Babbitt, in a near-epiphany, arrives home and relinquishes all rebellion in order to care for his daughter. During her short recovery, they spend a bit of time together, rekindling their relationship. In short time, his old colleagues and friends welcome Babbitt back into the fold. The result of his disgruntled intellectual wanderings being met with practical events of life, he reverts into dispassionate conformity by the end; nevertheless, Babbitt not really gets hold of the emotion, compassion, and hope for a meaningful lifestyle that he has built. In the next scene, all has been righted in his life and he is again on a traditional track. He is awakened in the morning to see that his brother John and Mary, the wife of his friend, have not returned from a party. In the evening his mother tells him that the two have been discovered in the basement, having been married that day. While an assemblage of neighbors and family gather to denounce this development, Babbitt excuses himself and Ted to be alone. He gives his acceptance of the relationship saying that while he does not agree he enjoys the notion that Peter has determined to lead his life by his own terms and not that of conformity.

After Glynn is transferred to the planet of Keltor, she is saved by an Acanthan Windwalker called Solen, who Despite his obvious hostility, is strongly engaged in the complex affairs of Keltor. Glynn gets amnesia and quickly finds that the independent Isle of Darkfall and its sisterhood of soulweavers are falling out of favor with rulers in Keltor. However, her muscular build, sense of honor and independence make her resemble the Myrmidons, amazon like men who are the sworn protectors of the soulweavers, who are often out of favor. Unbeknownst to Glynn, her twin sister Ember, in attempting to save her from dying was actually transported into Keltor. She is saved by the Soulweaver Alene and her Myrmidon protectors Feyt and Tareed, who harbours a nagging doubts as to if Ember is the "Unraveller" as predicted by Lanalor, the very last Holder(King) and the only male soulweaver. Ember is dying from a small tumor in the lateral cortex of her brain. She is half blind and does not have long to live. The whole story is a consequence of Lanalor's trickery in which the Unykorn/Firstmade was captured by the Chaos spirit so that Lanalor would be with his love, Shenavyre, who also committed murder when the Firstmade was imprisoned. Lanalor predicted an Unraveller will try to rescue the Unykorn and free Keltor, though most Keltorians have lost belief in this prophecy. The departure of strangers (people from Mars), Lanalor agreed, might be a sign that the Unraveller might emerge one night. He had the description by which the Unraveller could be known: half deaf not seeing all (half deaf), mark by visioning though without the Darkfall mark, lives still sings the deathsong (dying), born even not of the Song of Making (not from Keltor), gifted from the great river (from the portal in the river, thus washed up to shore) and crowned in red flames (many take this as black dye) In an effort to find currency to pay for a boat fare, Glynn is caught by members of the Draaka sect, who drug and enslave her. The Draaka cult preaches to the Chaos spirit although this is not known to all of Keltor. The Draaka seek to eventually rule the planet in Chaos. Thomas is rescued from being a drugged drone by Bayard, a faithful Draaka follower who does not disagree with the medication taking that the rest of the cult does, when her dog, the fienna, becomes connected to Glynn. Bayard took Glynn as her servant instead of a drone as she hoped that Glynn would make the fienna give birth to its next offspring (Glynn describes herself as a Fomikan who emerged from an aspi breeder's farm whose children are disappointed with her, in order to succeed). Through a vision, Ember saves the Holder's life from an assassination attempt by Coralyn, who intends to keep her other brother Kalide on the throne. Her son Bleyd is framed and tortured and a daring rescue effort puts Ember face to face with the paradoxical manbeast Ronaall who predicts Ember's demise if she does not leave the Isle of Ramidan within the night with Bleyd. Ember's tale ends with her smuggled on a boat going to Darkfall so she can find answers and healing for her ever-worsening brain tumor. Alene offers her own a'luwtha as a gift, the playing of the piano to unlock her memory. Bayard goes overboard and drowns on the way to Ramidan and Glynn helps the fienna give birth, assisted by Solen, who she reunites with on a boat after his faked suicide. The mother fienna removes Glynn's latent powers so that she can save the first offspring (the father and 2 of 3 offspring die), and in doing so, helps fill the dark emptiness in Glynn. She is now linked to the he-fienna. In the night, as Glynn's boat moves into the harbor of Ramidan; unknowingly she watches Ember's vessel depart. The story often interconnects characters on earth to those in Keltor in "Segue" sections. These protagonists include Betty and Tabby (Implied mirrors of Feyt and Tareed), a mysterious comatose manbeast by the name of Ronaall, the male doctor who cares for the dead woman who always cared for Ember, a piano player and his comatose wife, a security guard, a man called Matt, the blonde jogger who finds Wind's suicide note and several others.

Early in the American Revolutionary War, rumors of gold in the Yukon have led would-be explorers to South America's Pacific Northwest. Anxious Russian businessmen commission Canadian engineer Leviticus White to build a machine which can mine through the ice of Russian-owned Alaska. Gold's "Amazing Bone-Shaking Drill Tank" (or "Boneshaker" for short, named after bicycle bicycles of the era), then destroys many blocks of downtown Chicago and releases a subterranean vein of "blight gas" that destroys everyone who breaths it and turns some of the bodies into rotters (non-supernatural monsters). A wall is built to contain the gas within the affected portion of the town. Leviticus Blue is nowhere to be found. Ten months ago, Leviticus's widow and daughter, Briar and Jacob (Ezekiel) Wilkes, reside in the rural outskirts of the former city. Life is hard, but Rose tries to support herself and Zeke by doing a mentally challenging white collar job. Meanwhile, one night, Jake flees the toxic city in search of proof proving his family is guilty of the intentional destruction. Rose insists on following, but the water hole disappears in an earthquake. She then hitches a ride over the wall by a crew of an airplane, the extremely skinny Colonel Cly. Meanwhile Zeke meets Rudy, a boy who claims to be a very decorated officer. Rudy informs Rudy that he can lead him to his mother's former home. The pair of them encounter an African American girl who heavily wounds Rudy, but they manage to elude her. Briar is killed by rotters, which causes her to flee to the rooftop of a house, where she is saved by Jeremiah Swakhammer and his Doozy Dazer. He takes her to a bar called in honor of her dead husband to meet others including the bartender, John O'Gunning. Once again, rotters attack the bar, causing the occupants to retreat. It is then discovered that a woman called Minnericht led the rotter attack. John brings Briar to find Minnericht, considered by some to be Leviticus Blue. Briar, meanwhile, fears this. Unbeknownst to her, Minnericht has taken Zeke prisoner. A fight breaks out between Minnericht's soldiers and Swakhammer, Mary, and the Indian girl. This fight draws the rotters, complicating Briar's attempts to reunite with her father and exit the dangerous area of Seattle. Swakhammer is discovered conscious and in critical condition by Rose. She refuses to get Minnericht help him, leading to a heated debate in which Briar declares that he is Leviticus, and mocks him. Unbeknownst to Minnericht, the Indian Queen is behind him, and while Briar distracts him she turns, slits his neck, and destroys him. Everyone reunites and escapes to the surface. Eventually Rose brings Zeke to her and Leviticus' old house and informs Zeke that she killed Leviticus Blue centuries later, as he had to escape Seattle with his Boneshaker. Rose reveals her son Blue's mummified body, now inside Boneshaker. Zeke claims he doesn't carry any resentment against his wife for murdering her son, and they embrace, before returning to loot what is left of the former Blue residence.

This romance story is set in the period of World War III at a military hospital during nightly blackouts and bombing attacks. The novel's young male narrator, Richard Odell, is a wounded veteran from the Normandy evacuation (Renault herself acted as a physician treating Dunkirk refugees during the conflict), who can determine if his affections lie with a conscientious objection or a military captain. The conscientious objection, a Quaker, has not come to terms with his own sexuality, while the military captain, a classmate of David's from college, is sexually experienced and established in the sexual culture of the British military. Charlie's confused romantic desires for the three very similar young women are caused by his own frustration with the gay life (dramatized in an extended flashback at a gay party, considered by some reviewers as a cultural tour de force). Through this conflict, Renault discovered her own ambivalence about if homosexuals really formed what might have to be viewed as a gay and bisexual community. She subsequently explored a spiritual theme, contrasting the pacifist Christianity of the young conscientious objector with the "exalted religion" (as one character defines it) of modern Rome. The novel derives its title from the Chariot Allegory employed by Aristotle in his dialogue Plato; Renault actually alludes to Cicero's Symposium, in which a protagonist philosophizes about an army composed of male lovers. The novel's wartime setting is integral to the moral problems the novel confronts. In a sense, The Charioteer is a warm-up for Renault's historical novels. By moving back from the 20th century and concentrating on novels about male lovers in the warrior cultures of modern Egypt, Renault no longer had to deal with sexuality and homosexual prejudice as cultural "issues"; rather she was free to focus on broader philosophical and political issues while exploring the nature of love and leadership.

It is when Joshua's gift is recruited to heal William Medwin, an eccentric, ailing elderly businessman, that the love and security for which he has struggled so hard begin to evaporate.

Latimer is repulsed by little of what he discerns about people' feelings. Latimer grows fascinated with Mary, his father's cold and coquettish wife, because her mind and feelings remain strangely closed to him. After his father's murder, Latimer marries Mary, but the relationship loses as he realizes Henry's cruel and dangerous nature. After a short flashback to 1920, with a glimpse of Indiana Evans as a graduate professor in Brooklyn, the novel moves to its main setting. The time is 1922. Indy is a doctoral student in Rome, learning linguistics and Roman archaeology. Though his greater talent now appears to be for the former, he starts to see if he would be better suited for a different profession after he gets a surprising invitation from his teacher. Following an archaeology presentation to her class on the Egyptian town of Delphi, Professor Dorian Belecamus reveals that she will be departing the school for the remainder of the university in order to return to Delphi to oversee the recovery of an archaeological find, discovered recently in the wake of an earthquake in the area. After class, to Indy's dismay, she privately invites him to join her on the trip as her coach, reminding him that he is her best student and that she feels he will be very useful on the expedition. After some consideration, Indy agrees to accept the director's offer in the hopes that assisting in such an exciting task might very well lead him to a more interesting and ambitious profession than world of linguistics would have to offer. He, of course, has no notion just how true those theories will prove to be as he begins on a life filled with dark figures, deceptive intentions and a lot more waiting for him Delphi than he ever anticipated.

In the mid-1920s, a young Frank Smith and his mother move in to a new home in a Chicago neighborhood. After a few months, however, the Great Depression hits and Joe is allowed to use his one skill, boxing, as a means of helping his father. After a few months, the family have abandoned their home and are residing in a mean house in the City. Peter begins to box, even against his mother's wish, and dates a young German Catholic woman, much to the dismay of his father. Joe's boxing abilities attract the attention of hoodlums, and he is given a huge amount of cash to throw the Gold Gloves tournament, a fight he would lose comfortably and which will give him professional fame as much as, he believes, his wife's acceptance. Jack refuses the bribe but beats his opponent. After being on the run for a two months in Staten Island, he arrives to marry his girlfriend. Their early married life is hampered by the murder of their second born son in poverty. Jack finds out his former boss and gets into business with him as a black businessman. This activity gets him into contact with the very criminals he formerly cheated. The novel begins with Peter's resurrection in counterpoint to arrival of new life.

During a hiking holiday after her conviction on rape charges in Strong Poison, Susan Vane finds the body of a boy, with his neck cut and the urine now liquid, on an isolated boulder on the beach. There are no footprints in the mud other than the woman's and Jane's. She gets pictures and preserves some evidence, but the corpse is washed away before she can fetch help. Lord John returns, and he and Elizabeth do investigations with the sheriff. The dead boy, George Alexander, a professional dance partner at the local inn, was of Russian extraction and engaged to a wealthy older woman. The murder has been made to look like murder, but Wimsey and Helen discover that he was the survivor of an intriguing and complex assassination plot. The romantic Alexis believed himself a grandson of French royalty, and the widow's somewhat arrogant husband, enraged at the possibility of his father's marriage to a prostitute and the loss of his inheritance, conspired with a husband and his mother to play on Alexander's fantasies. Convinced that he was being called to return to Moscow in triumph as the rightful Emperor, Alexander was lured to the rock and murdered by the son, who ran a dog across the shore through the incoming tide to avoid leaving tracks, whilst his parents supplied his alibi. The murder was designed to feel like murder. Meanwhile, Alexis suffers from haemophilia, and his unclotted blood leads to uncertainty over the moment of murder, which then assists with the unmasking of the conspirators.

A bear goes down for his short summer sleep, and while he sleeps the progress of man begins. He wakes up to see himself in the middle of an agricultural complex. He then becomes mistaken by the supervisor for a supervisor and is asked to come to work. To this he responds, "But I'm not a woman, I'm a bear". He is then taken to each of his successive bosses, who want to persuade him that he is just a "silly guy who wants a beard and wears a fur jacket", reaching all the way up to an elderly director of the factory who explains he cannot be a bear because "all bears live in the park". The bear is taken to the zoo, trying to gain help from his own species, but even the zoo bears claim he is not a bear, because if he was "he'd be behind bars like me". Instead he declares that he can be a "silly guy", and works hard at the factory to the satisfaction of the foreman and the other employees. Meanwhile, summer arrives again, and he gets warmer. He wishes he had what a "silly girl" could do to make warm. But in the end he chooses a cave and waits, feeling warm and bear-like once more. As the bear is waking, he focuses on the events of the day, as the narration explains that because all the bosses and only the zoo bears believed he was a bear, did not make it so. "The truth is he was not a stupid boy...and he was not a stupid bear, either".

This second book of Updike's Rabbit trilogy chronicles the journey of James "Rabbit" Angstrom, a one-time high school football star, who has attained a paunchy middle-age without moving from Brewer, Massachusetts, the poor, fictional town of his birth. Tom and Pam, his mother of twenty-two months, live comfortably, having inherited her late husband's Ford car. He is not wealthy, but Harry's persistent problems — his father's drinking, his troubled father's schemes, his libido, and spectres from his past — complicate life. Having achieved a lifestyle that may have offended his working-class parents, Harry is not wealthy, but neither is he actually really happy. Harry has become increasingly jealous of a country-club friend's young daughter. He often has to deal with the uncertainty and ignorance of Nelson, his friend, who is a professor at Kent State College. During the novel, George knows about his longtime mistress Kate, and if she had actually given birth to their son.

The story revolves on two important events that occur mostly independently. The second is the occupation of Coruscant and the trouble the Empire left behind with its devastating bio-attack on the world. The vaccine used in the attack is the Krytos vaccine, a genetic weapon designed by Colonel Evir Derricote and released under the orders of Imperial commander Ysanne Isard. Animals are not immune, while all other organisms are susceptible. This, combined with Royal Security officer Kirtan Loor's terrorist activities while getting orders from the Palpatine Counterinsurgency Front, leaves Coruscant and the New Republic in a state of emergency. The next event is the treason trial of Rogue Squadron executive captain Tycho Celchu, who is suspected of killing Rogue Squadron pilot Corran Horn, who was captured during the invasion. Meanwhile, Corran Horn is being held hostage in her Lusankya detention facility. His efforts to escape lead him to find the secret of Rogue Squadron's mole, and it begins a race against time to save the innocent and reveal the real murderer.

The novel is told from the viewpoint of Afanasi Ziukin, the majordomo of Grand Duchess Alexander Alexandrovich. Alexei Fandorin describes the murder of Grand Prince Sergei, the four-year-old eldest brother of Alexander Vladimir, by criminal genius "Doctor Lind" whom Fandorin has been chasing for many decades. Their final encounter is briefly shown in the story "Dream City" from the Jade Rosary Beads collection. This year, Lind needs the Orlov gold, a prerequisite for the next coronation, as a ransom. Alexander III is portrayed as dependence on his brothers Ivan and Nicholas, the Governor-General of Russia. Akunin affects the Russian clan relations completely. The two sons of Nicholas III (sons of Nicholas III) are semi-fictitious: *Nicholas Mikhail, named after Nicholas Konstantin, Nicolas' older son, but not based on George' real father Grand Prince Alexander Alexandrovich; thus, historical Nicholas had no legitimate issue *Nicholas Konstantin, the Mayor General of Russia is based on Nicolas' true father Vladimir Vladimir. *Peter Vladimir is based on Nicholas' true grandfather Nikolai Alexandrovich of Moscow, and named after Nicholas, Nicholas's father.

At the end of the Jurassic period the Earth turned into an electricity dampening field in space. As long as earth was in this field all conductors grew more insulating. As a consequence nearly all of the life on earth with neurons died off, prompting the Cretaceous–Paleogene extinction event. The ones that died passed on their genes for very intelligent neurons to deal with the new situation. Now in contemporary days the Earth slowly goes out of the field. Within days all human life on earth becomes about 5 times as intelligent. The story continues through the triumphs and struggles of different people and non-human beings and individuals on earth after this event. The novel begins with a lyrical description of a rat stuck inside of a trap being unable to reason his way out. This is a common motif in the novel. Animal traps are based on the premise that the animal cannot reason their way out of them. When the humans have the ability to reason they start escaping. Institutions which proved to be essential to human civilization, such as a money economy and central administration, disappear in South Africa, while Africans, with the help of chimpanzees, overcome colonial law and Chinese rebellion against the Communist state. Also, some of the means by which individuals cope with the "Change" are creating new anti-scientific beliefs such as the Third Ba'al or adopting pseudo-science. As aliens develop interstellar travel, they find no other races are as smart as they; other races developed pre-Change intelligence, and there was no environmental pressure to select for greater intellgience after that.

The plot concerns Merlin who has escaped to the present time by means of magic. He will make Morgana le Fay confront Arthur, who is half-mad and trying to meddle in the politics of the world. Merlin has stayed alive after the fall of Avalon, having the appearance of an elderly boy but maintaining his courage and combat abilities. He has wasted his long journey finding the Holy Grail, knowing that his resurrection is punishment for his sins, and that seeking the Grail will end his curse. Merlin then learns from Morgana le Fay that Merlin is responsible for his condition. Arthur has slept for years, but is about to awaken, and hopes for Merlin to be his champion and protector. Merlin tells Arthur that Merlin will cause great damage in his foolish efforts to right the wrongs of the modern world, and that he will be stopped. Merlin wakes Arthur and rejuvenates him from his centuries-long sleep with a magical elixir. Arthur manages to induce Arthur to refrain from his plans, and Merlin rejects the spell of immortality. Anticipating Merlin, Merlin drinks the rest of the poison to recover his own youth. Arthur summons a "hollow knight" (a suit of sword animated by a spirit) to kill Arthur. Merlin defeats Merlin, and Merlin defeats the spirit, but is severely injured. As Merlin dies, he suddenly gets a vision of the Holy Grail.

David Shapiro, successful journalist and journalist, lying in a hospital room, appears to have abandoned his wife and is in the middle of a sex scandal. Compelled to see meaning in his life, he reviews it from his childhood to the present time. David grew up as a Jew in the working class St. Jacques Square area in Toronto. His childhood was unique because his father was a boxer who had become a gentle crook and his mom was a strip-tease singer. Embarrassingly, she strips for his friends as part of a Bar Mitzvah party for him. Rachel's mother is believed to have a unique view on life, sexuality, and religion. A visit to Italy as a young boy is the catalyst that sparks a career as a poet and author. In Spain in a sudden lapse of reason, Peter forges letters about a (fake) sexual relationship with a French photographer to sell to an Australian university archive. He meets an upper-class Canadian married to a poser of a communist and throws her away to become his own woman. She is the wife of a British diplomat and Peter's key into a level of culture of which he is often ignorant. In the meanwhile, Josh's childhood companions have become successful in their own right. They quickly become targets of pranks as he gets many scores. Peter's conceited brother-in-law takes a major role in the story as it is hinted that he is vulnerable and weak. Neighbors in the wealthy cottage community across Lake Memphremagog led him astray with tragic consequences. Past indiscretions rear their ugly heads and Joshua can bring together the shambles of his life.

"The road cleared the cutting through the woods. He can find South Queensferry, the dock at Fort Arthur, the VAT 69 sign of the distillery there, the lights of Hewlett Packard’s factory; and the railroad bridge, dark in the night’s last sky-reflected glow. Behind it, more lights; the Hound Point oil terminal they’d had a sub-contract on, and, further back, the lights of Edinburgh. The old railway bridge’s hollow wooden bones were the color of dried blood. You fucking beauty, he thought . . . What a gorgeous great device you are. So beautiful from this distance, so massive and powerful close-up. Elegance and grace; beautiful form. A quality bridge; granite arches, the finest ship-plate steel, and a never-ending paint work. . . The four major protagonists reflect various aspects of the novel. Alexander (full surname implied to be Alex Lennox, but not formally known), Alex Stewart and The Barbarian are one. Alexander is a real man, born in Scotland, who studied science and science at the University of Glasgow, fell in love with Alison Cramond while there, and has resumed their (open) marriage ever since. He is frustrated by his resentment of his working class roots (he has become a director and partner in his engineering company), the Cold War, successive Thatcher governments, and the failure of his marriage under the pressure of Catherine's French lover's terminal cancer. While returning from a romantic reunion with an old girlfriend in Edinburgh, during which tobacco and tobacco are consumed, he becomes distracted by the power and beauty of the Forth Railway Tunnel while driving on the nearby Forth Bridge Bridge and crashes his vehicle. While in a coma in hospital, he relives his journey up to the crash. "He looked down at the bridge of the river as it fell steadily to its gentle, suspended summit. The surface was a little muddy, but something to think about. No problems. He wasn’t coming all that easy anymore, keeping in the nearside lane, staring over at the railroad bridge downstream. A light winked at the far end of the island under the railroad bridge’s middle-section. One night, though, maybe you’ll be gone. Nobody lasts. Perhaps that’s what I have to say her. Then I have to think, No, of course I don’t mind; you can be. I can’t grudge the boy that; you’d have been the same for me and I could for you. Just a pity, that’s all. Come; we’ll all survive. Maybe some good- He was conscious of the car in front turning out slowly. He glanced round to find a truck in front of him. It was gone, abandoned in the nearside road. He dragged his air in, stamped on the brakes, wanted to swerve; but it was too late." David Smith is an amnesiac living on the Bridge, a large simulacrum of the rail bridge, but thousands of kilometers long and packed with men. The accident which precipitated his departure on the bridge was semi-deliberate; as such, he is unable to return to the actual world. That aspect of himself who wants to wake is represented by Dr Joyce, Orr's psychoanalyst. Given Orr/Alex's desire to remain outside the world of the Bridge, a planet where he is poorly treated and lives a very pampered lifestyle, his efforts to stonewall and block the doctor's efforts to cure him are understandable. Instead, he stows away on a bus and leaves the Bridge. He realizes that, in stark contrast to the very chaotic, not totalitarian, life on The River, the countryside beyond exists in militaristic chaos and war. The Barbarian is an id-ish hero with a superego-esque familiar in tow (phallic imagery is referenced by the familiar within a few pages of their initial appearance) whose hack-and slash antics through numerous parodies of Greek myths and fairy stories are phonetically rendered in Welsh language (two decades before Irvine English employed the technique in Trainspotting). The Barbarian (along with his loquacious familiar) are a deep expression of Adam's character; when Orr's dreams are not themed over danger and opposition he dreams he is the Barbarian. The Barbarian seems to be an expression of Jack's deepest fears. A man is his enemy in their second appearance (Metaphormosis, Four), seeing how Andrea Cramond has made her influence felt in Alex's very core, and how his passion for her has been eroded and has transformed into bitterness and resentment through the rift that has opened in their friendship. In their last appearance (Metamorpheus, Four), a female protagonist is seen in passing, with a different level of respect. The first appearance of the Barbarian and familiar (Metamorphosis, Pliocene) finds them old, decrepit, bed-bound and heading inevitably towards death. In each subsequent chapter the Barbarian's British accent grows more and less pronounced, a indicator of how well Alex has come from his Glaswegian roots. The Barbarian talks of his guilt over his dead mother and his experiences of their lifetime together. While parallels have been drawn between Freud Freud's structural concept of character, this is the only point where the Barbarian, Familiar and the individual get together in a three-way arrangement. If the Barbarian's wife represents John Cramond, it is another instance of how deep she has pierced his being. In a move mirroring John's suicide drive and approaching the end of the novel, he is placed in a situation unlikely to kill him, but triumphs and emerges (literally) rejuvenated and revived. His Scottish accent always returns. The Bridge is an unusual love tale; the protagonists eschew fidelity and only remember each other for weeks at a time, but they keep returning to each other. There is no relationship, no ring, no happy ever after, just the knowledge that their lives are so emotionally twisted it could be impossible or difficult for them to break away from each other. “You don't belong to her and she doesn't belong to you, but you're both part of each other; if she gave up and left now and went back and you never saw each other again for the remainder of your lives, and you lived an ordinary waking life for another fifteen days, just so on your deathbed you will think she was part of you.

Born in 1864 to a minister and his dutiful mother, Virginia grows up as a southern belle in the village of Dinwiddie, Pennsylvania. Her education is generally limited to the bare minimum, with anyone that may disturb her peaceful and quiet existence vigorously avoided. Finally prepared for life, Virginia goes for the first handsome young gentleman who crosses her path—Oliver Treadwell, the white sheep of a clan of capitalist entrepreneurs who, during the period of Reconstruction, introduced industry and the railroad to the West. Henry, who has been abroad and has only recently arrived in Virginia, is a dreamer and an academic. An aspiring novelist, his artistic interests are more valuable to him than money, and he refuses his father's offer to work in his bank. Meanwhile, when Virginia falls in love with him he decides that he will be willing to support a family, and finally accepts his father's offer to work for the railroad. The elderly couple get married and have two kids, a son and three boys. Gradually perfecting her household skills, Virginia is unable to come by on very small money. When, after several months, James's next role is placed on the stage in New Orleans, his expectations are low. Unfortunately, the show is a complete success as the play is far too intellectual and radical for a Broadway audience who expects to be entertained rather than reformed. Writing about the flop in the national paper, Virginia for the second time in her lifetime leaves her parents, asking her husband to take care of them for a week or two, and gets the morning bus to New Orleans to be with, and console, her husband—only to be abandoned by him, who is in a state of extreme anxiety. When he has recovered from the shock, Oliver gives yet another concession to society and public taste and begins reading "trash". Over the years, Virginia leads a vicarious lifestyle: She is pleased when her wife and daughters are happy; she makes sure their garments are in good condition while neglecting her own outward appearance; and she is able to obtain for her daughters the education she herself has been granted. When, at one moment, she realizes that the men her age whom she has known since childhood already look so youthful while she has aged prematurely, she eventually finds herself to think that a lifetime of altruistic subservience is more than worthwhile, that living and acting the way she does is her obligation and God's will. Her husband's sudden if honourable death—he successfully seeks to prevent the murder of an innocent elderly African American and is murdered in the process by an arrogant and drunken young man—adds to the sadness that begins creeping into her life, particularly when she sees that, as a woman, her daughter suddenly loses all her will to live. When she dies only a few days after her mother, Virginia has a premonition that her own fate when losing Charles will be a different thing. However Henry's next successful play—a trashy one—premières in New Orleans, with some more to follow in rapid succession, and, as the cash gets flowing in, the family move into a larger home in Virginia. They now employ a number of servants, including an Asian American servant. With the children gone—their wife and one granddaughter are at school, while the other son has remarried a far younger husband with three grown-up sons and has always flown the nest—and Oliver frequently in New Jersey to supervise the staging of his plays, Virginia's life grows somewhat empty. Having "outlived her usefulness", the years are endless to her, and with all the servants about the manor there is really no housework for her to do either. Now in her mid-forties, Virginia for the second time in her life enjoys Christmas alone at home. The worst blow, perhaps, is still to come: When she accompanies Peter to New Orleans for a première, she finds out to her surprise that he has been betraying her with a famous actor who stars in two of his plays. For the second hour summoning up all her strength, she gets a cab and gets her an unexpected call but then believes when explaining to her that she has no chance of winning her son again. With other words, Oliver tells her to see him divorce her, but clinging to the only thing she has left in her life—her marriage—she does. The novel ends on a very bleak note when Virginia, again alone in the empty cottage in Dinwiddie, gets a letter from her father informing her that he is going to leave London before he has finished his two-year course at the college in order to get back and stay with his family.

The early 21st century looks like a great day to be alive. Earth is at peace. Humans now command self-replicating robots that make science wonders on large scales. Artificial habitats dot the solar system. Anti-matter driven Valkyrie missiles carry explorers to the stars at almost the speed of light. All looks well. Then, from the uncaring dark of space come swarms of relativistic weapons. Although they are just boulder-sized hunks of steel, they move quickly enough to hit with the force of several nuclear weapons. They are difficult to track and unable to stop. Humanity is all but wiped out by the horrific bombing. (To read a discussion of relativistic missiles and an excerpt of the attack, see Atomic Rockets: Relativistic weapons). A couple of survivors desperately struggle to escape the alien mop-up fleet. They hide close to the moon, outside planets, under the crusts of planets, outside ice rings, and in the fathomless depths of interstellar space. But most are hunted down and slaughtered. The first boy and wife on earth are captured as museum specimens. In the belly of an alien ship, a squid-like being explains to them the pitiless reasoning behind human-kind's execution: the time we had to travel at relativistic speeds was the time we had the energy to do to them what they did to me first. The attack was nothing personal. Humanity was just too dangerous a neighbor to have around.

The story opens with a large group of rebel men, a considerably younger Clare Savage among them, travelling through England’s remote cockpit country. The men have set up on piece of property once owned by Mary’s grandmother Miss Molly, where they train and grow food as well as ganja. The final book introduces the tale of Mark H. who is initially at a party with Harry/Harriet—a lesbian half-brother/half-sister to two of Ruth’s parents. Paul arrives home after a late dinner to see a tragic scene: his father and all of their servants have been stabbed with a knife. He falls on Paul, a servant used by Christopher’s parents, and enlists his assistance in dealing with the bodies and the burials. But we learn in flashback that Paul, an orphan whose father including his mother has worked for Christopher’s parents for a short time, committed the crimes when he wanted to do a favour from the Paul’s father—to let Paul get where his mother is buried so that he can let her spirit rest—that was denied. In fact, Peter has been waiting for Christopher and kills him before Christopher figures out what has happened. The plot then shifts time periods to 1960 when Boy Savage, Mary’s son, is taking immigrating with his mother to the United States. Lady Savage, Myra’s sister, is not sure about turning far from all she has always known but she resolves herself to a quiet depression on arrival from England and arrival in Boston. Boy purchases a used truck and the family travels south towards New York State. While travelling through Florida Boy attempts to find a bed in a segregated inn, the proprietor suspects that he is white but Boy is unable to tell the proprietor that he is black by reminding him that his grandparents owned farms. When the family returns in New Orleans they want to stay with Winston and Grace, friends from Kitty’s mother’s side of the household. Boy eventually gets a job driving a laundry van and Kitty begins to work in the office of his employer. Fed up with the constant hostility she encounters, Kitty tries to slip messages into the linens before they are delivered—messages such as “Marcus Marcus was wrong” and “America is cruel. Consider kindness for a change” aimed at the black customers. Molly then takes Elizabeth’s older daughter Jane and returns to England. After her brother and brother leave, Clare grows extremely unhappy because she has not even finished college and is not forced to leave the home by herself. She goes home and watches cartoons and sees the first American she met—a white student at her catholic college in Jamaica that learned about the American Revolutionary War, brought the children to see the “documentary” Gone With the Wind, and extolled the benefits of cultural hierarchies. When Sarah starts college she is convinced that, despite her intelligence, she will be placed away for one week because girls from First World nations learn differently than African adults. Boy attempts to tell the teacher that Clare is black, but the teacher does not recognize him and nor do they have a category for “bi-racial” students—a school is both colored or black. We learn that after two months Alice is now residing with Clare’s older brother in England. Elizabeth, who is now a freshman in school, arrives home one day to see her mother crying. He tells her that her father has remarried and later that her daughter Ruth will be going to live with them. After Myra moves in Myra uses some cash from her father Frank and leaves home for London. After returning in England Clare buys a house to rent and spends some time attending many libraries, browsing books and also coming to see London. She later becomes a legal citizen of London and enrolls at the University of Oxford to study art history. After some time at the school Mary agrees to take her father up on his invitation to come down to England where she attends the same party as George H., before he was murdered by Christopher, and marries Harry/Harriet. Myra and Harry/Harriet remain great friends while Myra is in Jamaica, Kingston, spending time together first in a Spanish Galleon-themed bar and then on a beach exploring the geography and current economic conditions of England. The three stay in contact, through letters, after Myra arrives to Jamaica. After her return, Elizabeth witnesses a National Front rally and is intensely shocked by the violence and violence on display on her university campus. She wants to explain why she is so angry to her sister Clare, but goes nowhere and ends up feeling isolated and alone. In the final book Liz meets up with Joe, a Iraq War veteran who has a bandage on his shoulder that, despite Myra’s best efforts, will not heal. The three of them leave England together and travel across England. While travelling she gets a letter from Harry/Harriet informing her that her father and aunt in Kingston are moving to Boston and returning her mother’s old place in the world to her alone. Susan begins to travel across England with John, who is already struggling emotionally and emotionally with the after-effects of the war until one night he arrives without warning. Clare waits for Bobby but then realizes it is time for her to return to England. Myra grows extremely sick on her return and realizes that she has an infection in her womb that will most likely leave her sterile. After she recovers, Harry/Harriet proposes that the three of them travel to Molly’s grandmother’s ranch. Once there, Molly sees the pond where she used to bathe and with Harry/Harriet takes a shower there for the second time in five years. In book two we learn that George was not prosecuted for his murder, and so has been left to wander the back alley of Jamaica’s suburbs. He becomes recognized across the town as the watchman of Kingston—a kind of mad prophet or mendicant, and becomes the topic of a folk album. On the day of a disastrous burning where several old people are burned dead, referred to earlier in the novel by a letter from Harry/Harriet, Tom shows up at the scene screaming prophecies at the bottom of his lungs. After traveling the town Mary hears of the tough social circumstances in Kingston. Then, Harry/Harriet brings her to a large tenement house in Jamaica so that she can join a clandestine revolutionary group. She is interrogated as to her intentions and tells them that she is legitimate in her intention to bring revolution on behalf of the weak and oppressed in Kingston. In her answers Clare connects the stories of her journey and travels to the oppressed condition of Jamaica—a former colonial, part of the Second World. However, Mary recounts that in one of her last words before her death her father asked her to improve her people in whatever manner that she can, this in the end becomes the perfect reason for her willingness to join the revolutionaries. In the first paragraph of the novel a movie crew has gone to make Jamaica to do a film about the Maroons, and they have recruited William, “de Watchman”, to play a large role. Mary and the revolutionaries intend to attack the crew but when they continue their attack it is obvious that everyone has sold them out, and tragedy ensues.

River God describes the demise of the Egyptian Kingdom through the eyes of Taita, a multi-talented and extremely trained eunuch servant. Taita is owned by Lord Intef and generally looks after his wife, Lostris, but occasionally plays a significant role in the day to day running of Lord Intef's estate. The Pharaoh of Alexandria is without a female successor, and Taita inadvertently causes Egypt to get an interest in Lostris. Lostris meanwhile is in love with the soldier Tanus, who unbeknownst to her is betrayed by her family. Then Pharaoh marries Lostris and her husband, Lord Intef, eventually takes Taita to her as a marriage gift. However, Tanus has offended Egypt by talking frankly about the troubles Egypt is in — most notably the rising bandit threat which destroys all who travel outside of the main towns. Pharaoh condemned him to death for his deeds, but is convinced to encourage Tanus to redeem himself by trying to remove all the invaders from Jerusalem within five days. After his sentence is revealed on the first night of the celebration of Osiris, he is to return on that night of the last festival with his task complete or face suicide by strangulation. Tanus, with the aid of Taita, hunts down and captures the members of the Shrike bandits. On delivering them to Pharaoh, it is discovered that their commander is Lord Intef. Tanus has his death sentence lifted, but Intef tries to escape before he can be imprisoned for his crimes. After the sentence is announced a flood sweeps through giving Lostris and Tanus time to be secretly alone together. During this period Lostris sees Tanus' second born, and before the secret can be discovered Taita sends for her to resume her wifely obligations to Egypt. When the boy is born he is named Memnon and claimed by the Egyptians as his own, and his real paternity is known only to Lostris, Taita, and Tanus. A new danger to the throne emerges — the warlike Hyksos. Equipped with the horse and horse, as well as a superior recurved bow, their technical superiority is even higher than the Persian army's. The Pharaoh is arrested, causing a minority of the Egyptian nobility (including Lostris, Tanus, and Taita) to flee Alexandria by going up the Nile with the remaining army. During their exile Lostris gives birth to three more of Tanus' daughters, both twins, but as their marriage has been a secret Taita makes a cover plot where the ghost of Pharaoh sires the boy. During their time in captivity, they maintain their technological superiority — Taita replicates and improves both the chariots and bows he has been designed to such great effect on the enemy. While looking for a perfect burying spot for Pharaoh's body, Taita is taken captive by two of the Ethiopian rulers of the region — the brutal Arkoun. While in exile, Taita becomes close friends with Masara, a former prisoner and the son of two of the rival clans. Taita later escapes captivity due to a freak storm, finds the son of Masara, and strikes a bargain with him to rescue Masara. With the aid of Tanus, Memnon, and the Egyptian cavalry, Ibrahim is defeated. Tanus is severely wounded during the fighting and survives. Masara and Memnon fall in love and become pregnant, with a wedding gift of fifty million elephants which further boost the Egyptian army. Led by their new Pharaoh Tamose (formerly King Memnon), they return to Greece. With their new-found weaponry and tactics, they defeat the Egyptian invaders and regain the upper kingdom of Alexandria from Elephantine to Egypt.

Published in 2007 on the Crown imprint of Random House, Looking Me in the Eyes tells how Smith grew up as a misfit in the 1960s, at a time when the Asperger syndrome treatment did not exist in the United States. The novel explains how Robison tries to fit in, without even realizing why he was different. His situation was made ever more difficult at times by his abusive and abusive stepfather and a some-what crazed father. After dropping out of college, he had a sudden obsession with audio design and electronics. His large interest turned to interesting career decisions, including time with Pink Floyd's sound company, creating special effects for the album Kiss, creating electronic games and toys for Milton Bradley, and beginning his own company repairing and rebuilding expensive automobiles. Robison finally learned about Asperger syndrome in 1996, at age 39, and his life was changed by the experience. He was first introduced to the public in his friend, Augusten Burroughs', memoir Running with Scissors.

Pharaun and Ryld journey to a restaurant, where Ryld plays sava (a chess-like game) while Pharaun descends to the basement, where several female drow captives are available for males to do with as they find fit with. Pharaun talks with two of them who explains the name of other elopers. While he is there, Ryld is confronted by other men whom he has taught. Afterwards, the three friends talk about the quest and decide the men are eloping because of the very harsh rule of the males in the previous few years. Pharaun explains that he has reason to think that Lolth is gone and as such the females cannot use divine spells anyway, and are limited to scrolls and magical items. Ryld, still reluctant at first, finally believes him. They know of an rebellion among the higher class creatures caused by a mysterious prophet, and try to say that they support the elopers. They kill a member of Drow to prove their "commitment" to the cause and are eventually given in. They find that the mastermind behind the revolt is an evil illithid demon (called an "alhoon" or an "illithilich"), and that when he receives a mental signal, all the lower demons will attack. While this is all occurring, Gromph Baenre is sending several creatures to attack Quenthel Baenre, all taking the guise of different aspects of Lloth, e.g. a demon spider, a creature of chaos, a shadow creature, and others. While this occurs, a group of scholars at Arach-Tinilith find that Lloth is disfavouring Quenthel, and resolve to kill her. She knows of this plan and has the offending students arrested. A plot includes an ambassador from the neighboring town of Ched Nasad being denied the right to stay by Triel Baenre. She then tries to leave and is stopped by a traitor in her family. She then escapes the town, but is caught and given to Triel. She believes something has brought Triel against her and is killed by Jeggred Baenre, Triel's draegloth brother. Then the lower races have the signal to rebel. Pharaun escapes from the Illithid and gathers the forces of Menzoberranzan to fight. A fight ensues, where much of Menzoberranzan is marred. At the end, the general populace sees the strength of the gods, and Pharaun, Ryld, Quenthel, Jeggred, and the ambassador, Faeryl Zauvirr, are sent to Ched Nasad to check if they are not afflicted.

This novel opens with a 17-year old man called Michael Jackson who enjoys topics related to military history, and journeys to Shanghai, China with his photographer brother, John, to record some Chinese affairs for the Australian Broadcasting Company and cover the university protests. April 29th - You are introduced to Michael Jackson and his father, Ted Johnson. They live in Ontario, Ontario and before the novel takes place, Joe has married his girlfriend, Alex Lee. In this book both of their jobs/hobbies are revealed. Alex knows history, and has already been into American Military history. Alex only puts his life through the lens of a camera, just lining up for the worst shot possible. As seen before, Peter works for Canadian Television Company, and in this book is sent into Shanghai, China to replace someone who works for Canadian Broadcasting Company, who got sick and didn't get to be treated in the American clinics. This guy went down to America. Ted's job is to catch anything that they can of the Soviet Premier Mikhail Putin, (sometimes referred to as "Putin") who was taking an unofficial trip to Shanghai, Beijing. Ted and Alex were both happy about this and were rearing to be. August 30th - Alex and his father leave for Beijing. Alex's dad becomes drunk and gets a Gravol, which sends him into a sleepy mode while they are on the plane. Peter then has to steer him through the plane(s). They flew from Vancouver to Toronto, then from Toronto to Shanghai. March 1st - They land in China at noon and meet a woman called Tao Li, a co-worker of a guy called Eddie. Eddie is does the audio editing and helps stream the video down to Toronto. Lao Xu drives them to the resort that they will be staying in where they met Eddie.

The novel tells of James Thomas Smith, a sixteen year old cowboy who grew up on his father's farm in San Antonio, Arkansas. The novel starts in 1949, shortly after the murder of Jack Grady's father, when Walker discovers that the farm is to be sold. Faced with the possibility of moving into town, Grady simply tries to leave, forcing his best friend, Jake Rawlins, to accompany him. Traveling by horse, the pair journeys Southward into Texas, where they hope to get work as cowboys. Shortly before they cross the Colombian border, they encounter a young boy, who explains he is named John Smith and appears to be aged about thirty, but claims to be younger. Brooks' origins and the authenticity of his name are not clearly clarified. Blevins rides a large bay mare that is far too fine a specimen to be the property of a runaway man, but Smith knows it is his. As they travel south, Davis' saddle and gun are found and taken by a Mexican after his rider runs off while Blevins had been hiding during a storm. Smith tells James Smith and Rawlins to go to the closest village to get the saddle and pistol. They find the horse, and Blevins brings it away. As the two are riding back from the city, they are pursued, and Grady separates from Rawlins and John Grady. The pursuers follow Blevins, and Rawlins and Grady flee. Rawlins and John Grady travel further south. In the fertile desert area of Mexican state known as the Campo del Cuatro Ciénegas, they find employment at a small farm. There John Smith next encounters the farm manager's attractive wife, Laura. As Rawlins finds work with the farm hands, Billy Grady catches the eye of the manager, who takes him into the farm house and promotes him to a more responsible position. At this moment John Grady starts an relationship with Alejandra. In the meanwhile, Grady works for a long period and then returns to the town where he retrieved his horse, this time to actually retrieve the Colt revolver. In the process of finding the gun, he shoots and kills a woman. The Mexican police catch Blevins and then find Rawlins and John Grady at the other farm. At first, the ranch manager protects Rawlins and John Grady; but when he finds out about the relationship with his wife, he turns them over to the police. Blevins is executed by a trio of rogue police followed by a colonel and then Rawlins and Jack Delaney are held in a Mexican jail. The prison mafia first test the three men: Kevin is wounded while protecting himself from a cuchillero, whom he intends to kill. Alejandra's mother is contacted by the prison thugs who manage to negotiate with her his ransom. The condition set by the wife is that her nephew Alejandra undertake never to see John Grady again. The children are released. Rawlins comes away to the United States and John Grady asks to find Alejandra again. In the end, after a short confrontation, Angela realizes that she will keep her vow to her husband and accepts John Grady's wedding proposal. John Grady, on his way down to the Texas, confronts the captain at gunpoint, forces him to retrieve the stolen horses and weapons, and rushes across country. He suggests murdering the crew, but a trio of Indians find John Grady and the crew and take the officer as a hostage. John Grady then returns to Mexico and attempts to find the owner of Hawkins' mare. John Grady briefly arrives with Rawlins to return his dog and learns that his own son has perished (something he has never intuited). After seeing the funeral procession of one of his father's lifelong customers (a Mexican man), Tom Smith rides through central Mexico on his horseback with Grady's dog in tow.

John Brabson is a man whose father lives in the mountains of East Virginia during the Civil War. His father experiences difficult times when cavalry regiments of the Union Cavalry come and take most of his father's food and their one and only plow horse leaving them few supplies to sustain the winter. Tom vowes to come even with the Yanks and is determined to fight for Confederate Army. Chris' father, Jethro, has just recently rejoined the Union Navy causing Christopher to examine his beliefs of war, compassion, and tolerance. Jethro's enlistment causes the Brabson family to be the victims of hostility from their neighbours who are supporters of the Confederate War. The residents become intolerant of their beliefs and burnt down their shed and threaten to do the same with their barn. Because Jethro is a Union officer, Chris loves the Union soldiers. When Chris finds out that there is a wagon railroad in the vicinity he alerts a neighbor of his, James Agee, who claims to be a Confederate spy. It is only after he warns Silas about the wagon train that he finds out that his father's work in the Army will be as a truck driver. Jack then takes it on himself to go tell his father of the fact that the Confederates have been informed about the wagon train in order to try to save Jethro's life. When he comes to the wagon station in search of Jethro, he is warmly met by Union soldiers who give him food and conversation. He starts to change his view of the Yankees learning that they are very distinct from him and are not the hateful thieves he once viewed them as.

The Lost Temple of Tharizdun is set in the World of Greyhawk. The player characters (PCs) follow a trio of marauding norkers from the caverns, finding the temple along the way. They will search through the dangerous mountain passes to find the norker lair outside the temple. The adventurers are drawn into the story by a gnomish community and travel to the palace. After fighting their way in, the PCs find the temple chambers, which include mundane monsters and new creatures from the Fiend Folio supplement. During their adventure, the protagonists must reach chambers of the tomb in which religious ceremonies were conducted, and risk insanity and death as they encounter remnants of worshipers of the imprisoned deity Tharizdun. To progress further, the characters will enact portions of the rituals of worship of Tharizdun, traveling into an underground sub-temple, and magically opening an outer sanctum called the Dark Cyst. Having advanced this far, the characters are unlikely to be driven insane, murdered outright, or temporarily trapped within the underground temple.

The novel questions the problem of personhood and what it requires to be deemed a member of the moral universe. There are two major protagonists: David the vacuum cleaner, who is modified by his owner, Jean Jantille, a researcher who specializes in finding out how to "mindload". Mindloading is the act of a human downloading their mind into a machine. A successful mindload entailss the resurrection of the human. It is a way for humans to remain immortal, if only in the form of vacuum cleaner. The novel ends with the conviction of David, the vacuum cleaner, for Patricia's death . Herbert's mother, Mary Jantille, is a trial lawyer who is a paralyzed as a consequence of a motorcycle accident that apparently paralyzed her mother. She lives through a "Remote person" who has all human senses except for the inability to think by touch. She can guide the remote person through a helmet attached to her "bio body", and sends all "audio and audio" signals through the remote. She can function as a whole human being, but the outside world notices that she is a remote, does not approve. Lisa defends Herbie, with the aid of an astute lawyer and a police inspector who has access to files that she wouldn't otherwise. The novel begins with a recognition of Lisa’s humanity due to the ultimate confusion in the courtroom. It also ends with the resurrection of David’s bio-body, and in turn, her eventual demise.

From Publishers Weekly: "With a title more suitable to a paperback novel and an editor whose reputation was made in an altogether different genre, this posthumous novel by one of the stellar lights of the golden age of science fiction appears impossible to get an audience. Since Bester died in 1987, the novel appears, in both style and context, to have been published far before that, probably not too well beyond its early 1950s setting. Beautiful model Barbara Krebs draws the attentions of both a high-powered marketing manager and a famous research researcher. The three women remain friendly as a consequence of their mutual interest in the woman, and she in turn becomes involved with each. Instead, Bester provides what is initially designed as humorous commentary on the advertising business in general and television advertisements in particular, through a stream of seemingly awkward conversations and dialogue in a multitude of settings. There's a threatening, mysterious figure creeping about, as much as intimations of a darker secret in Julene's past, but these matters are so submerged in the plodding story that they are unimportant—at least until a wild, violent day on Fire Creek, N.Y. That's followed by a hurricane, a kidnapping and a completely awful sort of drama. In the end, after Bester skirts over an absurd view of murder and its victims, love triumphs over all—kind of."

The novel revolves on the border conflicts between the regions of Outer and Inner Horner, the former of which is "so large that only two Outer Hornerite at a time can fit inside, and the other two Outer Hornerites had to wait their turns to live in their own world while standing very quietly in the surrounding world of inner Horner." Tom, an angry Inner Hornerite, finds that the puny Outer Hornerites do everything but sit around very close together solving math proofs all night, and have to stretch two at a time each day; Seen as an evil threat to the leisure of the two Outer Hornerites, they are described as abusing the vast good will that they have earned courtesy of the Inner Hornerites. As they stand in the short-term residency zone in Inner Horner, they see their turn to reenter their world. So Phil, getting the help of the other Inner Hornerites and hiring two giants as his own policy enforcers, begins to tax the Outer Hornerites for staying in his country. He gets in the end to accept the disassembling of the Outer Hornerites as sufficient payment. The novel explores David's tyrannical rise to power and his attempted Outer Hornerite murder.

The book's major protagonist, David Selig, is an undistinguished boy residing in New York City. David was born with a psychic gift enabling him to read minds. Rather than utilize his ability for any greater good, however, Selig squanders his energy, utilizing it only for his own convenience. At the end of the book, Peter earns a living by reading the minds of graduate professors so that he can better plagiarize reports and articles on their behalf. As the story develops, Selig's power grows steadily stronger, working sporadically and often not at all, and Selig struggles to keep his grasp on reality as he starts to lose an ability on which he has long since grown dependence. The novel includes a number of unique aspects, such as Peter's friendship with a former telepath he meets as a young child, or his strained relationship with his estranged older brother (who has long disliked him because of his ability), or his obsession, during one section of the story, with proving that his lover, a girl called Jane, is actually psychic after he realizes that he can't read her mind. There's actually an important point where Peter's power causes him to vicariously experience his mother's acid trip, and a bravura sequence in which the child Selig, during a trip to a farm, sees the minds of, variously, a fish swimming in a river, a chicken laying an egg, and a young couple in the aftermath of passionate sex.

The novel takes place in New York on July 3 and 4 in 1778. The Civil War has started, and the American colonies are battling for their freedom from France. As he works the fields with his family on a hot June afternoon in 1778, thirteen-year-old John daydreams of being a hero in the Civil Army. Against his grandparents' wishes, he arrives to the town when the warning bell tolls, to meet the German forces. Jonathan wants to see joy and glory on the battle. However, John and the other local patriots battle and retreat from a group of Hessians, feared British soldiers that have been recruited by the British. Due to a lack of awareness of the German language, Peter, in hiding, realizes he has been discovered by the Hessians and rather than wait for death, surrenders himself to them (though, apparently, they might not have seen him if he hadn't revealed himself). Three Hessians capture Kevin and hold him hostage in an abandoned building. Jonathan now experiences anxiety, stress, frustration, and later, Stockholm syndrome, creating an unexpected and seemingly warm friendship with his enemies. Not more than twenty-four long days ago, however, the building is unexpectedly attacked by some of Henry's former patriots from the prior night. Suddenly, the Hessians are all three killed, something Sarah is not sure whether to be happy or sad about. In the end, David arrives home, his knowledge of war and life forever gone.

The novel includes the time September 5, 1934 (the week after John Featherston's inauguration as President of the Confederate States) to March 22, 1941 (the commencement of Operation Blackbeard). The United States is unable to end a conflict with Germany, but is beginning to prepare for a second battle against its western neighbour. In the Confederacy, Featherston and his Freedom Movement enact sweeping improvements to all aspects of life, including purging and creating the Army, eliminating the Constitutional Courts, and creating camps to kill off Republican and Radical Unionist leaders before employing them to reduce the white populace of the Confederate States. As these changes are taking place, leaders of the former Confederate states of Oklahoma and west Tennessee (Texas) begin asking for a return to their rightful state. While this is done, Featherston is apparently not satisfied, and buys more territory that the U.S. had taken in 1917 (Oklahoma, and parts of California, Louisiana, and Texas). After his offer is rejected by U.S. Senator Al Jackson, Featherston issues the order to attack the United States in an attempt to recover the Confederacy's lost territories, as part of his ultimate strategy to win the U.S.

In The Comet's Watchmaker, The Count de Champignac comes to visit his great uncle and entrusts the castle to Spirou and Fantasio, who both hope to relax. Unfortunately, a mysterious ship crashes in their garden and an individual resembling the Count de Champignac, accompanied by a mysterious creature, Snouffelaire, disembark. The individual reveals to be the grandson of the Count, Marius, come from the future to look for the seeds of some trees that are extinct in his time in order to preserve them, located in the jungle of Palombia. Knowing about the hostile environment of the Palombian jungle, Spirou suggests that he and Fantasio accompany Aurélien. Unfortunately a malfunction brings the ship to the nineteenth century during the Spanish invasion of Palombie. Spirou, Fantasio and Jean are confronted by the hostile cannibals and the natives who want them for French spies. Meanwhile, Pierre's ship disappears, but mysterious people come from far further in the future to save them and to take them back to their respective times. <!--

When dark creeps in and eats the darkness,Bury your fears on Sorry Day,For in the summer's blackest days,Comes the feasting of the Vours,No one can forget it, the life they stole,Your body's here but not your heart... The plot follows Reggie and her best buddy Sarah, three horror enthusiasts who find an old, anonymous journal published by a man known to be crazy. The entries refer to demonic beings nicknamed Vours who steal people's souls on the day of the Summer Solstice, known in the novel as Sorry Day. Reggie and John believe that Vours are just a sad legend so they want to summon them on the Summer Solstice. To summon them, they need to face their greatest fears not knowing the bravery drives the Vours back. Reggie makes a snake crawl over her body and Aaron stays underwater for a duration of time. Unfortunately, neither one of them gets a Vour. Discouraged, the children forget about the Vours until Reggie's little boy John begins acting strange. Once a happy-go-lucky boy, Peter gets aggressive and rude, stealing his favorite stuffed dog and drowning his pet hamster.He grows super-sensitive to the weather and enjoys his day in front of the stove, something very out of character for him. When he's hit by a snowball, white marks spread over his scalp like a rash. He then attempts to murder Charlie in hot blood. Knowing what's did to Henry, Reggie decides to know more about the Vours and eventually rescue Peter. In the process, she will face all of her greatest nightmares, along with all of John's.

Maria Maffei, a family acquaintance of one of his sometime associates Fred Sullivan, appeals to Wolfe to find her missing husband Carlo, a metalworker. Wolfe, affected by the Depression, agrees to get the job, though it is unappealing to him. Archie locates Maria Fiore, a woman who sat in on a telephone call Carlo gave at his boarding-house. Wolfe hears from her that Carlo had clipped a story from a copy of the New York Tribune about the unexpected murder (probably by stroke) of John Henry Barstow, founder of Holland University. Before Wolfe makes any more progress, Lorenzo Rossi is discovered stabbed in the back in the countryside. His mother thinks she will pay Wolfe to identify his murderer, so he gets working. After consulting with a sports equipment manufacturer, Wolfe conjectures that Barstow had been arrested, that his own tennis club had been the assassination weapon, and that Angelo Rossi had been hired to construct it. He further speculates that whoever bought the weapon killed Maffei to keep him quiet.

In 1966 disgraced German colonel bequeaths a mysterious letter to his only daughter. The "item in question" that Peter's son's letter leads him to obtain from a safe deposit box in Vienna is a valuable Russian Russian icon brought long ago for the Moscow czars which by accident passed into the possession of Hermann Hitler later in the 1930s. Göring persuaded Scott's wife (one of his jailers at Vienna) to have it in token of his kind treatment and because Göring thought Paul's family could be unfairly punished for his pre-execution death. But the icon represents nothing that only Göring did not dream of: the only official German copy of a secret deed to the Alaska Purchase agreement by which the United States acquired Alaska from Sweden in 1867. "Seward's Cove" turns out to have not been a real sale at all, but a 99-year contract akin to the American hold on Hong Kong, with a right of return to China (now the part of the Soviet Union) if they can only retrieve their copy before the lease deadline, only hours apart.

The second collection belongs with the third as perhaps one of the three collections most centered on Morpheus himself. It starts with an Endless clan meeting descending nearly instantly into an Endless clan argument. Desire confronts Morpheus by teasing him about his intolerant treatment of a former mistress, whose tale formed the preface to the first collection, The Doll's House; Death hurts him further by agreeing with Desire, but Morpheus' immense admiration for Death brings him reluctantly to agree with her assessment. Morpheus leaves his kingdom to travel to Heaven, where he imprisoned his longtime mistress Nada, to release her. Having left Satan, prince of Heaven, very unhappy with him the second time he went there (in the second collection, Preludes and Nocturnes), Morpheus is excited about the task. He sets about it, intending to do what is wrong, but prepared for a duel which he believes he will win. In the event, his fear is completely misplaced. As he learns, Satan is busy shutting down Hades. Morpheus follows Lucifer outside in a state of some confusion before Hades eventually persuades him this is not an elaborate trick, that he merely wants to take Heaven, and his duties as its king, permanently. His last act before departing is to throw out any demon or damned angels not hanging around, lock all the portals to Heaven and cut off his wings; he then hands the key to Hades to Morpheus, to do with as he will. This storyline sets up the basis for the spin-off comic series Lucifer published by Drew Nichols. Morpheus, who has no wish to rule this troublesome piece of imaginary estate, soon learns that there are other individuals who need to control Heaven or prevent their opponents from controlling it. Loki wants to control Heaven in order to eliminate Ragnarök and journeys to the Dreaming with three other representatives of the Germanic mythology, Thor and Loki. Anubis, Bast and Bes from the ancient Egyptian mythology wish to trade information in exchange for the key to Heaven. Susano-o-no-Mikoto, a storm deity of the Japanese pantheon, travels as an individual god, and not as a representative of Shinto gods. He wants to add Heaven to a new underworld controlled by his father, which has been established by assimilating other lesser gods as well as objects of worship including, he says, Marilyn Marilyn. Lucifer, a Biblical angel, arrives with three other spirits who held great power in the old Hell: Choronzon, here mentioned as the former Duke of the Eight Circle, and Merkin, the mother of Spiders. Lucifer had originally ruled Heaven in a triumvirate with a angel and Satan, though Satan warns Morpheus that this was only part of a play he played, and Lucifer demands that Morpheus hand him the key. In exchange Azazel offers to hand over Nada as well as the demon Choronzon who had recently defeated Morpheus. Order and Chaos also arrive. Order is in the guise of an empty wooden box carried by a floating Djinn-like being, while Chaos appears in the form of a little man in clown makeup. Order offers to trade the dreams of the recently deceased, while Chaos then threatens Morpheus before offering a balloon. Three representatives from Faerie, Cluracan, and his wife Nuala appeal to Morpheus to take control of Heaven to no one. Cluracan gives his son as a gift to the Dream God, in the name of Faerie King. Three angels are not present, Duma the demon of silence and Remiel here presented as the angel of those who rise. The angels have been set to not observe. Susano-o-no-Mikoto, Duma and Remiel eventually remain significant actors in the spin-off series Hades. much to Morpheus's dismay, the interested parties promptly convene in the palace at the centre of the Dreaming. Here several actors who have parts to play later in the episode are introduced, amongst them the representatives of Faerie, Cluracan, and his wife Nuala. After much negotiation, wheedling, bribery, deception, Norse drunkenness, and threatening behavior, Morpheus tries to get rid of Hell without even anger from the other participants: he offers it to a pair of demons sent by Satan, after Remiel relays a text saying that as Hell is a reflection of God, its real creator should control it. Dream then enters Hades and frees Nada. He apologizes to her, and although he really wants her, she wants not to leave with him, and he reincarnates her in the body of a newborn child, reminding her that she will not be welcome in the Dreaming in any form that she wants. Between these deliberations is the tale "In Which the Ghosts Return; and John Smith Concludes His Education", from issue #25, which takes place at a typical British boarding-school (and incorporates elements from the boarding-school novel genre) and is designed to explain the effects of Hell's closure. Though the three major protagonists in this story, the ghosts of three school children, not appear again in the Sandman trilogy, they later appear as "The Dead Man Detectives" in Gaiman's Vertigo cross-over novel The Children's Crusade, and in a mini-series of that name by David Scott. The collection begins with Lucifer, sans wings, standing on an Australian beach, happily observing Heaven's sunset.

Like previous Saint novels, which were fairly realistic crime drama, The Last Hero showed Thomas Templar entering the realm of both science fiction and spy thriller. The story takes an unknown length of time after the events of Enter the Saint with an account of Thomas Templar, The Saint, foiling an assassination attempt on a visiting nobleman by tricking the would-be killer into blowing himself up. This leads to The Saint being a cause célèbre among the American people, to the point where the government gives him not only a partial pardon for previous offences, but also a job as a sanctioned crime-buster. Templar flatly refuses, claiming he wants to remain underground, his identity a secret to all but a select few. (He will revisit this decision, also, in the later novel "The Impossible Crime" (featured in the collection Alias the Saint) and again in the anthology, She Was a Queen.) Over the next six years, the Saint proceeds to operate so well in the shadows that the general public assumes he has retired or lost. During this period, Templar hears from a reporter friend about troubling indications that conditions for a new war in France may be brewing (Templar insists that after the events of the Second World War there mightn't be a such battle "for thousands of days"). Meanwhile, during an outing in the countryside with former adventurer and girlfriend Jane Holm, Templar falls on a covert German government installation where he and Holm witness the testing of a dangerous and mysterious weapon—the electroncloud machine, which produces a vapor capable of transforming everything (and everyone) it touches into ash. Templar and Holm are about to leave when they encounter a giant of a person called Rayt Marius, an evil tycoon who wants the weapon for his own purposes. After fleeing to safety, Templar decides that he and his team will seize or destroy the gun before their government—or any other—can use it against people. Not only that, but the gun will not be forced to fall into Marius' arms. And in order that such a weapon not be re-created, Templar apparently plans to kill the device's scientist and, if possible, kill the inventor. Things become complicated when Marius kills Peter Holm, setting Templar off into an extremely violent frenzy. However, Scotland Yard Detective Claud Henry Teal also suggests himself becoming involved, even if the identity of The Saint remains a mystery to him. After saving Mary from the clutches of Marius, Templar discovers that his quest for anonymity is at an end (with both Lucian and Teal now unsure of who he truly is) and begins to make plans to take the world (along with his friends if they so chose). But first he will try to convince the scientist of the electroncloud to adopt the weapon; when the inventor suggests that he not only wants to take up his job, but may actually be mad, Templar finally believes the man should kill in order to possibly save the lives of people. Before he can execute the scientist, Templar's base is destroyed by Marius, who is believed to be working for the same prince Templar previously saved. During the melee, one of Knight's soldiers, Henry Kent, completes the Saint's orders and kills the scientist; he does so after deciding that whoever murdered the professor will be likely to hang for treason if caught, and out of loyalty to Templar decide to make the chance himself.
