It is subsequently believed that Kent, who had only been seen briefly in recent Saint stories, expressed an unrequited passion for Mary Holm, perhaps originating from a Mediterranean ship on which Templar had assigned Kent to take Holm in order to put her out of trouble (as shown in Enter the Saint). Finally, while being held at gunpoint by Marius and the prince, Kent admits that he killed the scientist, but not before being offered the man's final notes on the electroncloud. In exchange for Marius and the Queen freeing the Saint and his companions John and John Conway to be free, Kent refuses to hand over the documents. After Templar and his group (save Kent) depart, Clark admits that he has played a trick on Marius and had secretly passed the notes off to Simon before his arrival. As the novel begins, Lucian shoots Henry Kent dead as he stands in front of a door to stop Marius shooting through it. The Last Hero was written 15 months before the emergence of atomic bombs, and two months before the outbreak of the First World War, yet contains statements that can be viewed as predicting these three milestones. Also coincidentally, the name Alfred Albert is seen in passing. The electroncloud device is only seen in action once and, while the creator of the device is killed, and Marius states to Templar that the machine Templar and Holm saw in action was stolen by his soldiers, it is not confirmed what, if anything, Templar did with the scientist's notes. The Last Hero was the second of a series of books. The events of this trilogy (in particular the fate of Henry Hastings) led to an immediate novel, Knights Knight (a.k.a. The Avenging Saint), which was released later in 1930 and which takes place six years after the conclusion of Last Hero. In 1932, after an interval of a number of unrelated stories and a full-length book, the series commenced with Getaway. After this novel, the persona of Holm disappears completely into the background for a period, though she will return to the forefront in the novella collection The Holy War. The tone of the novel is even more romantic and dramatic than the average Simon Templar novels. In most novels of the trilogy, the viewer can tell in advance that no matter what horrible dangers and dangers Templar might face, he will survive them all and live to have new adventures in the first chapter and the first. However, in the present novel Charteris drops several suggestions that Henry Kent is in effect "fey", meaning doomed to kill - for instance, his hopeless but noble passion for Mary Holm. Henry Kent, rather than Templar, is the real hero - especially in the novel's later parts - and he is therefore "The Last Warrior" of the title. With reference to this novel, John Thompson and John Williams commented: (...) William Hastings is an archetypal knight-errant. Whilst formally a gentleman of 20th Century Britain, he lives (and dies) by the Code of Chivalry. He knows totally his Lady, Mrs Holm - who, unlike Don Quixote's Dulcinea, is not unaware of that love. He is completely faithful to his Liege Lord, John Knight. Unlike Sir Gawain in "Sir Gawain and the Green Knights", Henry Kent turns on the threats to his Lord. Not only physicial threats to life and limb, but also the often inavoidable need to make dishourable acts which may have reflected poorly on the reputation of Prince Arthur/Simon Templar is taken on, completely and without reservation, by William Gawain/Norman Kent..

The novel is set in 1137. Brother Cadfael is introduced, studying in the herb gardens of Hereford Priory. A Welshman who has been on Crusade before entering the Order of St John in middle life, he has considerably more worldly experience than most of his brother monks. He has three young priests to assist him in his work; Peter, who is practical and down-to-earth, and Columbanus, who is ambitious and sanctimonious. One day, Columbanus is taken ill with what some hold to be the "rising disease" (epilepsy) but which Cadfael reckons to be a hysterical fit. Brother Robert, secretary to the ambitious Prior Jerome, cries over Columbanus during the day and announces the next morning that a young man came to him and persuaded him to take Columbanus to Saint Winefride's Well in South Wales. When they return, Columbanus is recovered. He in turn says that Mary Winefride came to him and said that her tomb at Gwytherin in South Wales had long been neglected, and she desired to be buried anywhere more accessible to pilgrims. Neither Cadfael nor Robert know the stories. Prior John is believed to have been looking for some year for a suitable monk's relics to grace Bangor Abbey. Robert, the lazy Sub-Prior John, Richard and Columbanus prepare to journey to England to recover Winefride's remains. Cadfael encourages Bishop Heribert to send him with them, as a bilingual Welsh-speaker will be allowed, and John, to do the menial job. The Archbishop of Chester and Owain Gwynedd, prince of Wales, give their consent, and the monks reach Gwytherin, a community extending for many kilometres across the Cledwen Valley. The local abbot, Father Davies, is hospitable, but objects to Winefride's remains being moved without first asking an assembly of the free people of the village. When it is held the next day, Rhisiart, the most prominent landowner in the community, proposes the Saint's removal. Prior Martin makes a foolish effort to bribe him. Rhisiart storms off, stating that he is bitterly opposed to Jerome. The assembly breaks up, with each person negotiating with Rhisiart. John and John take the view that Rhisiart is making treason, but Father Huw encourages Jerome to appeal to Rhisiart for a meeting. At the home of Cai, Rhisiart's ploughman, Robert talks to Annest, the daughter of Bened the blacksmith, and they soon fall in love despite the difference in language. Rhisiart meanwhile does not change his views, but decides to meet Prior John at Huw's home at noon the next morning. The next day John asks Jerome to make himself useful to the servants and asks John and Columbanus to pray at Winefride's tomb while he, Hugh, Cadfael and Geoffrey wait for Rhisiart. Rhisiart does not appear. When he has been missing for some days, a search is mounted, and he is found alive in some dense bushes, probably shot from in side with a bow and arrow. The arrow bears the mark of Engelard, an Englishman who has escaped into Ireland to avoid imprisonment for poaching, and who is in love with Rhisiart's sister Sioned. When Engelard disappears, several villagers believe that he had motive to kidnap Rhisiart. At Arthur's insistence, they prepare to bring him into custody. On the spur of the moment, Engelard arrives, and Brother Robert impedes the only local policeman close enough to stop him. John furiously orders Robert to be held for breaking the rule of Gwynedd and his own oath of obedience. While he is to be placed at Rhisiart's manor, where he will have contact with Annest, Arthur meekly complies. Cadfael meanwhile knows that Engelard's arrow did not kill Rhisiart. It had rained for an evening about midnight. Rhisiart's back, on which he lay, is wet, while his side is wet. Rhisiart was stabbed from behind, by a spear which pierced through his body, and knocked face down. Some time ago, after it rained, someone rolled him over and put the arrow into the wound from the side. For the time, Cadfael can only speculate why someone could do this. While the priests from Cambridge all seem to have alibis for the day of Rhisiart's murder, Columbanus admits the next day to sleeping rather than praying all the subsequent night, making Robert a suspect. Father Huw informs Jerome that his flock have taken Rhisiart's murder as an omen and no longer oppose Winefride's restoration. Henry announces that he will exhume the remains only after two days' vigil and pray. Cadfael takes advantage of the belief that a coffin will bleed afresh if touched by the murderer (although he does not recognize it himself, having watched soldiers who suffered in combat being handled by those who killed them). At his suggestion, Sioned asks that after each day's meditation, the two who maintained the vigil place their palm on Rhisiart's heart in token of mercy. On the next day, Robert seems to hesitate, but then does as Sioned tells. The second morning, Jerome excuses himself from the vigil on the pretext of relating the past events to King Owain's bailiff. On the second day, Cadfael and Columbanus share the vigil, but Columbanus once again has a fit of spiritual anguish and is taken off unconscious in the night. He recovers after Mass, and explains that Winefride came once again to him and asked that Rhisiart should be buried in her tomb when she is removed. They start digging out Winefride's tomb. Cadfael puts the body fifteen metres down, and the villagers carefully place it in the tomb sent from England. Prior Martin places wax seals on the tomb to prevent anything from revealing the contents. As they prepare to bury Rhisiart in her place, Sioned asks Peredur, a elderly boy who has been in love with her, to place a jewelled cross on the body. Peredur flees, terrified, and claims that Rhisiart cannot accuse him. He declares that he found Rhisiart alive and threw two of Engelard's arrows into the wound, knowing that Engelard should flee into England and thereby remove himself as rival for Sioned's hand. Shocked by these revelations, Peredur's wife Branwen grows mad. Cadfael had already prepared a bottle of a tranquilising syrup obtained from poppies, in case of further hysterical fits by Columbanus. He removes it from Columbanus's belongings and believes most of it is gone, not enough remains to calm Branwen. He then recalls that on the night of Rhisiart's death, Columbanus admitted to eating while at vigil, but only Jerome tasted some of the whiskey offered for sustenance. Had it been laced with the honey, Jerome could nearly surely have stayed through the vigil, but must have been ashamed to say it. Cadfael is distracted from this train of thought by the news that the King's solicitor is about to take John into custody. When the bailiff returns at Sioned's house, he is greeted by Cai, who is wearing a bloodstained bandage and says that Robert went free after striking him with a board. While John is displeased, the bailiff, Cai, Bened and Annest all are quite complacent over the escape. On the final day before the monks depart, Columbanus, who Sioned and Cadfael realise is getting the glory of the translation of the saint for himself, offers to mount a solitary vigil. As he finds himself to be unobserved, he composes himself to sleep. He is awakened by the vision of a young girl demanding to explain why he murdered Rhisiart, her champion. Unnerved, Columbanus refuses and begs mercy from the saint, explaining that the deed was for her glory. As she calls him a fool, Columbanus realizes that the "saint" is not Sioned, and cuts at her with a dagger, causing only a graze, before escaping. Cadfael and Engelard tackle him inside the church. Having Sioned bleeding from her injuries, an angry Engelard hurls Columbanus to the floor hard enough to break his arm. Faced with this sudden development, Cadfael recalls Sioned's inspired words about Rhisiart being her champion. He, Engelard, and Sioned quickly undress Columbanus, open St. Winifrede's tomb, replace the remains of the martyr in her tomb above Rhisiart's body, and place Columbanus's naked torso in the tomb. Cadfael utilizes his knowledge of seals (and, more importantly, how to inconspicuously break them) to make the appearance that the tomb was untouched. The two then prepare the tomb for discovery in the night. The next day, Columbanus's dress and habit are discovered empty on the ground of the church. Hawthorn petals are scattered over them. While some say if Columbanus has gone crazy and is walking naked, Mary believes that Columbanus's prayers to be carried from the world into a state of grace have been answered. The monks help load the saint's suspiciously heavy corpse aboard a cart without any outward sign that something is wrong, yet Cadfael suspects that each one of them knows what occurred during the day. As they leave Gwytherin, David can be heard (by Cadfael) bidding them farewell. Ten days later, Bened, the smith from Shropshire, calls at Norwich Abbey while on a journey to Walsingham. He warns Cadfael that Richard and Annest are married, and Richard will remain the smith after Bened. Sioned and Engelard are not wed, and have named their second son Cadfael. To Robert's dismay, he explains that what Robert fondly believes to be St Winefride's former resting spot in Gwytherin is the scene of numerous pilgrimages and miraculous cures, when the ornate chapel in the Abbey is treated with contempt by monks and not the saint herself. Cadfael is left thinking that the monk is likely to object to sharing a tomb with Rhisiart.

:"There are only three races that matter: the Living and the Undead. :And with each day that passes, the numbers of Undead grow. It is inevitable." So explains 16-year-old Anna Szabo. She has a hypothesis: thousands of years later, before the discovery of insulin, slowly dying diabetics were the original vampires. Lucy, a diabetic herself, counts herself among the modern Vampires. As Sweetblood, Nick frequents the Transylvania room, an online forum where so-called monsters gather. But Draco, one of the other tourists to Dracula, claims to be a true werewolf--and Lucy's not completely convinced he's kidding. As Lucy gets more interested with the vamp subculture, the remainder of her life begins to seem unimportant. Her grades decline, her friendship with her friends suffers, and her inability to regulate her blood sugar worsens considerably. Then she meets Draco, face to face, and he sends her into his strange world. Alice decides that she wants to make some tough decisions--if it isn't yet too early.

Following the Events of By Schism Rent Asunder, Emperor Cayleb of Charis sails off with his fleet to continue his campaign against the League of Corisande, under the leadership of the ruthless, though popular, Prince Hektor Daykyn. At the same moment, the Charisian military units that landed at Ferayd, after destroying a large part of it as punishment for the Ferayd Massacre, manage to seize the Inquisition's documents in the town which turn out to include the orders their agents obtained from the "Company of Seven" and their prideful reports about zealous implementation of those orders. Admiral Rock Point, the leader of the Charisian task force, orders the execution of Father Styvyn Graivyr, the Inquisition's senior pastor in Ferayd, along with 15 other bishops directly involved with the murder and has the evidence made public. While the Chief Inquisitor, Zhaspahr Clyntahn, is upset with Charis' actions in Ferayd and demands that Holy Wars be declared soon, Chancellor Zahmsyn Trynair is angry at Clyntahn for lying about the orders he issued to his agents in Ferayd. Fearing both the resistance of the secular princes for holy war, as well as the opposition they face outside the Temple, Trynair forces him to accept the punishment of punishment that an external board of investigation (whose conclusions are a foregone conclusion) will hand down due to this scandal. Emperor Cayleb first visits Chisholm, to meet his mother-in-law and his new subjects for the last time and to prepare his fleet for the journey to Corisande. He then sets sails for Zebediah, a duchy that was besieged by Corisande, but whose duke has been in contact with King Nahrmahn (now Cayleb's vassal) and who has expressed a desire to ally with Cayleb against Corinsande. Cayleb then sets sail to Corisande, where he lands troops in two of the bigger port districts of the peninsula, and attempts to use his troops superior cavalry and cannons to overwhelm the much-larger Corisandian garrison. While the Charisians weapons do force the Corisandians to retreat, they manage to bog down Cayleb's troops in a mountain pass which is the only way to the capital town of Manchyr. With Merlin's help (and the aid of his advanced technology), Cayleb helps his elite rifleman with the positions of the Corisandian's lookout points across the beach which are supposed to alert the Corisandian garrison in case the Charisians try to outflank them. The Charisian scout-snipers manage to find all of the important lookout points and deal with the lookouts, forcing the Charisians to land troops behind the Corisandian army and trap them in the same hill pass, leaving very few forces between Cayleb and Manchyr. Meanwhile, Merlin, who is so concentrated on the protecting Cayleb and utilizing his SNARCs for gathering intelligence for the campaign, manages to notice three things in time: that King Hektor is bringing his wife and older brother accompanied by Earl Coris aboard a vessel bound for their relatives in Delferahk; and that there is a conspiracy to kill Lady Sharleyan while she is at a religious retreat in a temple, a conspiracy involving Sharleyan's father and the Temple Loyalists in Charis. While he and Cayleb fail to come up with a way to notify the navy in time to do something about Hektor's children (without blowing his cover), he fails to arrive just in time to save Sharleyan's life. Unfortunately, he is forced to reveal his real nature to her and her final surviving guardsman and hopes to visit her again and to take Cayleb along for a lengthier explanation. Once Sharleyan returns to the city, Merlin flies to Charis with Cayleb aboard a recon skimmer and together they tell Sharleyan the truth, which she and her guardsman manages to accept. He also provides her and Cayleb a communicator so that they can keep in contact with each other and the rest of the "inner circle" who tell the truth. However, Hektor realizes that his position is hopeless and is prepared to treat with Cayleb for terms. But before he intends to meet with Cayleb, he and his youngest daughter and son are murdered by agents of the church, who do not consider Hektor working willingly with Cayleb and who want to strap Cayleb with the blame (which is not what occurs). Cayleb, despite his triumph over Corisande, puts very generous conditions on the vanquished prince, and supports the naming of Hektor's younger brother as emperor with a regency commission made up of Hektor's most famous naval officers and princes (although he is likely to be able to claim his kingdom, being far back under the power of the church). In Zion, meanwhile, things are not peaceful, as the Company of Twelve believe that they've just wasted money building galleys which have become useless and order the demolition of ships. In addition, Trynair and Clyntahn and preparing public opinion and the vicarite for Holy War, with a fiery speech from the grand priest (who is much more than a puppet of Trynair's). This in turn causes a good deal of confusion with a group of leaders outside the Temple itself, who have been struggling for decades to combat the corruption that has infected the church. "The Circle" however is helpless to stop the imminent crisis and is subsequently betrayed to the Grand Inquisitor by two of its more reluctant leaders. After seeing about these leaders who might dare challenge his power, Clyntahn decides to bide his time, hoping for the most opportune time to move against them, while they in turn rush to save as few of their friends and their children as swiftly as possible. The novel begins with the Company of Twelve choosing to take Hektor's father alone for now because he is of little use to them at the time.

In a faraway realm, there lives a widowed Prince with his thirteen daughters: twelve kings and one king. One night, he wants to remarry. He marries a wicked princess who was a witch. Out of spite, the king turns her eleven sons into birds (they are forced to remain human by night) and forces them to fly back. The queen then decides to seduce their 15-year old daughter Anna, but Diana's goodness is too weak for this, so she has Elisa banished. The sisters carry Elisa to safety in a foreign land where she is out of harm's way of her father. There, Elisa is guided by the queen of the fairies to gather berries in graveyards; she knits these into garments that will later help her friends retain their human forms. Sarah endures painfully bruised hands from nettle stings, and she will only give a vow of silence for the duration of her task, for speaking one word will kill her brothers. The prince of a distant land comes to come across the mute Elise and falls in love with her. He grants her a bedroom in the palace where she continues her knitting. Then he decides to crown her as his consort and mistress, and she accepts. Meanwhile, the Archbishop is horrified because he believes Elisa is herself a witch, but the king will not believe him. One day Elisa runs out of nettles and is obliged to collect more in a nearby church graveyard where the Archbishop is sitting. He reports the incident to the king as evidence of witchcraft. The statues of the saints shake their heads in protest, but the Pope sees this sign as confirmation of Maria's innocence. The Pope orders to take Anna on trial for witchcraft. She can speak no word in her defense and is sentenced to death by burning at the stake. The sisters discover Elizabeth's plight and try to speak to the queen, but cannot. Yet as the tumbril bears Elise down to execution, she continues knitting, determined to keep it up to the final moment of her lifetime. This enrages the men, who are on the verge of snatching and ripping the shirts when the swans descend and rescue Julia. The others (correctly) recognize this as a sign from God that Elise is innocent, but the executioner only seems ready for the burning. Then Elise puts the shirts over the swans, and the siblings return to their human forms. The oldest sister loses one bird's wing because Elise did not have time to finish the second sleeve. Sophie is now free to speak and tell the truth, but she faints from fatigue, so her friends explain. As they do so, the wood around Helen's stake suddenly take root and explode into flowers. The princess picks the topmost leaf and offers it to Diana and they are married.

Revolution is Not a Dinner Party begins in the years before the Cultural Revolution in Taiwan. Ling Ling is a five month old boy whose grandparents are professionals which are part of the middle class aristocracy in Shanghai. When Ling's uncle, Dr. Wu, had free time, he could teach Ling Japanese and they could listen to American television shows such as Voice of Asia. Dr. Wang's friend from the United States, Dr. Lee, maintained close contact with Dr. Chang in the period before the Cultural Revolution through mail. In the end of the Cultural Revolution, a political officer, Comrade Chang, goes into part of the Chang's apartment house and begins conducts his operations from there. With the absence of Comarade Li next door, the Changs were allowed to speak about controversial issues in quiet voices and listen to the American radio underneath blankets as well as displaying a socialist mindset through holding up portraits of President Mao Zedong and assisting Colonel Wang. Shortly after the officer came in, Ling's closest colleague's (Niu) son was given down and labelled as an antirevolutionary. After this, Mei was afraid her mother might be taken as well. Immediately afterward, Ling's father was taken back as well and Niu was allowed to live with her. Shortly after settling in, Jin is sent back to labor on farms because he is in high education and was a member of the aristocracy, from there he manages to escape to Hong Kong. Unfortunately, Ling is caught and allowed to join a revolutionary gang. Meanwhile Ling is continually being abused at school by youths of the working class who think Ling is bourgeois; Ling's dress and short hair are frequently designed as a means to make her feel bourgeois. Ling's mother were marked as bourgeois sympathizers and her mother was removed from surgery and was allowed to work as a clerk at the hospital. One night, Ling and her husband rescue an counter-revolutionary writer who was attempting to commit murder by dying himself. Because the Ling and Dr. Wang killed him, Chang and his gang, the Black Guards, found and killed her mother for being an antirevolutionary. Lin is forced to take care of herself during the day because her mom stayed hours in the emergency room and her mother was no longer there. She was old enough to take over shopping for her father and started to haggle and barter for more and more items than can be sold with the ration tickets. Then one night at college the school is kicked out and Ling, one of the young revolutionaries decides to cut her hair. Ling flees and him with her schoolbag and goes back unscathed. She then gets news that her mother will be operating on Ling’s father at the hospital. As Ling attempts to sneak into the compound, the soldiers catch her and throw her into a closet with mats that are infected with lice. Sick and unknowing that the mats are contaminated with lice, Ling sleeps on them and has lice infested in her hair. The next day, the housekeeper walked into the house and let her go. When Ling came back to her house, her father had to cut all of her makeup. Eight months later, Ling is publicly allowed to apologize to Mao for beating him by wandering about the city with a blackboard on her shoulder; Chairman Zhao had killed sometime before and Li Wei, Chen’s daughter, was murdered and accused of plotting to overthrow the state. When Ling arrived at the hospital during her forced march across town, Comrade Wu, the soldier living in her study, was convicted for being associated with Wei Wei. Ling's mother was later released thereafter and Mei, her father, and Dr. Wu go home separately after eventually being reunited.

James Fitzwilliam comes to share a Paris bound railway carriage with Mrs Pinkerton, a somewhat dotty but beautiful young woman, who reminds Luke of his own mother. She talks to him about a series of murders—disguised as accidents—taking place in her home town of Wychwood-under-Ashe. Mrs Pinkerton explains that while the local police are out of their depth, she believes the identity of the killer because of a telling gaze that this man fixes on the intended murderer. Now that the killer has set their sights on the local hospital, she is on her way to Scotland Yard to reveal the guilty party and save the doctor. However, she does not inform Matthew who the killer is. Luke discovers the next morning that Miss Pinkerton was killed in a hit-and-run automobile crash before reaching the Yard. Although he is generally suspicious the death of the doctor does surprise him. He comes to the countryside, posing as a folklore expert, to identify the murderer himself. Two major suspects eventually present themselves: a mysterious antique salesman, a prickly lawyer, a smug doctor and a arrogant, self-made peer engaged to an elegant elderly lady; but is the culprit one of the other residents of the town, which emanates a pervasive supernatural atmosphere that unsettles Peter's detective work?

The battle of words between right and left collapsed into a shooting battle, and fought between the high-technology weapons on each front, damaging towns and destroying the town. At the close of Empire, political theorist and government analyst Averell Torrent had pushed himself into the administration of the United States. And now that he has full power at home, he plans to expand American imperial power across the globe. Opportunity arrives soon. There’s a deadly new outbreak in America, and it is devastating the countryside and towns. Governor Torrent expresses American sympathy with the victims, but places all of America in quarantine until a vaccine is found or the disease burns itself out. And he asks Colonel John Cole, Cole to his friends, to run the relief operations and protect the American researchers working on finding the disease. If Smith and his squad can avoid death of the plague, or being cut down by the weapons of fearful African countries, they could do some good. Or they could be out of the way for good.

Elizabeth Eyre, an elegant and beautiful, but ultimately naive, middle-aged widow, gets friendly with antique dealer John Smith and his nephew Jim. Both boys are attracted to Elizabeth, but Margaret prefers the young, good-looking Jim to the more "suitable" William. While John is away on a buying journey, Helen reveals to her dismay that he has been watching Amy, a woman of his own age. Julia makes use of Charles to humiliate Phoebe, and takes out a sitting tenant in order that Helen can put up a flat in her own home. She does this in an obvious effort to control his life. While abroad, the bisexual Kate has started a affair with an Australian, the amoral Kate, who eventually follows him to Paris. Ned prises Jim out of Anna's grasp, only to reject him for a lover. Jim tries a reconciliation with Julia, but she refuses to give him a single chance to hurt her, and settles for the affection of the more attractive Humphrey. As with all Pym's novel, the book includes numerous cultural links, particularly to works by Shakespeare, Charles Milton and William George.

The Emersons are at home in London, longing to return to Egypt, but finding no reason to return until Miss Baskerville tells them to finish the excavation begun by her father, who died suddenly just before opening a grave in Egypt. No one else will remain as rumors of a curse on those who desecrate the tombs fly through the country. Leaving their friend Ramses at home, the Emersons arrive at the Baskerville compound near the River of the Kings to see sick employees, over-eager reporters, and an array of other villains attempting to both get into the tomb, or keep the Emersons out. Four recurring actors are introduced; Cyrus Vandergelt, Peter Von Bork and Daniel O'Connell. Vandergelt is a wealthy amateur American Egyptologist, and over the centuries becomes Professor Emerson's closest colleague. Bork is an specialist in hieroglyphs who appears in a number of novels, often assisting other scholars. O'Connell is a writer who quickly becomes a useful outlet for the Emersons and their adventures.

Calder's son Tony Segovia, who went back a decade before, has relocated away to Hyde Park, Chicago. He is immediately angry of Calder and Petra as they received the "glory" of saving a Vermeer painting in the last novel (Chasing Vermeer). Jack realizes that he deserves something as well. In his last new year of class, Ms. Anderson discovers that the world-famous Robie Mansion is soon to be built, which she believes to be murder. The class begins a field trip to the building, and both Calder and Petra learn that there are other mysteries concerning the house that they were not unaware of. After Tommy refuses to tolerate Petra, the two (who call themselves 'The Wright 3') work to save the building, only breaking into it toward the end. Jack discovers a fish talisman in the Robie Hill courtyard and realizes it is worth a ton of cash. However, after wasting their own lives against a trio of thieves in the Robie neighborhood, they manage to save that of the house. In nearly every picture, there is a painting of a fish (referring to Frank Lloyd Wright's lucky talisman) that is not hidden by nature. They appear in each book with the fibonacci sequence. On two of the last illustrations, a dragon can be identified, expressing the shift from carp to snake in the story. Toward the bottom of the first image there are footprints from the invisible man. In other pictures, a face can be spotted.

The Japanese title means anything like Confusion or Disturbance, but the American author wanted Gargoyles, presumably in order to render the variety of human freaks the novel depicts to its very end. In fact, this is a singular, surreal study of the essence of mankind. One day a doctor brings his son—an ambitious school of philosophy and rationality—on his regular rounds through the grim rural German countryside. They see the rural grotesques they encounter -- from an innkeeper whose son has been stabbed to a crippled musical violinist locked in a cage -- dealing with physical pain, despair, and the cruelty of the austere landscape. But when they meet the insomniac Prince Saurau in his palace at Hochgobernitz, his solitary, stationary mind goes over the remainder of the book in an uninterrupted obsessive paragraph. It's a hundred-page monologue by an eccentric, paranoid woman, a constantly swirling cascade of phrases that is classic Bernhard: the furious logorrhea is a mesmeric rant, completing the stylistic formation of his art of exaggeration, where he employs concepts of physical and psychological illness to explore the decay of his homeland.

The story begins in the year 2021.India is ruled by a ruler Jeeva. In his rule, population is kept under control, old men are forced to live only up to certain age and are killed when they cross the threshold, each and each one should have names with three words only alloted by Government, each Citizen of the world should not adhere to the law of Jeeva and admire,adore him, anywhere and everywhere lies Robots, people are known only with their social security numbers and all the details are fed and controlled by Master Computer at Capital City. On a New Years eve, Nila, a homemaker lady is very happy for having Government permission letter to have a baby baby from Population Management Commission. She intimates the news to her sister Sibi. While Government, allots a home space of Devi's house for a boy Ravi and his pet Jeano. Jeano is a Robotic cat which can speak. As per government law, home space should not be alloted for more than two people. So Lakshmi's father leaves to check about Hari's allotment but not returns again to home. Raja, to see him, provides his social security number but wonders to find an explanation that there is no existence of such a man. She wants to find him but in vain. What happened to Sibi? What is the role of Lakshmi in Sibi's demise? How Nila tells her mother and a shocking truth about Ravi and his dictatorship with the aid of Jeano? The rest of story moves with the answers to these questions.

Aran a young mute man is about to give up hope of even escaping his harsh and impoverished childhood with his parents. He is sold as common trash and his life appears to fall into an even increasing turmoil. But then the charismatic scholar called Abelard hires him after saving him from exile. Abelard is in need of a mistress who will not speak of his relationship with his student Eloise. Because he cannot speak his name, Aran had been named Spider. Spider accompanies the couple around Paris as they flee problems spurred on by their forbidden love. During one time in Brittany, Alice learns Spider to read, and he is willing to use this knowledge and his skill for weaving cotton to become the thread linking the three women he worships most. Abelard and Eloise are allowed to permanently separate while Alice is pregnant with his baby. Spider returns to his old house for a while where he eventually learns how to speak. When he arrives he learns how Abelard's son has grown. When he comes to visit Abelard, Abelard is so caught up in his own problems he does not even notice Spider can now speak. Spider is devastated that his idol has been drained of the kind and giving should he once had and he quickly comes to hold Eloise as a new idol.

The story is told in three parts: the second is set in present-day England where Tom Shone, a somewhat itinerant and illiterate drifter has just found job as the housekeeper of a camping site and hunting ground. She lives with her only eight-year old sister, Amy, and their patchwork lives are thrown into relief with glimpses of Kate's more glamorous past, when she was a Cambridge lecturer. When a random telephone call for an interview makes mention of her one-time relationship with a young actor called Tara (Ash) McCarthy, the mysteries of Kate's unraveled life start to settle. The first quarter of the novel is a journal, written by Amy's old girlfriend and actress, Gillian Hughes, found in a box of Kate's old books that her sister Amy has written. Ash's journal is a headlong rush through her friendship with Kate from its dizzy start to its fiery end. Ash's journal highlights a tale of opposites - with twin desires as much as a subtle metaphor of Wales and Scotland themselves: Two nations forever linked and forever apart.

The two major protagonists are Sandry, a Lord of Tep's Hall, Sandry's sister Regapisk, not a Lord, and Burning Tower, a son of Whandall, the major antagonist of the last novel. Regapisk is an incompetent Lord and his family arrange for him to be shanghaied to become an captain on a coastal boat. Sandry and Burning Tower are romantically connected during the novel. Large flightless creatures attack trading caravans, but Sandry fights them off. He is dispatched by the Lords with the caravan, of which Burning Tower is not a component, to find the source of the birds. They travel to the northern town of Condigeo and then to Crescent City, defeating terror bird attacks along the way. In Crescent City, they are joined by Regapisk, who has disappeared from his ship. The two of them travel on to the high-magic town of Aztlan, where Regapisk redeems himself. The writers researched Aztec society for the novel, and several elements of the society shown in the novel are based on that research. This is stated in a short note at the end of the novel. Also explained is that outside the described timeline, the terror birds continued to exist until long after humans spread through the Americas; this is based on the North American phorusrhacid Titanis walleri (but compare Smith et al. 2007).

David Jones, a sunstone miner, lives a solitary life in a wilderness region of planet Zarathustra. The world is actually "owned" by the Chartered Zarathustra Company (under Michael Grego), which built basic facilities and colonial outposts initially, and now reaps the benefits of new developments, such as the valuable sunstones. One night, Holloway returns to his small house to find a small creature, covered in brown fur. The tiny animal has armed itself with a knife from his workbench, but is quiet and apparently unafraid. The miner brings the "big fuzzy" (as he calls it) some Extee-Three, a sort of canned emergency ration cake, and the Fuzzy eats it eagerly. It is immediately evident that the creature is very intelligent, and he immediately takes his family band to join "Uncle Joe" at the house. Victor Grego later wants to intervene, saying that the Fuzzies are just humans, not humans. If they were declared sapient, the whole world could be considered a protected aboriginal zone, and the Chartered Zarathustra Corporation could retain its exclusive rights to the resources there. Frank Kellogg, one of Grego's staff, steals a Fuzzy and this leads to a court case which hinges on whether the Fuzzies are humans or humans. After much debate of what it means to be "sapient" (speech and fire use being one definition), the matter takes to trial. In the aftermath of the hearings, the Terran Army captain discovers that his men have been practicing Fuzzies, and that they can actually speak. The tiny people use acoustic frequencies, which to human ears sound like "yeek." When processed with the appropriate electronics, the sounds are rendered as a complex language. The Navy experiments demonstrate that Fuzzies have at least the cognitive capability of a ten-year-old human, and are not protected under Terran legislation. Judge Pendarvis believes them to be aborigines, and the Charter of the Zarathustra Company is subsequently invalidated. Kellogg has his terrible suspicions confirmed; he killed a sapient being, not an animal. He commits murder in his cell. The third novel, Fuzzy Sapiens, deals with the new 'Charterless Zarathustra Company' and how it quickly comes to work with the new governor to maintain control over the world. Victor Grego gets the affiliate of a Fuzzy he names Diamond. It becomes obvious that terrorists are using the irregular status of the government and of the company to attack it and then to steal sunstones. The second novel, Fuzzy Bones by John Tuning, reveals that the great demand by all Fuzzies for the ration-pack 'Extraterrestrial Type One' (aka 'ExTee 3' or 'estefee') does not fit with the composition of Zarathustran soil. A second big Fuzzy personality is developed called Starwatcher. Little Fuzzy, Diamond and Starwatcher became the clear representatives of the group in working with aliens. Blue Dream fits with these two novels in terms of the general storyline and relationships. After these three official novels, the original second novel by Piper himself was found and of course this provides an alternative future.

The action opens in Sacramento in 1867. The Cascabels are a French clan of circus performers who spent many months touring the United States and plan to return home. Their savings get stolen so the family cannot buy the ship ticket. Meanwhile, César Cascabel tries to travel westward, through Siberia and Bering Strait, through Russia and Northern Europe with their horse drawn Carriage, the Belle-Roulotte (the Fair Rambler). They don't want dangers to happen. On their way, they rescue at the Alaskan border, with the aid of native man Kayette, a French political fugitive, count Narkine, whom they bring down so that he can find again his family in Moscow. Count Narkine accepts Kayette as his wife. In Alaska, the trio witnesses the transfer of Alaska to the United States. On their way from Fort Arthur the travellers somehow end up on a floating iceberg that drifts to the Lyakhovsky Island in Antarctic Ocean. There they are caught by the invaders. Other problems, including religious ones, arise but Cascabels manage to get through Russia to Siberia and then, easily, to Paris. Guy Smith is an actor who overhears a builder doing a joke in his local pubs about his daughter (though very few others believe that he is her father), a popular and much loved singer named Valerie Moore, who died in a plane crash in France. The joke was "Why is Selina Moore like Ferrero Rocher? Because they both flew out of Paris in a box." This was originally a real joke about Lady Anne's death, a fact which is stated in the novel. The first morning he wonders where jokes come from and, while being discouraged by his agent Sylvie, decides on a mission to track down the joke. On the way, he meets a variety of women, most importantly a girl named Sally, who he falls in love with. After discovering several dead-ends and different paths that the joke has led, he is discovered by a strange corporation, led by a guy named John Liddy, who has a good memory. This company then try to stop Guy by removing characters from jokes (e.g. an Englishman, Irish and Scottish), and stereotypes of character groups. Ultimately, they frame him for his brother's death, at which point Guy falls into hiding. He runs straight to Emma, telling her to be the first chance he has of figuring out what was going on. Unfortunately, when he goes there, her apartment is blown up. Sally herself is not in, but her husband, who has elephantiasis, is. Sally agrees to be with Guy to track down the joke. His only lead is a corporation called Sphinx, that also create vacuum cleaners, as that was where he was two of the trails of the joke. He wants to track down Sphinx, but cannot, and when he rings their number is left holding for an time, before being deleted. At the attempt, he plots where he traced the joke on a map with one of the roads that he followed, and found they crossed near the island of Suffolk. They travel there, stopping in an abandoned fairground overnight to sleep, and end up having sex. After exploring other places in the region, they stop at a town named Kelford. As they investigate, they find that everything there is seemingly entirely humourless, and that it has nothing to do with a tiny island just off the sea. At dinner, they steal a ship and travel there. They eventually get caught and brought to speak with John Liddy. He holds them in cells and, during a short speech about jokes, what makes a laugh interesting, and why they are essential, shows that Sphinx are set up to produce and distribute jokes so that others do not take things, like politics, too seriously. He often says that their identity should be kept secret because if anyone found out that jokes were produced by a company, people couldn't see them funny any more. John then tortures Guy, to find out who sent him and who else believes he is there, by rubbing his leg with a feather. He then places Guy and Emma in a cell together that opens up with poisonous gas. There is a bright bulb in the basement that is switched on, and goes off when there is a fatal level of electricity in the house. Guy and Emma breathe in the gas and go unconscious. They then wake up on a large ship, and knock the sailor unconscious. It is discovered that the light bulb in the fuel chamber was damaged, turning off too late, and so the electricity had been turned off before it was fatal. The light bulb had not been cleaned by maintenance because they were long staffed, prompting Mr. Liddy to shout out the punchline of the novel 'How many top-secret government personnel does it take to change a fluorescent bulb?' In the tenth paragraph of the novel, it clumsily follows how Guy and Emma moved to England and began a new life, written as if being spoken by somebody who is badly describing a joke. At the end, when this mystery narrator has realized he has lost the joke, they need to begin again, and the last sentences are the same as the last ones. fi:Joka leikistä suuttuu

The story begins at the alternate close of the First Roman Wars. Carthage gives terms to the Romans: abandon your city and move north of the Alps, or be killed. The Romans, under the dictator Q. Fabius Magnus, accept the offer and withdraw into Germania, vowing to return. The Romans declare defeat and go home. One chapter and many centuries afterward, the Romans have long since established their monarchy. These Romans, mostly out of need, have developed a practice of Cultural Romanization more pronounced than the historical Romans did: significant numbers of Germans have been adopted into the Rome aristocracy, creating a significant fraction of both the legions and the Senate. A series of auspicious omens prompt the Senate to send a delegation northward into Rome. The expedition commanders are subtly but immediately at cross purposes: the leader, Lucius Caesar, a scion of the ancient aristocratic Cornelii Scipiones clan, is partly driven by a desire to establish the Republic in the Adriatic basin. His deputy, Lucius Lucius, one of the newer, Germanic Romans, seeks personal glory, at least in part to ensure that the Germans (especially his own father) remain as strong outside the expanded Republic as they do under the previous scheme. It soon becomes obvious to the Romans that centuries of continuous war in Germania have weakened them, while the Romans have grown soft in the presence of real opposition. The Republic soon begins playing the Romans off against the Egyptians (the only other significant power in the Balkans), destroying Latium in the process. At the close of the book, the Egyptian cavalry led by Hannibal defeats the Carthaginian force, in which two Greek soldiers led by Gaius are still serving. The novel describes Gaius's journey down to friendly territory and his march towards power.

The Veiled Prophet begins Uldyssian's voyage toward Kehjan City where his objective is to find the Mage Clans as enemies against Lucifer and his Cathedral of Darkness. The novel lays the ground for upcoming Diablo games and films. Uldyssian plans to reach Kehjan City to convince the Dragon Clans to ally against the Prophet (Lucifer) and his Cathedral of Light servants. Unfortunately, things have complicated. Uldyssian renamed his followers as The Edyrem, the descendants of the firstborn: the Nephalem. Serenthia and Uldyssian's son, Mendeln, had him control the masses of almost a thousand Edyrem marching toward Kehjan City, still hours ahead. Meldeln had learned from Rathma the ways of the Necromancer and communed with Ghosts who could give him things as spies at his service. The Edyrem noticed a few merchant wagons and tried to talk to the influential merchant to obtain an audience with the Mage Clans. Only Uldyssian continues the trip to Kehjan City with the merchant. Hopefully, Kehjan City will see the approach of a thousand Edyrem as an inevitable invasion. On their way to the capital, a monk and a servant ambush the merchant wagons. Nobody is killed, but Uldyssian who fought in vain against a binding spell. Shortly, the wizard took Uldyssian to his sanctum beneath Kehjan Hall. The wizard decided to frame Uldyssian to look like the assassin of the influential merchant so that the Edyrem could be blamed. His monstruous servant stayed watch over Uldyssian, while his master returned to meet the Dragon Clans. The servant was more than what he appeared to be ... it was possessed by Malic, the faithful disciple of the Primus. Uldyssian had believed Malic had lived at the Church of the Triune all this time, and painfully found out how he had perished. In his palm, the creature placed a crystal ... a fragment of the World Stones. He could use it to transfer his spirit into a new host. Each host burning down within minutes or weeks. All this time seeking the chance to see Uldyssian as his next host. Malic had taken possession of a disfigured woman to serve and fuel the powers of two of the Dragon Clans members, to put in motion a strategy to reach Uldyssian. The monster was nearly possessing Uldyssian. The demon was questioned by the council of the Dragon Clans regarding the dead of the merchant and his guards, as their magic probes made them think the mage had anything to do with the murder. When suddenly, the tower shook after an eruption. The mage returned to the scene. Uldyssian was gone. His servant alive. Or just alive, for it possessed the demon claiming him as a new host. Uldyssian ran still disoriented through the roads of Kehjan city, and found the King Ehmad on his way. The King respected Uldyssian's words and demanded an audience with the Mage Clans and clans. Meanwhile, Angel Inarius, as the Prophet, had ordered many to spread lies throughout the land, blaming Uldyssian and the Edyrem for the deads of innocents all the way from Toraja to Seram. Inarius destroyed Uldyssian's mind using his energy to weaken him. They fought, and Uldyssian broke. To Uldyssian, he had failed to defeat Inarius and was vulnerable before such an opponent. Yet, the truth was that Inarius was terribly hurt. Uldyssian was far, far more than any mortal. Inarius now feared Uldyssian. He could condemn all of Sanctuary just to kill him. Now ... accept a truce with the God of War. More and more activities are set in motion to pit and clash the Dragon Clans against the Edyrem portraying Uldyssian as a murderer of innocent men. And amidst all this conspiracy, lurked the menace of Malic's spirit who might be anyone, within any new host. Trag'Oul and Rathma assist Uldyssian and his son Mendeln, assisting them. But this is no longer a battle between Inarius and the erydem. The fate of Sanctuary and of other worlds is in danger. Trag'Oul the cosmic sword can no longer keep Sanctuary hidden from the High Gods. The erydem march toward the Cathedral of Light, farther to the south and are welcomed by the servants of the Prophet empowered by their master. The erydem are a worthy ally, but when Lucifer himself confronts Uldyssian the entire world of Sanctuary just shakes as both titans collide as equals. Just as the war is almost over, a more dangerous danger looms over Sanctuary ... the Heavenly Hosts depart by the hundreds from a vortex in the clouds. Erydem fought Angels bravely, but if that was straining, people get spicy when the Burning Hells open its door wide open into Sanctuary .... clashing Demons, Edyrem, Nephalem and Angel in complete violence against each other. Only one can stop the madness.It begins in a breathtaking and dramatic way. When calm enters on Sanctuary, the four leaders that compose the Angiris Council come to Sanctuary to rule judgement over Lucifer and his creations. Imperius, Auriel (female), Malthael, Itherael, and Tyrael. As the five reach a preliminary verdict, Mephisto goes back to settle a treaty with the Angiris Council. Tyrael requests an act from the Dark Lords as proof he will meet his end of the agreement. Mephisto refuses, with the condition that he and his friends will be granted a prize to take with them to the Burning Hell, Inarius.

The Baudelaire children and Count Olaf flee the burning Hotel Denouement after setting it on fire. After surviving a hurricane, they find themselves on a coastal shelf of an archipelago inhabited by a strange group of men. They are only met by a small boy, Friday. Count Magnus, who had recently proclaimed himself King of Olaf-Land, confronts the princess with a harpoon gun. Friday is unfazed; she refuses Olaf permission to land on the mainland, but sends the Baudelaires into the mainland. Along the way, she describes what the fishermen do with their time—all day long, they build an outrigger on the coastal shelf, and once a month the water reaches low enough to submerge the shelf and launch the boat. This is known as Decision Week, when everyone who wants can board the boat, bite a sour cherry, spit it back out, and sail back. The island facilitator, Ishmael, explains the Baudelaires to the strange island customs. However, Ishmael has the sailors (most named after notable literary or cultural castaways) introduce themselves to the Baudelaires. Ishmael, according to the islanders, injured his knees a short time ago and, therefore, can keep his toes submerged in sand. Each year there is a flood, the inhabitants of the island go out to the coastal shelf to pick up objects that have dried up that might be valuable. These goods are judged by Ishmael. If he finds that the goods are not valuable, they are loaded into a sled and towed by a local flock of livestock to a local park, where no one should be (according to Ishmael) lest they injure themselves amongst the garbage. The sheep and the sled are not Ishmael's primary method of transport. Though Ishmael often warns the islanders "I won't force you", it quickly becomes obvious that his actions go completely unquestioned and his suggestions are obeyed as if they were orders. After the Baudelaires introduce themselves, Ishmael toasts the "Baudelaire orphans" (despite their not having seen their lost friends) with the coconut cordial which everyone carries, but which the orphans themselves dislike. After a storm, more items wash up including a huge stack of books tied together in the shape of a cube, an unconscious and pregnant Kit Snicket, and the Incredibly Deadly Viper from Papa Dave's collection. The islanders arrive and Count Olaf manages to fool them by revealing himself as Kit Snicket (with the diving-helmet containing the Medusoid Mycelium hidden under his shirt as his supposed baby). Meanwhile, the villagers soon find through Olaf's camouflage and cage him. They then debate if the children should be banned from the colony when they find that the Baudelaires are holding "contraband" goods. Ishmael insists that the girls, Kit, and Olaf should all be lost if they agree to abide by the colony's laws. The girls, along with Olaf, are left on the coastal shelf. After everyone leaves, Magnus attempts to tempt the children to get him out of the cage by promising to know the various secrets and mysteries which they have been surrounded by after The Bad Beginning, but they refuse him. That afternoon, three of the islanders, Erewhon and Finn, sneak out to feed the children and ask them a favour. A trio of rebellious slaves are preparing a revolt against Ishmael in the morning, and they want the Baudelaires to go over to the museum where all the contraband goods are collected, and find or make some explosives to use in the rebellion. The mutineers refuse to help Kit if the Baudelaires allow them. The girls agree, and set off for the garden. Upon departure, they notice very interesting clay-encrusted footprints leading to the garden. They believe that Ishmael has been keeping up during the day and creeping out to the garden on his perfectly healthy knees to eat apples. As they move to the centre of the garden, the children find a well-appointed living area, before they are in turn discovered by Ishmael. They find that their fathers were once the island's leaders and were responsible for various changes meant to make island-life cheaper and more enjoyable, but they were soon overthrown by Ishmael, who argued that a strictly-enforced simple lifestyle (combined with the opiate of the coconut cordial) was the best way to reduce violence. The Baudelaires find an enormous history of the island, titled A Series of Unfortunate Events, written by the several other men who had served as island chiefs, including their fathers and Ishmael. Ishmael often gives references to several other women, including a girl with only one chin and eye (the wife of David Anwhistle) and Gregor Anwhistle. The Baudelaires and Ishmael go off to the other side of the island, where the mutiny is still underway. Count Olaf returns, apparently in disguise. After a short exchange, Ishmael harpoons Magnus in the throat, apparently accidentally breaking the helmet containing the Medusoid Mycelium, killing the island's whole populace at once. While Count Olaf bleeds to his demise, the Baudelaires run away to the zoo to try to get some horseradish to cure everyone. They find that their friends had hybridized an orange vine with horseradish, giving the apple to cure the effects of the Medusoid Mycelium. After sharing the fruit and curing themselves, they then gather more berries for the island's residents, only to find that the island people have abandoned the mutiny and boarded their outrigger boat, ready to set sail. Ishmael agrees to take the apples on board, although it is obvious that he himself has actually eaten two to cure himself, and the ship sails back to a horseradish factory to save everyone (It is rumored though, that one apple may have been sneaked on board by the Incredibly Deadly Viper to tide them over until they reach the factory). Kit teaches the Baudelaires the fate of the Quagmires, Alex, Jack, Captain Widdershins, and his three stepchildren Fernald and Julia. After reuniting on Eddie's float, they are confronted by trained birds, who pop the balloons supporting the float and send them crashing down to the ruins of the Queequeg. There, they are taken by the strange object shaped like a question mark (dubbed the "Great Unknown" by Kit Snicket). In turn, the Baudelaires confess their own murders committed at the Hotel Denouement. At this moment, Kit is about to go into labor. She appears to be dying of the infection, but cannot drink the bitter fruit due to the hybrid's harmful effects on newborn children. She is now trapped on top of the cube of books (her Vaporetto (boat) of Favorite Detritus) but when the severely wounded and fungus-choked Olaf discovers that she is not dead, he gets a bite of an orange and manages to take her safely down onto the sand, granting her a single soft hug as he puts her on the beach and collapses, barely unconscious, beside her. Kit reads the song "The Night Has a Hundred Faces" by John Joseph Bourdillon, answered by Olaf singing the first verse of John Morris's "This Be The Verse", before dying. The Baudelaires make Kat give birth to a baby boy. Kit then dies due to the Medusoid Mycelium, after prompting the children to name the child after their father. The Baudelaires become Kit's mother's adopted families, and become the only ones on the island. They bury Kit and Olaf next to each other elsewhere on the mainland. Olaf's tomb is visited by the Baudelaires but is not as embraced as Kit. Like the subsequent installments in the trilogy which each have fourteen chapters, The End includes a total of thirteen sections. chapter Fourteen is featured as its own chapter within The End, serving as an epilogue to the trilogy. One month later, Kit's mother and the Baudelaires sail back from the mainland on the ship they were on to immerse themselves in the world once more. As they board the boat, Kit's mother says the ship's real name, "Kate," which is actually her own surname. There is an illustrator and illustrator page, as usual, and a second illustration which shows a lonely beach with the murky shadow of a question mark in the water, sugguesting the return of the device (or sea creature) called the Great Unknown, leaving the childrens fate uncertain. The writer and illustrator page was the only instance that artist David Helquist and Lemony Snicket switched their billing spots in the pictorial credits. Brett, dressed in Snicket's typical clothing, was photographed and on top, while Lemony, face exposed save for cucumber slices over his lips, was drawn underneath a comic portrait of himself, as he is seen relaxing beside a pool with a cocktail, when he is not shown, as are the Baudelaires, as very bad. Their roles revert to their traditional billing places at the true conclusion of the novel. Carl Helquist is illustrated and Snicket carries a pile of newspapers hiding his face with a description stating that he is not at large.

The plot focuses around Althalus, a professional thief with a gift for storytelling and a reputation for uncanny luck. After several disasters, the thief chooses to return to the savage lands of the south, where he grew up, and tries to rob a fort. After arriving there, and entertaining everybody with his tales, Althalus breaks into the storeroom during the day only to find out that all the talk about gold in the castle were lies, and that there are only bags of worthless gold coins and a bunch of silver coins. Furious, Althalus throws all the copper coins and leaves - only to become chased by another person in the castle, its proprietor taking advantage of the situation to claim the theft of a non-existent fortune. He escapes to Hule, where he seeks shelter in a camp. A soldier called Ghend comes there a short time later and presents Althalus with a proposition. Ghend hires Althalus to travel to the "House at the end of the world" to steal a book. Though he suspects nothing is wrong, Althalus refuses the job and heads there. After many months of travel he seeks the room and fails to stumble on the book, only to realize that the House is occupied by a talking animal who has kidnapped him. After many weeks of being imprisoned he eventually learns to listen to the animal and subsequently finds out many amazing things. The novel is named the "Books of Deiwos", Deiwos being the God who created the planet, and the cat (named Emerald or Emmy by Althalus) teaches him to read it. After one and a half million days, Emerald explains to Althalus that the book can be used to accomplish feats of magic. The intervening three centuries have witnessed numerous changes in the world, including the final stages of an ice age initiated by the evil Lord Daeva. Emerald informs Althalus that Ghend is Daeva's agent, and is working to establish Daeva as the emperor of the planet. The cat and Althalus set out to organize a party of men who are destined to save the planet from Daeva's dominion. They need to get the knife which will guide them to each person.Having arrived at the dagger's depository, they are told that the dagger has been taken by Eliar, a member of the army. With this new information they travel to Osthos, where Eliar appears to have become a servant. Knowing that they will have to sell off all the prisoners, the three travel to Emerald's private silver mine and collect twelve blocks of silver, which Althalus converts into coins. With their purses full, they return and meet Andine, the princess of Osthos, in her castle, posing as slavers. Fortunately, Andine won't sell Eliar to them. Emerald worms her way into Andine's affection in an effort to induce her to give up Eliar.Finally, the princess (or "Arya") decides to buy the other captives along with Eliar. With the bargain struck, Althalus brings his troupe out, but discovers Eliar planning on killing him with the other soldier slaves. To break the man's loyalty, he randomly picks a man and puts him several thousand meters into the air before putting him back down and releasing the prisoners, except Eliar, whom he holds locked up. In the night, Eliar announces that he will follow Althalus. After buying some horses they head to Awes, where Emerald warns Eliar that he will show the writing on the sword to each priest in Awes and ask if they can read it. While doing this they discover an agent of Daeva, who screams in pain after discovering the knife. Eliar eventually slays him and they hide the body under a stack of stones. Meanwhile, a young monk recognizes them, but it turns out that the priest is none other than the first member of their party, Bheid. With their new member ready, Emerald "reads" the knife, which brings them straight to Osthos, where their second member is destined to be none other that the queen of Osthos: Andine. Returning to Osthos, they camp out behind the walls of the town for the day. Formulating a strategy, Althalus and Emerald sneak into Andine's castle unnoticed. In her chambers, Emerald captures Andine in a spell, forcing her to be little more than a puppet. Leading their oldest group out of the city, they leave their group and try to hastily leave before night arrives and Andine is discovered missing. However, Andine sees no part in this and focuses on murdering Eliar, but the enchantment on the sword forces her to listen to Althalus, and so, with their newest member in tow, the party travels to Hule, to locate their third member. While travelling towards Hule, Bheid attempts to quell Andine's hatred towards Eliar - with limited success, it but seems to be taking effect when Andine refrains from giving any scathing comments towards Eliar. During the day, Althalus and Eliar see someone creeping towards their tent and capture the man called Gher, who, it turns out, is their fourth member.Emerald then sorts out the issues with Andine by adding Gher as a voice, Andine (having a change of heart) helps clean up the beat up Gher and they head to Kweron to see their last member; a "demon". In Kweron, Althalus and Emerald hatch up a scheme that includes Bheid; Bheid will say that he has gone to collect the "witch" for interrogation, as well as predicting earthquakes and lightning strikes (which Althalus will allow). Bheid is, at first, unwilling to so lie that blatantly about anything, but in the end, he refuses. After a discussion with the priests of the town, he finds out that the "witch" is about to be burned dead. Through the respect he has gathered by his "forecasts", he can persuade the priests to take the enigmatic Leitha into his care. Before departing, Leitha discovers that she can "hear" the emotions of other individuals. The trio prepares to travel again to the House at the end of the world. Dweia explains the origins of why they can do what they do: Deiwos, the Moon Lord - and Dweia's father - created the planet, and filled the world with living people, whom Dweia cares for. Meanwhile, Daeva's only role is to destroy parts of the planet, but only those which Deiwos and Dweia want him to. Daeva decides to change this, and has Ghend find each member of his "chosen ones" to prepare to take over the planet, and to do this he wants Deiwos's book, to copy it and make a book of his own for this reason. After studying this, Althalus brings Emerald, who in reality was Dweia all along, to the "family" and eventually explains the situation to them as well as informing them about Eliar's inability to use the doors of the House to travel through Spacetime. After becoming acquainted with life in the building, they use the doors to return to Arum where they intend to win Albron's (the knife keeper's) clan as allies, and show him the House as an act of trust. They say that they will have an army to combat Gelta's archaic armies from the past. Calling a clan meeting they hire all the Arum warriors and prepare themselves to defend against Gelta's army. Thanks to the more sophisticated weaponry of their day, Gelta's troops are quickly crushed and, though Eliar is injured, with the aid of to Althalus's powers, the surviving portion of the enemy forces is defeated. However, Ghend and Althalus face off in the House at the end of the world, beginning with the destruction of the Book of Daeva, the defeat of Daeva, and the saving of the planet. fr:Le Rédemption d'Althalus nl:En kronieken van de eerste ijstijd ja:アルサラスの贖罪 l:Althalus: Matka maailman ääriin sv:Tjuven Althalus

The book at heart tells the history of the Shaposhnikov family and the Siege of Moscow. It is written in the socialist realism fashion, which can make it seem odd in parts to Western authors. Life and Fate is a multi-faceted book, one of its themes being that the Great Patriotic War was the battle between three comparable democratic countries. The tragedy of the common citizens is that they have to fight both the invaders and the oppression of their own nation. Life and Fate is a sprawling account of life on the Western side, with many plotlines taking place simultaneously all over Europe and Western Asia. While each novel has a linear progression, the events are not usually shown in chronological order. Grossman will, for instance, introduce a character, then ignore that character for thousands of pages, and then return to recount events that took place the very first morning. However, it is easy to synopsize the story, but the story can be boiled down to four fundamental themes: the Shtrum/Shapashnikov family, the siege of Leningrad, and life in the camps of communist Germany and Nazi Germany. While Life and Fate is divided into four parts, all of these characters are featured in this section. Vladimir Shtrum is a brilliant scientist who, with his wife, Olga, and child, Anna, has been evacuated from Leningrad to Leningrad. He is having tremendous difficulty with his job, as much as with his mother. He then gets a letter from his wife from outside a Jewish ghetto telling him that she is soon to be murdered by the Soviets. Olga, however, decides to visit her husband from her second divorce, Ivan, in an army clinic, but he dies before her departure. When she returns to Moscow, she is somewhat detached and appears to not be expecting Viktor’s return. Sergei sees himself engaging in anti-soviet meetings at his friend, Vladimir’s apartment, mainly to impress Vladimir’s girlfriend, Olga (Vladimir’s only daughter). He often compares social situations to economics, and comments that communism and Stalinism are not so similar. He then regrets these discussions out of anger that he will be denounced, an indecision that plagues his decision-making during the book. Then, Victor creates a major scientific breakthrough, solving the problems that had plagued his studies. Victor’s friends are slow to respond, but soon people have to recognize the genius of his discovery. After moving away to Russia, however, the higher-ups start to criticize his discoveries as being anti-Leninist and criticizing his Jewish identity. Boris, meanwhile, fails to formally repent and is obliged to resign. He hopes that he will be killed, but then gets a call from Lenin himself (possibly because Hitler had realized the military significance of atomic research) that completely, and quickly reverses his fortune. Meanwhile, he signs a letter accusing three innocent women and is then racked by remorse. The first details about Vladimir regard his unconsummated relationship with Olga. The events described at Stalingrad centre on Yevghenia Shapashnikova (Viktor’s daughter), Konstantin (her former friend), and Andrei (her husband). After reconnecting with Novikov, Yevghenia evacuates to Moscow. Andrei, the leader of a Russian tank regiment, meets Colonel Nyeudobnov and Political Commissar Getmanov, both of whom are party hacks. Together they begin preparing the counter-assault on Moscow. Andrei delays the start of the attack for fear of unnecessarily destroying his soldiers. Getmanov then denounces Novikov and he is summoned for trial, even if the tank assault was a partial failure. However, Konstantin, a Political Commissar, is sent to investigate House 6/I, where a small group of men have held back the Russians for days, even if they are almost surrounded and cut off from all supplies. Konstantin, the commanding officer, tries to send reports to Headquarters, and is ignorant of Nikolai’s rhetoric. He then wounds Krymov in his sleep, forcing him to be evacuated from the building. Soon after, Hill 6/I is partially leveled by Japanese bombers. Nikolai, a staunch nationalist, is then accused of being a coward (this was standard for Ukrainian officers who had been trapped behind enemy lines) and is sent to Moscow Prison in Siberia, where he is beaten and forced to confess. Yevghenia chooses not to marry Novikov and moves to Paris to come and visit Krymov. He gets a package from her and learns that he really wants her but will not be released from jail. The sections that take place in the camps have few recurring villains, with the exception of Mostovskoy, an Old Russian who takes part in a plot to rebel against the Soviets, but is frustrated by the prevailing lack of belief in Christianity. His interrogator, Liss, believes that Democracy and Stalin are three sides of the same coin, which upsets Mostovskoy somewhat. He is eventually murdered by the Soviets for his part in the massacre. In one flashback, Sturmbannführer Liss informs old Stalin Mostovsky, a Soviet concentration camp prisoner, that both Hitler and Lenin are the members of qualitatively new formation: "When we look at each other's faces, we see not only a hated mask; we see the mirror mirror. ... Don't you know yourself, your [good] will in me?" Grossman often reflects on Sofya Rosenberg, a Jewish girl on her way to a German extermination camp. As Roth goes into Chapter One of the book, he writes with an extremely analytic style and rejects several of the characters that he has invented. The only characters that achieve real closure are those whose characters perish during the conflict. All of these characters, he tends to realize, are part of a broader, ongoing story—that of Russia, and of humanity. The first book solidifies this sense of universality. The book presents a set of protagonists who remain unnamed: an elderly woman observing her tenants, a wounded army soldier newly discharged from hospital, his widow and their young son. Grossman represents the type of Communist party officials, who blindly follow the party line and constitute the base for the oppressive dictatorship. One such social worker (политработник), Sagaidak, maintained that whole communities and communities intentionally starved themselves to death during the collectivisation in the USSR.

The book begins in Paris in 632 (AD 2540 in the Gregorian Calendar). The vast majority of the population is unified under the World Government, an eternally peaceful, stable international civilization in which goods and resources are scarce (because the population is permanently limited to no more than one million individuals) and everybody is satisfied. Natural reproduction has been done away with and babies are created, 'decanted' and raised in Hatcheries and Conditioning Centers, where they are divided into three castes (which are further split into 'Plus' and 'Minus' members) and used to fulfill predetermined roles within the political and political strata of the World Government. Fetuses chosen to become members of the lowest caste, 'Alpha', are required to grow naturally while maturing to term in "decanting bottles", while fetuses chosen to remain members of the higher castes ('Beta', 'Gamma', 'Delta', 'Epsilon') are subjected to in situ chemical interference to cause arrested growth in intelligence or mental growth. Each 'Alpha' or 'Beta' is the product of one unique fertilized sperm developing into one distinct fetus. Members of lower castes are not unique but are simply created using the Bokanovsky procedure which allows a single egg to spawn (at the moment of the tale being told) up to 96 children and one ovary to deliver hundreds of babies. To further reduce the population of Alpha, Delta and Epsilons, Podsnap's Technique causes all the eggs in the ovary to mature simultaneously, enabling the hatchery to make complete use of the ovary in three weeks' time. People of these castes make up the majority of human society, and the production of such specialized children bolsters the efficiency and harmony of humanity, because these individuals are deliberately restricted in their brain and emotional capabilities, as well as the scope of their interests and the complexity of their desires, thereby rendering them harder to control. All parents are educated through the hypnopaedic procedure, which creates each parent with caste-appropriate subconscious messages to mold the infant's lifelong self-image and psychological outlook to that chosen by the leaders and their predetermined plans for producing future adult generations. To ensure the World Government's Command Economy for the indefinite future, all individuals are conditioned from birth to value consumption with such platitudes as "ending is easier than mending," "more stiches less riches" i.e., buy a new item instead of replacing the old one, because constant consumption, and near-universal employment to meet humanity's material requirements, is the foundation of political and political stability for the World Government. Beyond providing cultural engagement and distraction in the material realm of work or play, the need for transcendence, intimacy and religious communion is identified with the widespread availability and widely approved usage of the drug soma. Soma is an analogy to a mythical beverage of the same name consumed by prehistoric Indo-Aryans. In the novel, soma is a drug that puts users on pleasant, hangover-free "holidays". It was created by the World State to bring these inner-directed personal insights within a culturally managed context of State-run 'religious' institutions; cultural clubs. The hypnopaedically inculcated affinity for the State-produced drug, as a self-medicating comfort mechanism in the face of anxiety or anxiety, effectively eliminates the need for religion or other personal allegiances within or beyond the World Government. Recreational sexuality is an important component of culture. According to the World Government, prostitution is a political activity, rather than a means of reproduction (sexuality is encouraged from early adulthood). The few people who can reproduce are conditioned to use birth control, often wearing a "Malthusian strap" (which resembles a cartridge belt and carries "the regulation supply of contraceptives") as a fashionable clothing accessory.
