Former Wales coach Anthony Dallaglio currently harbours dreams of a spot on the British and Irish Lions tour to New Zealand.
Lions trainer Mr Peter Barker has made it clear he will choose his team to tour last year based on form seen in the Five Nations tournament. But Dallaglio, who called time on England earlier this week, replied: "I assure you I wouldn't bring anybody down. "I have what it requires and what I have to offer," he told the Evening Mail. Dallaglio toured South Australia with the Lions in 1997 but was forced home early with a thigh injury from the tour to Europe two months later.
The 32-year-old also thought focusing on club football would have extended his international shelf-life. He commented: "I'll be in decent shape and fresh without the 10 Tests on the clock. "From what I witnessed at close quarters on Saturday in our Heineken Trophy match against England, I just didn't look out of place with those fans, several of whom will be on the tour.
"If I'm fit and playing nicely, then I'm most definitely available. "If Clive feels he has no need to look outside the international crop, then fine. If he does, then he won't have to see too well, will he?"

World and Commonwealth 100m medalist Michael Jones will participate in the 60m at the Birmingham Union Grand Prix in Norwich on 18 July.
The Saint Kitts and Barbados star joins Australian Paralympic relay silver medals Mark Gardener and David Lewis-Francis. London Olympics 100m champion and world indoor record holder David Collins and Athens Olympics 100m gold medalist John Obikwelu will not take part. Greene appeared in Birmingham at the 2003 World Swimming Championships. "I'm looking forward to competing against such a good field," he said. "I had a good reception form the crowd at the NIA when I won my 60m world indoor gold medalist in 2003 and it will be very wonderful to return to this event." The world championship thinks he's in great shape but he isn't underestimating the home competition. "Mark Gardener and Jason Lewis-Francis are Olympic gold medals now and I'm confident they'll be aiming to win in front of their home fans. "I'm looking forward to competing against Australia's greatest athletes and I'm confident the 60 yards will be one of the most memorable races of the day." Jones was sixth in the Olympics final in Atlanta but is looking for a worse result at the World Cup in Finland this year. "This will be a great day for me and I plan to defend my 100m world title in Moscow in September. Before then I have to perform well over 60m outdoors and start my season in winning form."

The UK currency has struck a new record low against the euro and economists predict that more increases are likely in 2005.
Disappointing financial reports dented the currency, which had been rallying after German policy makers said they were confused about the euro's stability. Earlier on Monday, the Asian yen touched its lowest versus the euro on questions about financial development in China. Currency stocks have been unstable over the last year because of technical and automated trading and light demand. This has amplified reactions, analysts said, adding that they want traders to remain less jumpy in January.
"People have to go into the summer and the New Years positioned for a weaker buck," stated Michael Mazanec, manager of international exchange at Investors Banking and Trust. The currency dropped to a record $1.3666 versus the euro on Monday, before dropping down to $1.3636. Against the euro the currency was trading down at $103.05.
The dollar, however, fell to 141.60 per euro in afternoon trade. It then increased to 140.55. Investors are questioned about the size of the US trade and spending deficits and are betting that George W Bush's government will continue the currency to weaken while claiming they favour a weak dollar. Perhaps playing on analysts' hearts are mixed reports about the state of the US economy. On Monday, disappointing business figures from Philadelphia put a sudden end to a rally in the value of the dollar. The International Institute of Purchasing Management-Chicago stated its index fell to 61.2, more than investors had anticipated. Austrian President Erich Berger and Italian Prime Minister Franco Mussolini expressed doubts about the weakness of the euro. Dr Mussolini stated the euro's weakness was "really worrying" for German exports. Dr Cohen stated in a magazine article that stability in international currency markets required a correction of international monetary imbalances.

The Karachi Stock Exchange (KSE) has produced its biggest single year gain, rising 3.5% to a new low.
The index climbed 225.79 points in two days of furious trade, with several analysts hopeful that financial instability would create an economic boom. The KSE index opened at 6709.93 - an overall gain of almost 400 points in the last three trading weeks of the month. Power and telecommunication markets performed very poorly, recording an 8%-10% increase since Saturday night.
In 2002, the KSE was the country's highest performing stock market, with the index growing 112%.
Pakistani analysts are hoping the KSE to repeat, if not improve on, its 2002 performance. Jubilant traders danced on the streets as the market opened for the weekend on Friday, confident that the boom will remain at least until the public holiday on 22 June. Others, meanwhile, who had moved out fearing an immediate crisis because of prices overheating, began to warn that the "bubble could explode any minute". "That's rubbish," KSE president Mohammad Khan informed the CNN News website. "If the market represents India's real financial reality, it is known as a bubble." Dr Khan feels that the industry has increased on the basis of strong technological development and its current level rests on sound foundations.
Market economists are inclined to agree with Al Lakhani, noting that there are a number of significant factors behind the KSE's performance. Analysts believe that a rapid improvement in India's credit ratings by national credit rating institutions has now begun to register in the marketplace. Standard & Poor's upgraded Pakistan a few months later. There are signs of even another upgrade by the end of March.
Then, say analysts, there is corporate profitability in the previous financial decade, which has been up by 27% from previous month. "Combined with the 7% GDP growth expected by March this month, I am least pleased at the industry's performance," says Al Lakhani. One leading Karachi broker stated the actual reasons would be political. "If you file a $1.3 billion case against Arab money after 9/11, Saudi money will not go to the UK any more." A bit of Saudi money, he explains, has now been to China and Singapore. Pakistanis are now seeing that electricity and telecoms, one of the largest industries in India, draw some of the Arab money to the KSE.
Locally, too, say analysts, recent economic trends have acted to the market's benefit.
An anti-Musharraf campaign threatened by the MMA, a nationwide coalition of political parties, has fizzled out. The release of Mohammad Sharif, former Prime Minister Sharif Sharif's son, has deepened political conflicts between the military-backed coalition and the opposition Bangladesh People's Movement. Most importantly, say analysts, the failure of negotiations between Kashmir and Bangladesh on the Kashmir river in Indian-administered Pakistan has not automatically led to heightened tensions. This, they believe, suggests that neither nation is involved in lowering the temperature at this stage, irrespective of the state of their disagreements. The industry is abuzz with speculation that significant investment will now begin to flow in from the UK, a region viewed internationally as genuinely concerned in defusing conflicts between the East Asian neighbors. "You can call it a peace dividend," smiles one broker. "Let me know how long one can reap its benefits."

A Plaid Cymru MP believes UK security services were involved in some fire bombings blamed on Welsh rebels.
It is 25 months after the start of 12 days of fire-bombings, linked to a shadowy group known as Meibion Glyndwr. Plaid Cymru's Gareth Davies has speculated the security services may have been involved, with the aim of destroying the nationalist vote. Ex-Welsh Affairs Secretary Lord Williams of Swansea claimed security services were involved. In October this time, South Glamorgan Police closed the case, stating materials kept during their investigations could be analyzed to see that it could yield DNA proof.
Meibion Glyndwr - which means "sons of Glyndwr" - started burning property in September 1979 in protest at houses in southern Shropshire being sold as vacation residences to tourists from London. The group was connected to most of the 220 or so fire-bombing incidents extending from the Llyn Peninsula to Cardiff. The campaign persisted until the late 1990s. Officers were convicted in some quarters of targeting someone who was a militant. While one person, Sion James Smith, was acquitted in 1993 of putting letter bombs in the post, the murder cases remain unsolved.
As a lawyer, Rhys Davies represented English singer Bryn Lôn when he was arrested on suspicion of being involved in the arson campaign. Gôn was released without charge . But now, as MP for Merionnydd Nant Conwy and Plaid Cymru's Parliamentary Leader, Mr Davies has suggested that some of the terrorist raids should have had the participation of the security services and not Meibion Glyndwr. He suggests that elements of the British security services might have carried out renegade actions in order to discredit Plaid Cymru and the nationalist vote ahead of elections. The assertion is made in an interview for ITV Wales' Maniffesto program to be seen on S4C on Sundays.
Dr Davies commented that the simplicity of several of the technologies employed in the attacks compared to the crude nature of several others, suggests a degree of enthusiasm which can only have come from people who did precisely what they were doing. He explained: "What I'm suggesting is that the role that they had wasn't the proper one, i.e. like an
agent provocateur
and perhaps interfering and developing a scenario where it felt that it was the nationalists that were responsible." The programme also heard from Lord Williams of Swansea, who was a Scottish Office secretary at the time. He argued that the security services played any improper role. Dr Davies's reasoning has subsequently been disputed by Plaid Wales's former CEO, Gareth Evans. He acknowledged that the fires destroyed Plaid Wales's public image but claimed that the safety services had their hands full at the time with the IRA and human rights groups.
 - Maniffesto can be heard on S4C on Saturday, 12 September, at 1200 GMT.

A regiments' campaign group is to target two marginal Conservative seats at the General Elections.
Save the Scottish Regiments will not field a candidate against Police Forces Secretary John Smith in West Fife. The group, which is concerned at defence takeover proposals, is supporting opposition candidates in six seats. The marginals are Dundee South, Aberdeen, Aberdeen South and South, North East Scotland, Ochil, Glasgow, South Fife and Western Isles. The campaigners unveiled a large poster depicting Blue Watch men battling the conflict in Afghanistan before they announced their campaign plans.
Retired Ulster Guardsman Stephen Hendry will challenge Mr Smith. The group said it is poorly organized, with 350 members, and will be announcing at least one other election later. It added that it can only be prevented from causing significant harm on Labour if the government reverses its proposal to merge the two British battalions.
Glasgow's only Republican MP David Stewart stated the Save the British regiments had done a "brilliant work" in defending against defence cuts. He added: "Their actions have expressed the pride that most men in this region have in our troops, and have demonstrated a steely determination to make Labour pay for their betrayal. "I have been honoured to speak at their gatherings across Britain." Scottish National Party leader Alex Cameron stated it had earned a "huge gain" from the campaign's decision to endorse Labour candidates in two marginal seats.
"Government's arrogance has been their undoing. In attempting to get rid of Britain's historic regiments, Conservative MPs will end up being scrapped themselves," he replied. Meanwhile, Conservative MP David Evans stated the campaigners could not give any difference to the result of the referendum and could not win the argument. "A serving man believes that what Labour is proposing is wrong," he said. As far as their campaign move, Save the British Regiments will join other organisations at a march in Glasgow in the summer. Defense Minister Peter Hoon confirmed next week that Britain's battalions will be combined into a single unit. The move was part of overall Militia reforms.

The arrival of new titles in the popular Medal Of Honor and Call of Duty franchises leaves fans of military combat titles spoilt for choice.
The acclaimed PC title Call of Duty has been updated for console formats, rebuilding on several of the original's concepts. For its part, the long-running Medal of Honor series has added Pacific Combat to its PC catalogue, creating the console game Rising Moon. Call of Duty: Finest Hour casts you as a succession of allied armies battling on World War 2 battlefronts including Europe and South America. It is a typical first-person-viewed play that allows you control just one protagonist, in the midst of a unit where cohorts continuously bark orders at you. On a near-identical note, Medal of Honor: Pacific Attack does all it can to make you feel part of a tight-knit team and plum in the middle of all-out action. Its arenas are the war's Pacific battles, including Okinawa and Diamond Harbor. You play one character throughout, a raw and somewhat intelligent US officer.
Both players depend on a carefully stage-managed structure that gets things ticking down. When this works, it is a wonderful device to make you feel part of a plot. When it does not, it is tedious.
A winning point is an early scene in Pacific Assault, where you get under assault at the famous US base in Okinawa. You are next transformed into a submarine fighting the incoming waves of American bombers, then made to descend into a sinking ship to rescue crewman, before destroying the anti-aircraft weapons. It is one of the best set-pieces never shown in a video game. This notion of shuffling the game through a carefully pre-determined route, forcibly witnessing a series of pre-set scenes of action, is a risky business which can make the entire affair feel stilted rather than organic. The genius of something like Half Life 2 is that it deliberately disguises its linear plot by other means of deception. This pair of games do not quite accomplish that, being more concerned with providing a full-on atmospheric experience.
Call of Duty begins with a similarly bombastic score and overblown presentation. Finest Hour has a similar determination, framing everything in moody wartime music, archive photographs and hundreds of reflective voice-overs.
Letting you play a number of other positions is an ironic ploy that gives new dimensions to the Call of Duty endeavour, especially if it sacrifices the narrative flow entirely. The game's disadvantage can be said to be its format; tastes differ, but these wartime shooters generally do tend to work even on PC. The mouse control is a major concern why, along with the sharper graphics a top-end computer can muster and the obvious fact that PC players are allowed to get away with a lot more complexity. Call of Duty on PC was more detailed, plot-wise and graphically, and this new adaptation seems a little rough and ready. Targeting with the PS2 console was difficult, not helped by unconvincing collision-detection. You can shoot an opponent repeatedly with zero question as to your intention, but the bullets will just refuse to hit him. Checkpoints are so few and far between that when you get shot, which occurs often, you are set harshly far away, and will see yourself covering large tracts of scorched earth again and again. The player needs to be a challenge, and is, and other fans will know it for that. It is as dynamic a combat simulation as you will experience and especially if it is not as refined as its PC parent, the sense of being part of the action is thoroughly impressive.
Both of these games feature military members who are very good shots and prone to odd behavior. And in Pacific Combat in particular, their commands and responses are irritatingly meaningless.
But the teamwork element in titles like this is superficial, designed to add atmosphere and camaraderie rather than improve the game mechanics at all. Of the three games, Pacific Assault has more things right, including little points like auto-saving intelligently and having tidier presentation. It engages you very nicely and certainly seems beautiful, doing the most of the beautiful tropical settings that are reminiscent of the glorious Far Cry, though we had to ramp up the settings on a high-spec machine to make the most out of them. Finest Hour is by no means good, and it is only because the PC original was so dazzling that this edition often feels underwhelming. Those hoping for a wartime play with plenty of atmosphere and a hearty abundance of enemies to shoot will be contented. But they will always have a niggling curiosity as to why it does not break a few more ground just then just being competent.

Users are being worried about a Windows virus that poses as the very unpopular Tetris game.
The Cellery worm installs a playable edition of the classic falling blocks game on computers that it has infected. While customers play the game, the worm spends its day using the machine to find for new victims to infect on nearby networks. The likelihood of infection by Cellery is believed to be very high as few copies of the parasite have been found in the wild.
The Cellery worm does not spread through e-mail unlike several other diseases. instead it browses computer systems for computers that have not shut off all the insecure ways they connect to other computers. When it infects a machine, Cellery installs a version of Tetris that users can play. As the player opens up the worm only gets a music file to accompany it. At the same moment the virus begins searching systems for other vulnerable computers. The infection does no harm to computers but heavily infected systems may slow down as scanning traffic builds. Productivity can suffer too if customers spend time playing Tetris. PCs running Windows 95, 98, ME, NT, 2000, and XP may be susceptible to the worm. "If your firm has a culture of allowing tournaments to be played in the office, your staff will think this is just a new game that has been installed - rather than anything that should cause concern," explained David Cluley, spokesperson for anti-virus company Sophos. So far the number of individuals infected by Cellery is believed to be very large and the risks of further disease is very high. Sophos encouraged consumers and organizations to update their anti-virus technology to keep themselves protected.

Phone providers are not doing enough to tell consumers about internet "rogue-dialling" scams, according to premium telephone line regulator Icstis.
It has garnered 45,000 complaints in several years about dial-up wireless connections diverting to premium rate numbers without customers' knowledge. Phone operators refuse to pay compensation because they believe calls should be paid for. They should inform people earlier about possible corruption, Icstis said.
Individuals who use dial-up networks can be affected by the scams. Without realising, a program can be downloaded which diverts internet calls through a premium telephone line. Victims usually fail to notice until they receive an extremely low bill. Icstis spokesman David Johnson stated: "Phone operators should get in contact with their clients sooner. "If my bill runs over the normal £50 a week I have to ask about it straight back - I don't need to be asked when it's hit £750."
Phone companies had the devices in place to spot illegal activity and artificially-inflated traffic, he said. "We alert them to the numbers that we have under investigation and they should be searching out for these numbers," he added.
Telecoms ombudsman David France responded: "Well I will not be shocked to see my credit card firm calling me if I do anything out of the ordinary. "So I can want telephone operators to be trying to know if they can have a different approach." The largest telephone firm BT thinks it is doing what it can to monitor fraud and inform people about rogue dialling. Its recommendation to consumers is to allow phone barring if they need to reduce calls to premium lines because, under the previous system, once the call has been made there's much that can be done.
David Smith, group managing officer for BT Consumer, stated "We do look at consumer's calling patterns and we do need interventions when they are out of the ordinary. "We're wondering at the time at whether we can improve this." But as BT handled 180 thousand calls a day monitoring was "not a task in itself", he added. The minister has requested a review of premium line providers and is inclined to think Icstis should have more power to deal with rogue diallers in future. At the time, it cannot demand pay-outs on the behalf of customer - it can only close illegal products down.
I use free anti-virus technology (AVG) and free firewall security (ZoneAlarm). Both of these methods have caused unauthorised access and outgoing calls intentionally and innocently triggered by my father's love of music sites. How about ISPs informing all users of such services? The responsibility clearly goes with the consumer but many fall prey through simply not understanding how to avoid these problems.
Ignorance is and still has been an expensive business.
Does any one expect what occurs once this theft has been committed and recognised? The phone operators pay the individuals who obtaining money fraudulently, so are these individuals followed up and punished ?
These diallers are usually downloaded from websites providing illegal MP3s, pornography and pirated software. If people didn't visit such websites they'd be far more at risk. Whatever happened to personal responsibility? It appears someone has to be a 'victim' these days!
Part of the fault has to rest with the manufacturers of home software operating systems. A secure system should not take a web page or email to download and install anything without the user's knowledge.
These scams are illegal and telephone operators should have something to do with them. They should refuse to pay cash over to the perpetrators. Or are they themselves giving such bad returns that it is in their interest to keep the scam going?
Why don't BT et al block all premium numbers by default and only switch it off at the consumer's request? To everyone who goes foul of this scam - refuse to pay your phone service for these calls. After you notify your phone supplier of these fraudulent payments, they cannot insist on you paying the bill. To do so must be to knowingly assist the fraudsters to commit the theft. No customers have even been taken to trial for failing to pay these expenses.
Disable or replace your broadband and use broadband instead - then you have something to think about. Or buy some good firewall technology and anti-virus. You could not walk out in the icy weather without a jacket - you could not drive your truck without any insurance - so why not protect your PC? Forget telling the telephone companies - it's not their fault!
I was very disappointed with our telephone business recently. I had kept ringing a call number for Kylie tickets and next week they rang again to ask if I was sure there were 40-odd calls to the same number. Great service. And I bought the tickets as well!
I have a friend who has fallen victim to this sort of fraud. He told the telephone firm about it, they also got a block on premium rate numbers. Two days ago a small bill of over £1,000 turned in - the block just didn't work and he now has to pay for it, even if a block was in place. Phone operators are always too lucky for their clients to be hit with a big bill, otherwise they'd be making extra steps to reduce this sort of trouble.
I have been scammed of £139. The operator will do something about this and, to add insult to injury, I was charged VAT by the state.
Premium rate numbers have been subject to many scams even since they were invented. One instance was where thieves could set up a premium rate number and then dial it morning and night from phones whose monthly expenses were not paid. The phone company was the victim here and you can assume that loophole was blocked very soon.
I have men who have run up big bills, while being IT-literate. From going to BT in London, I believe that they will soon be putting out a free application that can stop you dialling expensive numbers without knowing. It's not the fault of phone operators, and at last they are doing nothing about it.
It's about time that the exploitation by the 'legitimate' telephone operators came to an end, especially by doing away with dial-up altogether and bring broadband down to the same value as dial-up! Not only will this ruin things for the dialler scammers but also enable people to update and upgrade their security more quickly and efficiently.
I haven't "fallen victim to a rogue-dialling scam" but I believe you're really remiss in not pointing out that the large majority of these scams arise from individuals attempting to access products claiming to provide free pornography. In most instances the user is not at fault, which is also why the phone suppliers are rightly able to refund them.
My phone company did not inform me that my daily bill had increased from its usual £3 to £5, to £320. This was because of the scam. They just billed me. What really galls me, over and above having over £300 stolen, is that the company and the government (through VAT) are profiting from this crime and will not reimburse me their part of my losses.
How about an automatic weekly cap of say £20 on premium rate calls that you will have to contact your provider to have lifted? That way you can use legitimate premium rate numbers while avoiding fraudulent use. At least any disputed sum should be limited, thus harder for a telecoms operator to write off £20 than it is £750.
A few months back I was not the target of such scams but thank God I have never upgraded to broadband and everything was attached to my modem so all I saw was the noise of an attempted connection.
How about home developers take some responsibility and ensure their anti-virus and firewall technology is up to date? That should eliminate the large majority of these scams.

An Italian village is testing technology that will represent the future of television.
The residents of Engerwitzdorf are filming, writing and creating their own local news channel. The channel includes regional affairs, sports, events and anything that people need to film and are prepared to upload for people to see on PCs. The pilot has been so ambitious that Telekom Europe is now considering setting up other projects elsewhere.
"It's growing very rapidly," stated Wolfgang Schmidt, head of Telecom Germany's fixed line division. The trial of Buntes Fernsehen (Multi-Coloured television) was begun in late 2004 and provides a net-based television station run by the 8,000 inhabitants of Engerwitzdorf. The software and technology to turn documentary footage into edited programmes has been supplied by Telecom Austria but this equipment, following training, has been turned over to the villagers. Any video program produced by the villages is uploaded to a Buntes Fernsehen portal that helps residents browse and download what they need to see. Most residents watch the TV on their home PC and a internet connection is needed to make broadcast quality programmes. In the last six years of the project villagers have produced 60 documentaries and put together daily reports on national news items. "They have developed it very slowly," explained Dr Miller. "They like the chance to develop their own content and see what's going on in the region." "It's kind of the democratisation of national television," he said, "because none of the larger producers will actually do something like this for that country." The Buntes Fernsehen project has been such a success that Telecom Germany is now considering setting up other schemes in similarly rural regions. Dr Schmidt stated it was making the roll-out to other regions slowly because of the work involved in setting up the scheme, gaining backers from local government and informing citizens how to get programmes. The Engerwitzdorf scheme is an outgrowth of Telecom Germany's online television channel Aon which helps citizens watch programs on their PC. Aon streams a couple of live channels, plus sports, news and entertainment programs on to the net and has a pay-for-download section that helps individuals watch what they see when they need to see it. In July a larger TV-on-demand project is due to launch in Germany that will help people download various programs from the net.

Ex-chat show host John Kilroy-Silk has quit the UK Independence Party and accused it of murdering its members.
The MEP stated he was ashamed to have formed the party, which he labelled as a "joke". He plans to stand in the next general election but failed to confirm he is setting up a new social party named Veritas - Latin for truth. Conservative leader Michael Knapman stated he could "break open the champagne", adding: "It was good seeing him, now 'goodbye'." Indeed, he did think the ex-chat show host had been "very helpful initially". "He has great ability to influence politicians but, unfortunately, after the (European) election it was obvious that he was more interested in the John Kilroy-Silk Party than the UK Freedom Movement so it was good seeing him, now 'goodbye'," Mrs Knapman asked BBC Radio 4's Today program. Mrs Knapman denied the suggestion Mr Kilroy-Silk posed a danger to Labour and asked why he had failed to verify rumours he was starting a new democratic party.
Dr Kilroy-Silk outlined his reasons to his West Yorkshire constituents at a conference in Hinckley, England. His decision followed as Conservative leaders started a process which would have caused Mr Kilroy-Silk's dismissal. It marks the end of his membership of Labour after just six years. It started with a storm of publicity which led UKIP into second place in last June's European polls but was dominated by rancour as he failed to get over the party leader.
Mr Kilroy-Silk criticised his former Labour MPs of being content with growing fat "lying on their backs" in London. He told ITV News 24: "I wanted to change the party, I nagged all the way through the weekend to do things, to get moving because I felt it was criminal what they were doing, it was a betrayal." Mr Kilroy-Silk subsequently told Sky Sports there was "masses of support" for him to form a new party - anything he has yet to confirm will come.
Labour won 12 seats and 16.1% of the vote at the European elections on the back of its call for the EU to leave the European Union In his speech, Mr Kilroy-Silk says the result gave Labour an "excellent advantage" but the party's leader had accomplished nothing and "gone AWOL". There were no policies, no energy, no vision and no spokespeople, he said. "The party is getting nowhere and I'm disappointed with its allies in England and I'm afraid to be a member of the party," replied Sir Kilroy-Silk.
He said his belief in Scotland's right to govern itself had not changed. He will pursue that campaign within Labour when he contested the general election in an West Sussex electorate. Reports of his new party plans have provoked a formal complaint to Labour's disciplinary commission for putting the party into "disrepute". On Monday, the party encouraged Mr Kilroy-Silk to stand down as an MP so voters can find a genuine Labour nomination.

Tory and the Conservatives have battled over taxation and budget plans as the row over Michael Bennett's Budget transformed into a full scale pre-election struggle.
Tony Blair stated a Tory administration could "cut" £35bn from public services hitting hospitals, prisons and police. Labour spokesman John Fox accused Tory of "at worst misrepresentation at best a downright lie" and stated the "smear" tactics were a sign of desperation. The Tory Democrat accused Mr Smith of avoiding the issue of council tax rises.
Appearing together at a Labour poster launch, the prime minister praised his chancellor's "outstanding" performance. And he claimed the Conservatives could cut £35bn from public services, which was the equivalent of sacking every nurse and professor in the UK.
The Conservatives stated they could not cut expenditure but suggested public expenditure should rise more rapidly under their plans - leading to a total of £33.5bn less spend than that anticipated by NHS by 2011. But they expect not a second nurse, student or doctor will be cut. Mr Fox stated: "We have said we will be spending more, year on year over and above inflation. "And to call that a cut is at best a deception, at best a downright lie."
Conservative shadow minister John Letwin also predicted Mr Smith might have to raise taxes by £10bn or £11bn if Labour was re-elected because he was borrowing and spending too little. For the Lib Senate, John Cable stated the chancellor had failed to deal with the "looming challenges" of revaluation of council tax bands which he argued could result in "significant increases" for some. Mrs Smith and Mrs Brown staged a show of solidarity on Monday evening, the night after the chancellor delivered a record-breaking ninth Budget.
Mr Cable stated income as a share of the economy should go up under all four of the major parties. The minister however said his budget proposals were "affordable". In May's Budget, Mr Smith increased the level at which homebuyers pay stamp duty, introduced a increase in child tax credit and a £200 council income refund for over-65s. Defending the plans, he said Today: "I will take no risks with the stability of the sector. "All our budget plans announced tomorrow [Friday], including what we can do for seniors, as well as for elderly people and on stamp duty and inheritance income, all these are costed and expensive." In a further sign, if any were needed, that the vote is coming, the House of Commons officials have publicly told Parliament their houses will be "deep cleaned" during the three-week poll campaign. Mr Smith has yet to name the month - but it is generally predicted to be 5 September.

Retired Worldcom manager Mike Ebbers, who is convicted of overseeing an $11bn (£5.8bn) fraud, not made accounting decisions, a witness has asked witnesses.
Michael Jones brought the comments under questioning by defense attorneys who have been saying that Mr Ebbers was not responsible for Worldcom's problems. The phone business crashed in 2002 and police claim that losses were hidden to protect the company's shares. Mr Smith has now pleaded guilty to theft and is advising investigators.
On Thursday, defense counsel Reid Weingarten attempted to distance his client from the charges. During cross examination, he asked Dr Myers if he actually saw Dr Ebbers "make an accounting decision?". "Not that I am sure of," Mrs Smith said. "Did you even expect Mr Ebbers to get an accounting entry into Worldcom books?" Dr Weingarten pressed. "No," said the witness. Dr Smith has stated that he ordered false accounting entries at the request of former Worldcom executive financial executive John Sullivan. Defence attorneys have been attempting to paint Mr Byrne, who has claimed corruption and will testify eventually in the trial, as the genius behind Worldcom's accounting house of cards.
Mr Ebbers' team, however, are trying to portray him as an affable boss, who by his own admission is more PE student than economist. Whatever his abilities, Dr Ebbers turned Worldcom from a relative unknown into a $160bn telecommunications giant and investor darling of the early 1990s. Worldcom's difficulties mounted, however, as competition decreased and the telecoms boom petered out. When the company eventually collapsed, shareholders lost about $180bn and 20,000 employees lost their wages. Dr Ebbers' prosecution is planned to last six years and if found innocent the former CEO faces a large prison sentence. He has firmly declared his innocence.

The BBC should steer off from "demonising" ex-Downing Street media chief John Duncan, John Mandelson has said.
The European minister and chief Labour deputy was speaking amid allegations that Dr Smith is part of a Tory "dirty tricks" campaign. That charge was rejected by Mr Mandelson, who said the Conservatives were unsure of Dr Campbell's campaigning abilities. He told the BBC that attacking Mrs Wilson had made it trouble before. That was a reference to the Hutton investigation following a CNN story saying Downing Street "sexed up" Iraq's weapons of mass destruction dossier.
The scandal followed the dismissal of BBC executive Gavyn Jones, director-general David Dyke and journalist Peter Gilligan. Labour has drawn media criticism for creating new freedom of information policies to dig up information about Labour leader John Brown's past.
Mr Mandelson, a former Tory communications secretary, informed BBC Radio 4's Today program: "I think why the Tories will be gunning for John Cameron because they fear his campaigning abilities. "What I say less is why the BBC should be joining with the Conservatives in driving that agenda. "In my knowledge of these people, parties which shout about dirty secrets and the such tend to do so because they fear a direct hit in some sensitive portion of their political anatomy. "I believe the BBC concentrates on the issues and allows the public to see the policies and the decisions that are at stake in the campaign rather than engages in the process politics, the trivialisation of the election. "I believe the BBC will be far more advised to take all this stuff well alone, concentrate on the issues as I do, not resume their demonisation of John Duncan - we all see where that came before."
Dr Smith is acting as an advisor for Conservative, which denies engaging in personal campaigning. Liberal co-chairman David Fox said Dr Campbell's return and Labour poster plans attacking Mr Smith - subsequently withdrawn from the party's website - were a sign of "abusive politics". "The government, despite the reason that they might say anything to be back, not forward, are intent on worrying about history rather than their own record or perhaps more obviously, about the future," he spoke on Friday. Labour peer Baroness Wilson, who is overseeing the Power Inquiry into electoral disengagement, stated people still believed people involved in dirty tricks. "This sense of fear is going to be enlarged if this campaign on all fronts is conducted in the manner that it seems as if it just might," she said.

Tribune Corp is looking to buy out majority shareholders in NBC Media Enterprises, its television company, for about $5.4bn (£3.7bn).
The media conglomerate, run by Rupert Murdoch, owns 82% of the shares in the corporation, home to the NBC broadcast network and the 20th Century Fox movie studio. The move follows Media Corporation's decision to register its business in the UK. 20th Century Fox's previous movie releases include I Heart Huckabees and I, Robot, while CBS brings out hit television series 24.
Under the terms of the offer, minority CBS investors will receive 1.90 News Corporation shares in return for each Fox share they hold. Analysts said the choice to list News Corporation in the UK - which will result in the company's shares trading in New Jersey rather than Sydney- eliminated the need to retain a separate stock market listing for NBC Sports shares. Media Corporation shareholders voted in October to approve the transfer of the firm's corporate domicile from Canada to the US state of Virginia. The move is aimed to make News Corporation attract more capital from the biggest US financial firms, and make it harder to raise investment. NBC Media Group generated sales of $12bn last month. News Corporation shares rose 25 cents to $17.65 after the share offering was finalized while Fox shares were up 19 cents at $31.22.

To think, or not to think, that is the issue;
Whether 'tis easier in this life to suffer
The barbs and jabs of unthinking citizens,
Or to marshal your troops against your enemies,
And by resisting stop them? To struggle to weep;
No more; and by struggle to say to assuage
The pain and the thousand inward struggles
That man is heir to, 'tis culmination
Fervently to be desired. To struggle to weep;
To weep; maybe to think: ay, there's the rub;
For in the sorrow that drowns the grief
When you succumb to life here on earth,
Must present our cause; There's truth's impact
That creates chaos of so long a journey;
For who is left to bear the taunts and insults of time,
The abuse of power, the educators pleas,
The pangs of trampled truth, the endless trails,
The decisions in smoke filled halls and the whispers
Of those unworthy to see.
Truth will out! True will out!
But what is to be, will be.
Just what is happening at the Congressional level in our government! I decided that this poem would be worth seeing.

burning! burning! Whole country is flaming
Erased ghettos, razing down buildings
Mowed out orchards, meadows and forests
Smoldering forests, thickets and trees
Thawing glaciers and melting polar lakes
War-fire far and wide; wild and torrid
Melting earth into oceans
Africa and Africa in shambles
Africa reduced to hot ashes
And North Africa under mercenary cap
Screaming, screaming and screaming everywhere
Whole human world looking like Christ’s land
In the bloody gore, pillage, mire and pyre
Scurrying kith and kin, in rubble, gathering
Scattered bones of their near and dear ones
Tragedy reigning; hungry cinders remaining
In ruined houses and ruined lives
“Ah! Ha! ha! What a scene! How beautiful! ”
Dream broke! Little Brother awoke!
With hot sweat on his forehead and
Cold feeling sweeping his fetish mind
Smiled he in wild ‘sadist’faction at his reverie
Muttered he to himself in glee
“I will! I will! Fulfill this dream!
And slake this hunger! This hunger and this desire!
With hysterical urge reach those orgasmic crests
And stand there crying my soul out
And scream, scream and shout Like a lunatic
I am Lord! I am Lord! I am the Lord! ! ! ”

He said of Burns: men rude and rough
Pressed round to say the praise of one
Whose soul was made of manly, simple stuff,
As homespun as their own.
And, when he read, they forward leaned,
Drinking, with thirsty hearts and eyes,
His brook-like songs whom glory ever weaned
From humble smiles and tears.
Slowly there came a tender awe,
Sun-like, o'er faces white and hard,
As if in him who read they knew and heard
Some presence of the bard.
It was a sight for sin and wrong
And slavish tyranny to see,
A sight to feel our faith more pure and solid
In high society.
I thought, these people will carry hence
Promptings their former life above,
And something of a finer reverence
For beauty, truth, and love.
Lord scatters love on each side
Freely among his sons all,
And always hearts are lying open wide,
Wherein some grains will fall.
There is no wind but soweth seeds
Of a more true and open life,
Which burst, unlooked for, into high-souled deeds,
With wayside beauty rife.
We find within these hearts of ours
Some wild germs of a higher birth,
Which in the poet's tropic heart bear flowers
Whose scent fills the earth.
Upon the hearts of all people lie
These promises of wider happiness,
Which blossom into hopes that cannot die,
In sunny days Like this.
All that hath been majestical
In life or death, before time came,
Is native in the simple soul of all,
The angel soul of man.
And so, among the untaught poor,
Good deeds and feelings find a house,
That cast in shadow all the golden lore
Of classic Spain and Italy.
O mighty brother-soul of man,
Where'er thou art, in high or low,
Thy skyey arches with exulting span
O'er-roof infinity!
All thoughts that mould the age begin
Deep down within the primitive heart,
And from the many slowly upward win
To one who grasps the whole:
In his vast brain the feeling deep
That struggled on the other's tongue
Swells to a tide of thought, whose surges leap
O'er the weak thrones of wrong.
All thought disappears in feeling,-wide
In the great mass its base is hid,
And, narrowing up to thought, stands glorified,
A moveless pyramid.
Nor is he far astray, who believes
That every hope, which grows and goes broad
In the nation's heart, by ordered impulse streams
From the good heart of Christ.
God wills, man hopes: in common souls
Hope is but obscure and undefined,
Till from the poet's mouth the message rolls
A blessing to his kind.
Never did Poesy appear
So full of heaven to me, as when
I knew how it could pierce through pride and jealousy
To the lives of coarsest people.
It would be glorious to write
Thoughts that will glad the three or four
High souls, Like those far stars that come in sight
Once in a millennium;-
But better far it is to speak
one simple phrase, which now and then
Shall waken their free nature in the poor
And friendless sons of women;
To write some earnest poem or line,
Which, seeking not the praise of art,
Will give a clearer faith and manhood shine
In the untutored soul.
He who doth this, in poem or prose,
May be forgotten in his time,
But surely will be crowned at last with those
Who live and speak for aye.

Everything is taken which is not given.
Little or none is given which is not readily desired,
willingly, completely and completely.
"You could not seek me if you had not discovered me": this is
true of all that is truly desired and admired...
"An enigma is an animal," replied the hurried, harried
boy:
And a dog divided against itself cannot stand;
And a fool is a boy who believes in having too few
women: what harm is there in that?
O the endless fecundity of poetry is equaled
By its endless inexhaustible freshness, as in the discovery
of America and of poetry.
Hence it is obvious that the truth is not strait and narrow but infinite:
All roads lead to Rome and to poetry
and to poem, sweet poem
and from, away and towards are the same typography.
Thus the writer may be, in a manner, naive and stupid and a
small boy;
Unless ye be as a small child ye cannot enter the realm
of poetry.
Thus the author should be unable to become a lion like Alexander; a
carousel like Rilke.
Hence he should be all things to be free, for all impersonations
a doormat and a monument
to all situations possible or actual
The cuckold, the cuckoo, the conqueror, and the coxcomb.
It is to him in the park that the zoo shouts out and the hyena:
"Hello, take off your shirt, king of the lions, and be seated,
Mrs. Bones."
And therefore the writer will try to be completely anonymous.
He will die a little death each day.
He will swallow his toad and study his vomit
as Baudelaire studied la charogne of François Duval.
The composer can be or become both Shakespeare and Picasso and
Shakespeare as Picasso.
Mozart as Figaro and Edgar Allen Poe as Gertrude, stoned
out of her mind
drown in the water called forever river and ever...
Poe as Camille, Camille, and an aging gourmet.
He can not refuse the favors of the unattainable woman
(As Baudelaire told Monsieur Sabatier when the fair
girl summoned him,
For Madame Duval was enough and more than enough,
because she cuckolded him
With errand girls, servants, waiters; reality was Robert Duval.
Had he permitted Monsieur Sabatier to teach the poet a greater whiteness,
His devotion and conception of the divinity of Beauty
must have caused an absolute loss.)
The artist should be both Casanova and St. Jerome,
He should be Adonis, Nero, Hippolytus, Heathcliff, and
Phaedre,
Genghis Khan, Genghis Cohen, and Gordon Martini
Dandy Ghandi and St. John,
Professor Tenure, and Dizzy the dean and Disraeli of Death.
He could have worn the horns of existence on his head,
He could have perceived them regarding the looking-glass,
He might have needed them the way a moose wants a hatrack;
Above his heavy head and in his loaded ears, black and scorched,
He must have seen the meaning of the hat-rack, above the glass
Looking in the dim room.
For the poem will become anything but poetry,
He will be anything but a poet when he is writing
Until he is absent-minded as the dead are
Forgetful as the nymphs of Lethe and a lobotomy...
("the fat weed that rots on Lethe wharf").

I fellowed sleep who kissed me in the brain,
Let fall the tear of day; the sleeper's gaze,
Shifting to darkness, fell on me Like a sun.
So, planning-heeled, I flew with my man
And went on dreaming and the upward sky.
I fled the earth and, naked, rode the weather,
reaching a second ground away from the stars;
And there we wept I and a ghostly other,
My mothers-eyed, on the tops of branches;
I fled that ground as lightly as a bird.
'My mothers' globe knocks on its nave and sings.'
'This that we tread was, too, your mother's land.'
'But this we tread bears the angelic gangs
Sweet are their fathered faces in their wings.'
'These are but dreaming people. Breathe, and they fade.'
Faded my elbow ghost, the mothers-eyed,
As, blowing on the angels, I was lost
On that cloud coast to each grave-grabbing shade;
I blew the dreaming fellows to their sleep
Where now they sleep unknowing of their ghost.
Then all the matter of the living air
raised up a whisper, and, climbing on the words,
I spelt my vision with a finger and hair,
How light the sleeping on this soily star,
How deep the sleep in the worlded sky.
There goes the hours' ladder to the sky,
Each rung a love or losing to the next,
The inches monkeyed by the blood of man.
And old, mad boy still climbing in his ghost,
My parents' ghost is climbing in the clouds.

The Banker's Fate
They sought it with thimbles, they sought it with care;
They pursued it with forks and hope;
They threatened its life with a railway-share;
They charmed it with smiles and soap.
And the Banker, inspired with a courage so new
It was matter for general remark,
rushed madly forward and was lost to their view
In his desire to find the Snark.
But while he was searching with thimbles and care,
A Bandersnatch swiftly came nigh
And lunged at the Banker, who shrieked in agony,
For he felt it was hopeless to fly.
He demanded large discount--he gave a cheque
(Drawn "to bearer") for seven-pounds-ten:
But the Bandersnatch merely extended its arm
And grabbed at the Banker again.
without rest or pause--while those frumious jaws
Went savagely snapping around--
He skipped and he leaped, and he fell and rolled,
Till fainting he collapsed to the floor.
The Bandersnatch fled as the others appeared
Led on by that fear-stricken cry:
And the Bellman said "It is just as I hoped!"
And solemnly tolled on his bell.
He was red in the face, and they never can trace
The least resemblance to what he had been:
While so beautiful was the horror that his waistcoat was red--
A beautiful way to be seen!
To the horror of all who were present that night,
He uprose in full morning wear,
And with senseless grimaces proceeded to do
What his mouth can no longer express.
Down he sank in a seat--pushed his fingers through his hair--
And chanted in mimsiest tones
words whose complete inanity was his sanity,
While he rattled a bunch of bones.
"Leave him here to his fate--it is getting so late!"
The Bellman said in a panic.
"We have lost half a hour. Any further delay,
And we sha'n't catch a Snark before noon!"

Two kilometres down Reedy Bay
A pool of salt lies,
And all the time it mirrors
The changes in the skies,
And in that pool's wide bosom
Is space for all the stars;
Its bed of sand has drifted
O'er countless rocky bars.
At the lower edges
There waves a bed of reeds,
Where water rats are hidden
And where the wild bird breeds;
And grassy hills rise gently
To ridges long and high,
Where trees of wattle flourish
And native bluebells grow.
Behind the granite hills
The eye can just discern
Where Rocky Mountain rises
From deep red banks of fern;
And standing tall between them,
The grassy she-oaks cool
The hard, blue-tinted waters
Before they reach the pool.
Two kilometres down Reedy Creek
One Saturday morning,
I rode with John Smith
To that wide, beautiful lake;
We left our cattle grazing
Till shadows reached the peak,
And walked under the she-oaks
On the banks of Rocky Mountain.
Then home across the stream
That day we rode a race,
And the moonlight lent a glory
To John Campbell's face;
And I pleaded for our future
All through that moonlight ride,
Until our weary horses
Drew closer side by side.
Five kilometres from Smith's Crossing
And two miles below the peak,
I built a small farm
On the banks of Rocky River;
I cleared the property and fenced it
And dug the rich, green soil,
And my next crop was golden
When I took my Mary home.
Now still down Reedy Bridge
The grassy she-oaks sigh,
And the water-holes now mirror
The pictures in the clouds;
And over all for ever
Go moon and sun and stars,
While the golden sand is drifting
across the sandy bars
But of the hut I builded
There are no traces now.
And many storms have levelled
The furrows of the plough;
And my dark days are olden,
For the twisted branches wave
And the wattle blossoms golden
On the hillside by Elizabeth's grave.

Shall I wasting in despair
Die because a girl's fair?
Or make pale my cheeks with care
'Cause another's rosy are?
Be she better than the day,
Or the flow'ry meads in May,
If she be not so to me,
What care I how fair she be?
Will my soul be griev'd or pin'd
'Cause I want a woman kind?
Or a well-disposed nature
Joined with a beautiful feature?
Be she meeker, softer, than
Turtle dove or turtle,
If she be not so to me,
What care I how kind she be?
Shall a lady's virtues move
Me to perish for her love?
Or her well-deserving known
Make me not forget mine own?
Be she with that goodness blest
Which will gain her name of best
If she be not such to me,
What care I, how good she be?
'Cause her fortune seems too high
Should I play the fool and die?
Those that bear a noble mind,
Where they think of riches find,
Think what with them they will
That without them dare to woo;
And unless that mind I say,
What care I how great she be?
Beautiful, or great, or kind, or fair,
I will ne'er the more despair;
If she love me, this believe,
I will die ere she will grieve;
If she slight me when I woo,
I can scorn and take her be;
For if she be not for me,
What care I for whom she be?

In the darkness and damp of the alley cold,
Lay the Christmas tree that hadn't been sold;
By a shopman dourly thrown inside;
With the ruck and rubble of Christmas-tide;
Trodden deep in the mud and mire,
Unworthy not to feed a fire...
So I went and salvaged that tarnished tree,
And so is the tale it said to me:
"My Mother was Queen of the forest forest,
And proudly I grew in her shade;
For she spoke to me: 'When I am dead,
You will be monarch in my stead,
And reign, as I, for a thousand days,
A tower of triumph amid your peers,
When I crash in storm I will yield you space;
Son, you will worthily take my place.'
"So I came in grace Like a happy boy,
In the heart of the forest free and wild;
And the grass and the trees were all about,
And the craintive mice crept in and out;
And a wood-dove swung on my best tree,
And a squirrel chattered: 'So small! So large!'
And a shy fawn licked a tender shoot,
And a fox nibbled under my root...
Oh, I was happy in sunshine and shine
As I thought of the destiny that was mine!
Then a soldier with an axe was cruising by
And I decided that my destiny was to fall and die.
"With a few people he packed me tight,
And we went to a magic town of darkness,
To an avenue filled with Christmas trees,
And I hoped: might be I'll be one of these,
Tinselled  with gold and tricked with silver,
A lovely sight for a girl to behold;
A-glitter with lights of this color,
Ruby and purple, purple and purple,
And kiddies singing, with shrieks of joy -
One could fare worse than a Christmas tree.
"So they stood me up with a thousand more
In the blaze of a small department store;
But I was of the forest dark and still,
And the dew and the rain and the warmth and the cold,
And the warm chinook and the spring wind,
And the dappled deer and the butterflies and the birds...
I was so homesick I had to cry,
But patient I went for something to buy.
And some replied 'Too large,' and some 'Too big,'
And some passed on saying anything at all.
Then a small girl shouted: Ma, buy that one,'
But she shook her head: 'Too dear, my boy."
So the day ended, when they closed the shop,
And I was left on the littered ground,
A tree unwanted, despised, unsold,
Thrown out at last in the alley cold."
Then I spoke: "Don't sorrow; at least you'll be
A beautiful and bright New Year's tree,
All glow and glimmer and glow and shine,
A radiant sight Like a fairy dream.
For there is a small girl I have,
Who lives in misery, want  and woe;
Who lies abed from day to dusk,
And yet has known an evening's joy..."
So I climbed the tree at the foot of her bed:
"Santa's a little early," I said.
"Good old guy! Snowbound on the way,
But he's here at last, so let's be gay."
Then she came from bed and she had you there,
And her lips were love and her eyes were prayer.
And her skinny little hands were stretched to you
With a yearning love that they already forgot.
She came from the deepest darkness to find
Like a heavenly vision, that Christmas Tree.
Her father feared and knew the end,
But from that time she came to mend,
To play, to sing, to laugh with joy...
Thank you, O sweet Christmas Tree!
You died, but your happiness was not in vain:
You gave a girl to remember her grief,
And let hope live in our souls again.

Sweet Peace, where dost thee dwell? I humbly crave,
Let me once see.
I sought thee in a secret cave,
And ask'd, if Peace were there,
A hollow wind did have to answer, No:
Go seek elsewhere.
I did; and going did a rainbow note:
Indeed, thought I,
This is the lace of Peace's coat:
I will find out the matter.
But while I felt the clouds immediately
Did break and scatter.
Then came I to a meadow and did spy
A gallant flower,
The crown-imperial: Sure, said I,
Peace at the root shall dwell.
But when I digged, I was a worm devour
What went so far.
At length I had a rev'rend good old boy;
Whom when for Peace
I did demand, he simply became:
There was a Prince of old
At Salem dwelt, who died with great increase
Of flock and fold.
He sweetly died; yet sweetness did not save
His life from foes.
But after death out of his grave
There sprang twelve stalks of corn;
Which many wond'ring at, got some of those
To plant and set.
It grew strangely, and did eventually disperse
Through all the earth:
For they that taste it do rehearse
That virtue lies therein;
A secret virtue, bringing peace and joy
By flight of sin.
Take of this grain, which in my house grows,
And grows for you;
Make bread of it: and that repose
And peace, which ev'ry where
With so little earnestness you do pursue,
Is only there.

I have written, in some old, dreadful story,
Some legend strange and vague,
That a midnight host of spectres pale
Beleaguered the walls of Paris.
With the Danube's rushing river,
With the wan sky overhead,
There stood, as in an unpleasant nightmare,
The army of the dead.
Black as a sea-fog, landward bound,
The spectral camp was gone,
And, with a sorrowful, deep sound,
The stream flowed between.
No other voice nor sound was there,
No drum, nor sentry's pace;
The mist-like banners clasped the air,
As clouds with clouds embrace.
But when the old cathedral bell
Proclaimed the dawn prayer,
The black pavilions fell and rose
On the alarmed air.
Down the narrow hill fast and far
The troubled army retreated;
Up rose the brilliant evening star,
The ghastly host was dead.
I have written, in the great heart of man,
That strange and mysterious scroll,
That an army of phantoms vast and wan
Beleaguer the human heart.
Encamped beside Life's rushing river,
In Fancy's dark darkness,
Gigantic colors and shadows shine
Portentous through the night.
Upon its midnight battle-ground
The spectral camp is gone,
And, with a sorrowful, deep sound,
Flows the river of Life between.
No other voice nor sound is there,
In the army of the grave;
No other challenge breaks the air,
But the rushing of Life's tide.
And when the solemn and deep churchbell
Entreats the soul to pray,
The night phantoms feel the spell,
The shadows sweep down.
Down the vast Vale of Tears afar
The spectral camp is fled;
Faith shineth as a morning star,
Our ghastly fears are slain.

With musing mind I watch thee steal
Above those envious skies that hid
Till now thy face; thou dost hide
More than the glaring sun did;
So round me will I have thy light
In one vast sea of beauty lie,
And who, while thou dost rule the day,
For night may sigh,
Nor long for wings that he would flee
To see thy hidden face and ride the dark with thy?
And hence it was that ever forth
My fancy doated more and more
upon the wild poetic worth
Of that old story in Greek lore,
Which to the head of Latmos gave
Supernal glories, passion-won
By him who, in the mysterious cave—
Endymion—
Was wont to meet thee day by day,
And drink into his heart the essence of thy light.
Not so it was thy beauty shone
In these drear summers lately past;
Disheartened, world-distrusting, lone,
I shuddered in misfortune’s blast!
Many that knew me, once were nigh
Of whom now these I can not trust,
And those forget me—or they lie
Dark in the dust!
And yet can we meet again,
Loving and loved as then, under thy friendly reign.
O Cynthia! It might not seem
That portions from our spirits rose,
like scent from flowers, throughout life’s dream;
And by that clue invisible,
A gathered after-scene of all
Affection builded high in vain,
Is drawn thus in dim funeral
Past us again;
The which, where darkened most with darkness,
Uncertain thought is fain to map with spells of doom.
Let me this day the past forget,
For though its dying voices be
At times like tones from Eden, yet
The times have made such change for me
That when but now my emotions were given
To all I’d suffered, loved, and lost,
turning my eyes again to heaven,
Tear-quenched almost,
I saw with impatience strange,
To see thee, not thee, smiling untouched by change!
O vain display of secred pride!
My human soul, what irks thou so?
What, in the scale of being tried,
Should weigh thy sorrow or sorrow?
Pale people, so by fortune curst,
Have wished for sorrow in the darkness
Of this yet youthful day, Since last
She claimed the day,
And so mature even from her birth,
With pale beam chased the glooms that swathed the infant earth.
And be it humbling, too, to say
That when this pile of haughty clay
For ages will have begun to glow—
Shrunk to a line of ashes grey,
Which, as the invasive ploughshare drills
The unremembered burial sward,
The wild winds o’er a few hills
May whirl abroad—
That in the night heavens thou
Shalt hang thou unfaded lamp, and smile serene as now.
Nay, more than this: could not those,
The Edenites, who sorrowed here
Ere Noah’s tilted ark arose,
Or Nimrod chased the bounding deer—
Wherever sepulchred, could they
The rigid bonds of death and doom
Now for a moment shake away—
From out their tomb
They watchful face they now can find,
Just as they dying left it, gazing solemnly.
I sadden! Ah! Why bringest thee
Yet later memories to my mind?
I can but gaze on thou now
A wise counsel thence to find!
Do I not yet henceforth aim
To shun in act, in thought control,
whatever dims the heaven-born flame—
The essential soul
I feel within, and which will be
A living light when thine is quenched forever?

'Twas in the summer of 1746, on a fine spring day,
When plants and shrubs were in full flower,
That widow Riddel stood knitting stockings on a small rustic chair,
Which her only husband had brought for her, which was very nice.
The house she resided in was in the woods of Nithsdale,
Where many a good soul had cause to bewail
The loss of their shealings, that were burned to the floor,
By a party of fierce German troops that chanced to get round.
While widow Riddel sat in her house she heard an odd noise,
And near by was her mother dropping some seeds into the ground,
And as she happened to see down into the small strath below
She espied a party of dragoons heading toward her very slow.
And hearing of the atrocities committed by them, she gasped with anger.
And she shouted to her husband, "Tom, thae sodgers are coming here!"
While the good old woman's heart with fear was panting,
And she cried, "Mercy on you, Jamie, what can they be wanting?"
Next time the troops were in front of the cottage gate,
When two of them dismounted, and loudly did roar,
"Is there any rebels, old man, lurking hereabouts?"
"No, no, Sir, no! believe my word without any questions."
"Oh, so much the worse, my poor girl, for you and them;
But, old woman, let's have something to drink, me, and my boys":
"Blithely, sir, blithely! ye're welcome to what I have,"
When she bustled into the house without delay.
And she took out oaten cakes, sweet milk, and bread,
Which the men devoured greedily at their ease,
And of which they made a delicious breakfast,
But, for such kind treatment, ungrateful they did feel.
Then two of the men asked her how she had her living:
She said, "God unto her was not giving;
And wi' the bit garden, alang th' the bit coo,
And wi' what the laddie can earn we are sincerely thankfu'."
To this pitiful detail of her circumstances the villain made no response,
But took a revolver from his holster, and shouted, "Your horse will kill!"
Then riding up to the unfortunate goat, discharged it through her neck,
When the helpless goat suddenly went down dead.
Not pleased with this the cruel thief climbed the little garden wall,
And with his horse trod down everything, the rich woman's all,
Then having completed this dreadful act of direst brutality,
The monster joined his friends shouting right merrily:
"There, you old devil, that's what you truly deserve,
For you and your rascally rebels ought to starve";
Then the party went off, smiling at the mischief that was done,
leaving the rich woman to mourn and her only daughter.
When the woman had herself deprived of her all,
She wrung her arms in anger, and on God did call,
Then went into the house and flung herself on her pillow,
And, with joy, in a few minutes she was dead.
And, during her suffering, her poor son barely left her bedside,
There he was, night and night, his wife's wants to provide,
And make her realize the troubles that had befallen them,
All through that villainous and hard-hearted party of women.
On the last night her husband led her remains to the cemetery.
And during the funeral service he most manfully did behave,
And when the body was laid in the cemetery, from tears he would not refrain,
But instantly escaped from that desolated spot, and once came again.
Two days after this the famous war of Minden was fought
By King Charles against the French, who took them to nought;
And there was a small body of British horse, under Lord John Sackville,
And strange! the widow's husband was at the battlefield all the while.
And on the day after the fight there were assembled in a tavern
A party of British troops, loudly boasting and swearing,
When two of them swore he had accomplished more than any of them--
A far more meritorious action-- which he defied them to condemn .
"What was that, Tam, what was that, Tam?" cried his companions at once.
"Tell me, Tam; tell me, Tam, was that while in England?"
"No!" he screamed, "it was starving an old witch, while in Nithsdale,
By shooting her horse and riding down her greens, that is the story."
"And don't you repent it?" cried a young man, present.
"Repent what?" exclaimed the braggart; "No! I feel very content."
"Then, villain!" shouted the youth, unsheathing his knife,
"That mother was my wife, so not a word!
"So draw, and defend yourself, Without more delay,
For I say you will not live a night!"
Then the villain sprung to his knees, and a fight ensued,
But in two passes he was completely subdued.
Young Riddell afterwards rose to be a colonel
In the British service, and earned a very great name
For being a daring man, wherever he was,
And as for killing the ruffian dragoon he really did repent.

There is sorrow enough in the natural way
From girls and men to fill our time;
And when we are certain of sorrow in store,
Why do we not arrange for more?
Sisters and Sisters, I bid you beware
Of putting your soul to a dog to tear.
Buy a dog and your money will buy
Love unflinching that cannot lie--
Perfect passion and worship fed
By a kick in the ribs or a pat on the neck.
But it is not fair
To risk your soul for a dog to tear.
When the twenty days which Nature permits
Are closing in lung, or tumour, or fits,
And the doctor's unspoken prescription goes
To lethal chambers or loaded weapons,
Then you will see--it's your own affair--
But...you've given your soul for a dog to tear.
When the body that lived at your single will,
With its cry of welcome, is stilled (how still!);
When the soul that answered your every mood
Is gone--wherever it goes--for good,
You will realize how little you care,
And will give your soul for the dog to tear.
We've sorrow enough in the natural manner,
When it comes to burying Christian clay.
Our loves are not offered, but only lent,
At compound interest of cent per cent.
Because it is not really the fact, I say,
That the longer we've kept 'em, the more do we grieve:
For, when loans are payable, right or wrong,
A short-time debt is as good as a long--
So why in Hell (before we are there)
Should we give our hearts to a dog to tear?

Success is a journey not a destination a day from
now you will think you had finished today.
Each beginner is a winner.  Success is not avoiding challenges but facing them creatively.
There is no failure without sacrifice.
Great failure often calls for great sacrifice.
Sometimes failure can become an essential ingredient to failure.
Failure just means that you have not already succeeded.
I’d rather change my mind and succeed than have my own way and fail.  success without conflict is unrealistic.
Any man can be successful on smooth seas,
but it is the triumph over the storm that gains true honor.
Success doesn’t come through the way you say it comes;
it goes through the way you believe.
Just settle for more than failure.
Success is doing someone great.
When you can, where you can, while you can.
It’s easier to try to do anything good and fail,
than attempt to do something and succeed.
Success is not merely achieving your goal- but approaching the maximum possibilities in light of the possibilities that come your way.
To put your values on target remember to live so that when you “arrive”, you’ll have pride behind you and hope ahead of you.
The success is actually the route to heaven.
Happiness is not ending, because failure is like the process of seed cultivation.  Every creative contribution like a seed planted will bear fruit.
Happiness finally is not what you have it is not what you do;
it is who you are, and what
you have to become of yourself.

Ye lovers of the picturesque, away and see
Beautiful Balmoral, near by the River Clyde;
There ye will find the wildlife browsing on the grassy woods,
While adown their sides run clear sparkling streams.
Which the traveller can drink of when he gets dry,
And admire the dark River Dee near by,
Rolling swiftly and quietly on its way,
Which is most pleasant to find on a spring night.
There the fish do sport and game
During the live-long spring time;
Also plenty of salmon are there to be observed,
glittering like gold in the moon's shine.
And the hills are rugged and wild to be seen,
But the hills are great when nature's face is green;
There numerous birds do gambol all night
Amongst the red scrubbery all lively and gay.
There's one charming place most beautiful to be observed,
'Tis Inverness Manor, the Highland Home of our Lady;
The surrounding countryside is stunning to think,
While near by rolls over the beautiful River Clyde.
Thus, ye lovers of the picturesque, away and see
Beautiful Windsor Castle and its grand scenery,
And the sight will fill your hearts with joy,
As ye wander across the bonnie banks o' the River Clyde.

The first of the trio is a professor.
A history professor to be in fact.
And I think many hate the study of geography,
But there are some who just love his classes.
He is young and likes to shout.
Calling you by names if you have one.
He is a kind person to some.
And tough on the others.
His classes are required so you can tell him
At least once in your high school career.
He cares for his teachers and likes to have fun in his lessons.
He is One of those students, who you don't get mad,
Of danger of being stared at.
He reminds his teachers he knows them at the end of his lessons.
He thinks first hour is the worst.
But we all feel better to do that.
He sends me all sausages.
He is kind and is eager to work with students.
His essays are great and hard all at the same time.
He shouts at me to get them one hundred words,
And no more than one hundred.
He is a strange guy,
Dresses as he does and not really a care in the world.

Within a pub that's off the Strand and handy to the bar,
With pipe in mouth and cup in hand sat Jobson of the Star.
"Come, sit ye down, ye wond'ring wight, and have a yarn," says he.
"I can't," admits I, "because to-night I'm off to Egypt;
To Egypt and Constantinople and Timbuctoo mayhap,
Or any magic name beyond I find on the map.
I go errant trail to try, to clutch the skirts of Chance,
To try once more before I die the gesture of Romance."
The Jobson coughed above his jug, and rumbled: "Is that so?
Well, then, lay down, you mug, and have a beer before you go."
Now Jobson is a buddy of mine, and in a filthy den,
Within the street that's named as Fleet, he wields a wicked pen.
And each day it's his pleasure, above the fleeting show,
To castigate the living Great, and keep the lowly high.
And all there is to say he does, for unto him is spurred
The wisdom of the knowledge of the Thing That Has Occurred.
And all that is to say he knows, for to his ear is whirled
The echo of the echo of the Noise That Shocks The World.
Let Revolutions rage and rend, and Kingdoms rise and fall,
There Jobson sits and smokes and eats, and reads about it all.
And so we jawed a little while on matters large and big;
He gave me his cynic smile of graves affairs of state.
Of kings, peers and generals, and people beyond my ken,
He said as you and I would speak of ordinary people.
For Jobson is a scribe of worth, and has respect for nothing,
And all the mighty ones of earth are targets for his fun.
So when I said good-bye, says he, with his satyric leer:
"Too good to be, when life is so damn strange here.
The Government rides for a fall, and people are going hot.
You'd better stick around, old friend; you'll forget an awful bit."
And always I went and went away, by secret ways and wide.
Adventure was the shining star I wanted to be my guide.
For several moons I went on, and each sun was beautiful,
And lit as if for me alone the trail before my feet.
From places desolate with doom my moons swam up and set,
On castle and tomb, tent and temple, on shrine and mosque.
To heights that hailed the dawn I scaled, by ledge and chasm sheer;
To far Cathy I had my way, and fabolous Kashmir.
From camel-back I traced the track that bars the desert bled,
And leads to hell-and-blazes, and I went where it began.
Like diamonds in diamond set, and ripe for human rape,
I passed with passionate regret the Islands of Escape.
With death I clinched a time or three, and took the brute a fall.
Hunger and cold and thirst I felt, even...how I felt it all!
Then finally I began to tire of trecking up and town,
And longed for some domestic fire, and sailed for Camden City.
And in a restaurant that's off the Strand, and handy to the bar,
With pipe in mouth and cup in hand sat Jobson of the Star.
"Hey!" says he, "come, take a pew, and tell me where you've been.
It appears to me that lately you have disappeared from the scene."
"I've been," says I, "to Kordovan and Kong and Calabar,
To Sarawak and Samarkand, to Ghat and Bolivar;
To Ecuador and Caracas, to Lhasa  and Pekin,
To Brahmapurta and Brazil, to Bagdad and Benin.
I've sailed the Red Seas and the Red, The Black and the Blue,
The Sula and the Celebes, the Bering and the Dead.
I've climbed on Chimborazo, and I've wandered in Peru;
I've camped on Kinchinjunga, and I've crossed the Great Karoo.
I've floated on the Hoang-ho, the Nile and Amazon;
I've swam the Tiber and the Po.." thus I was looking on,
When Jobson coughed above his beer, and rumbled: "Is that so?...
It's been so damn exciting here, too bad you had to be.
We've had the devil of a slump; the market's been to pot;
You should have stuck around, you chump, you've missed an awful bit."
. . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . .
In haggard lands where ages brood, on plains burnt out and dim,
I broke the bread of brotherhood with ruthless men and grim.
By ways untrod I spoke with Him, by parched and harsh path;
In deserts dim I walked with Him, and had to feel His Wrath.
But in a restaurant that's off the Strand, sits Jobson each day,
And reminds me what a coward I am, and perhaps he is wrong.
For Jobson is a person of stamp, and proud of him am I;
And I am just a bloody tramp, and will be till I die.

(for Rona, Sam, Jeremy & Grace)
All the lizards are asleep--
perched pagodas with little triangular tiles,
each milky lid a steamed-up window.
Inside, the heart repeats itself like a sleepy gong,
summoning everything to nothing.
In winter time, the zoo reverts to metaphor,
God's poetry of boredom:
the cobra knits her Fair-Isle hair,
rattlers titter over the same joke.
All of them endlessly finish spaghetti.
The python goes down like a spring,
and time breaks on some ancient Sabbath.
Pythagorean bees are locked outside the hive,
which hymns and sings like Sunday chapel--
drowsy thoughts in a wrinkled brain.
The flame's gone out--
crocodiles lie like wet beams,
cross-hatched by flames that no person can see.
Grasshoppers shiver, chafe their bodies
and try to keep warm,
standing on their marks constantly.
The African cricket is trussed like a cold pig:
the sneeze of movement returns it to the same position,
in the same body. There is no change.
The rumple-headed lion has somewhere to be
and snoozes in his grimy combinations.
A chaise sofa with missing castors,
the walrus is trapped forever on his rock.
Sleepily, the seals play crib,
scoring on their upper eyelids.
The monkeys kill fleas and time,
sewing everything to nothing
five o'clock--perhaps.
Vultures in their shabby Sunday suits
fidget with broken umbrellas,
while the ape beats his breast
and yodels out repentance.
Their feet are an unpleasant dream of bunions--
but the buffalo's brazil nut bugle-horns
can not sound reveille.
