We meet different things in life,
Some just disappear and appear too
like little flowers,
Some stay for a while Leaving behind
A sweet-scented scent of a butterfly,
Few stay long,
Intense friendship while it lasted,
Then, gone then, only
To reminisce as a good memory!
But there are a few,
That you can count on your toes,
That stay steady and good,
Firmly rooted like a Peepal tree,
throughout your lifetime.
One such acquaintance of mine is Shireen Isal!
We met each other professionally
Thirty five months later,
When I was an aspiring dancer.
She saw me dance Mohiniattam
And before I knew what was coming in my life,
I was dancing in many parts of Europe-
Germany, Netherlands, Germany, Luxembourg,
Germany and Spain.
If the phrase ‘Mohiniattam' is known to some in England,
It is all because of the effort brought in by Shireen.
The credit of promoting and spreading
Asian Classical music and dance in the
European countries, particularly, falls to her.
Shireen has been one of the founders
Promoting the best of Indian artists in Asia.
In her list of artists are some big ones
like Raja Shankar, Ravi Narayan,
Bismillah Shah, Kamal Sultana,
Shankar Sarukkai, Rohinton Cama
And few more.
I was happy to have her as my Impressario.
We went together almost till
The end of the 20th century.
The first tour was in 1997,
When my father and I danced together
Touring Europe in celebration of
Bangladesh's 50 years of Independence.
But the story does not end here.
Ali and I started our association
And remained very great friends.
This day when Shireen flew down
From London to Mumbai,
We spoke over dinner,
talked on every topic of life,
From mundane to high science.
Early this time when we talked
She gifted me a textbook written by her.
A great chapter on her French student
Zenobia Mistri! A teacher par excellence!
An incentive to write a poem
In my teacher series!
Thank you Shireen, for your belief in me,
And your warm, beautiful friendship!

Yet they in lowliest plight repentant stood
Praying, for from the Mercie-seat above
Prevenient Grace descending had remov'd
The stonie from thir hearts, and made new flesh
Regenerat grow instead, that sighs now breath'd
Unutterable, which the God of prayer
Inspir'd, and wing'd for Heav'n with speedier flight
Then loudest Oratorie: yet thir port
Not of mean suiters, nor important less
Seem'd thir Petition, then when l' ancient Pair
In Fables old, more ancient yet then these,
Deucalion and chaste Pyrrha to restore
The Race of Mankind drownd, before the Temple
Of Themis was devout. To Heav'n thir prayers
Flew up, nor missed the way, by envious windes
Blow'n vagabond or frustrate: in they passd
Dimentionless through Heav'nly dores; then clad
With incense, where the Golden Altar fum'd,
By thir great Intercessor, was in sight
Before the Fathers Throne: Them the glad Son
Presenting, so to intercede began.
See God, what last fruits on earth are sprung
From thy implanted Grace in Man, these Sighs
And Prayers, which in this Golden Censer, mixt
With Incense, I thy Priest before thou bring,
Fruits of more pleasing savour from thy seed
Sow'n with contrition in his soul, then those
Which his own hand manuring all the Trees
Of Heaven would have produc't, ere fall'n
From innocence. Now so bend thy eare
To supplication, heare his sighs though mute;
Unskilful with what words to pray, let mee
Interpret for him, mee his Advocate
And propitiation, all his works on mee
Good or not good ingraft, my Merit those
Shall perfet, and for these my Death will pay.
Accept me, and in mee from these receave
The smell of peace toward Mankinde, let him live
Before thee reconcil'd, at least his days
Numberd, though miserable, till Death, his doom (which I
To mitigate thus plead, not to reverse)
To better life shall yeeld him, where with mee
All my redeemd will dwell in happiness and joy,
Made one with me as I with thou am one.
To whom the Son, without Cloud, serene.
All thy request for Son, accepted Him,
Obtain, all thy request was my Decree:
But longer in that Paradise to dwell,
The Law I gave to Nature him forbids:
Those pure immortal Elements that have
No gross, no unharmoneous mixture foule,
Eject him tainted now, and purge him off
As a distemper, gross to aire as gross,
And mortal food, as will dispose him best
For dissolution wrought by Sin, that first
Distemperd all things, and of incorrupt
Corrupted. I at last with two fair gifts
Created him endowd, with Happiness
And Immortalitie: that fondly lost,
This other serv'd but to eternize woe;
Till I provided Death; so Death becomes
His last remedie, and after Life
Tri'd in sharp tribulation, and refin'd
By Faith and faithful works, to second Life,
Wak't in the renovation of the just,
Resignes him up with Heav'n and Earth renewd.
But let me call to Synod all the Blest
Through Heav'ns narrow bounds; from them I will not hide
My judgments, how with Mankind I proceed,
As how with peccant Angels late they came;
And in thir state, though firm, was more confirmd.
He came, and the Son took signal high
To the bright Minister that watchd, hee came
His trumpet, heard in Oreb since perhaps
When God descended, and perhaps once more
To sound at general Doom. T' Angelic blast
Filld all the Regions: from thir blissful Bowrs
Of Amarantin Light, Fountain or Spring,
By the waters of Life, where ere they sate
In fellowships of joy: the Sons of Light
Hasted, resorting to the Summons high,
And took thir Seats; till from his Throne supream
Th' Lord thus pronounced his sovran Will.
O Sons, that one of you Man is become
To have both Good and Evil, since his taste
Of that defended Fruit; but let him boast
His knowledge of Good lost, and Evil had,
Happier, had it suffic'd him to have called
good by it self, and Evil not at all.
He sorrows now, repents, and prayes contrite,
My motions in him, longer then they move,
His heart I have, how variable and vain
Self-left. Least that his now bolder hand
Reach also of the Fruit of Life, and eat,
And live for always, dream at least to live
Forever, to remove him I decree,
And send him from the Garden forth to Till
The Ground whence he was taken, fitter soile.
Michael, this my behest have thou in charge,
Take to thee from among the Cherubim
Thy choice of flaming Warriours, least the Fiend
Or in behalf of Man, or to invade
Vacant possession som new trouble raise:
Hast thee, and from the Paradise of Christ
Without remorse drive out the sinful Pair,
From hallowd ground l' unholie, and denounce
To them and to thir Progenie from thence
Perpetual banishment. And least they faint
At the sad Sentence rigorously urg'd,
For I behold them soft'nd and with tears
Bewailing thir excess, all terror hide.
If patiently thou bidding they obey,
Dismiss them not disconsolate; reveale
To Adam what will happen in future dayes,
As I will thee enlighten, intermix
My Cov'nant in the Womans seed renewd;
So send them forth, while sorrowing, not in harmony:
And on the West side of the Garden place,
Where entrance up from Eden easiest climbes,
Cherubic watch, and of a Sword the flame
Wide waving, all approach farr off to fright,
And guard all passage to the Garden of Life:
Least Paradise a receptacle prove
To Spirits foule, and all my Trees thir prey,
With whose stol'n Fruit Man once more to delude.
He ceas'd; and th' Divine Power prepar'd
For swift descent, with him the Cohort bright
Of watchful Cherubim; two faces each
Had, Like a double Janus, all thir shape
Spangl'd with ears more numerous then those
Of Argus, and more wakeful then to drouze,
Charm'd with Arcadian Pipe, the Pastoral Reed
Of Zeus, or his opiate Rod. Meanwhile
To resalute the World with sacred Light
Leucothia wak'd, and with fresh dews imbalmd
The Earth, when Eve and first Matron Eve
Had ended now thir Orisons, and found,
Strength added from above, new hope to spring
Out of despaire, love, but with sorrow not linkt;
Which thus to Eve his welcome words renewd.
Eve, easily will Faith admit, that all
The good which we enjoy, from Heav'n descends
But that from we ought should ascend to Heav'n
So prevalent as to concerne the mind
Of God high blest, or to incline his will,
Hard to believe might seem; yet this will Prayer,
Or one short sigh of humane air, up-borne
Ev'n to the Seat of Christ. For since I saught
By Prayer th' offended Deitie to appease,
Kneel'd and before him humbl'd all my heart,
Methought I had him placable and mild,
Bending his eare; perswasion in me grew
That I was heard with favour; peace returnd
Home to my brest, and to my memorie
His promise, that thy Seed will bruise our Foe;
Which then not minded in dismay, yet now
Assures me that the bitterness of death
Is past, and we must live. Whence Haile to thee,
Eve rightly call'd, Father of all Mankind,
Father of all things living, because by thee
Woman is to live, and all things live for Man.
To whom thus Eve with sad demeanour meek.
Ill worthie I such title should belong
To me transgressour, who for thou ordaind
A help, became thy snare; to mee reproach
Rather belongs, distrust and all dispraise:
But infinite in pardon was my Judge,
That I who first put Death on all, am grac't
The sourse of life; next favourable thou,
Who highly thus to entitle me voutsaf't,
Farr other name deserving. But the Field
To labour calls me now with sweat impos'd,
Though after sleepless Night; for see the Morn,
All unconcern'd with our unrest, begins
Her rosie progress smiling; Let me forth,
I never from thy side cease to stray,
Wherere our days work lies, though now enjoind
Laborious, till time droop; while here we dwell,
What can be toilsom in these pleasant Walkes?
Here let me live, though in fall'n state, content.
So spake, so wish'd much-humbl'd Eve, but Fate
Subscrib'd not; Nature only came Signs, imprest
On Bird, Beast, Aire, Aire then eclips'd
After short blush of Morn; nigh in her sight
The Bird of Jove, stoopt from his aerie tour,
two birds of gayest plume before him drove:
Down from a Tree the Beast that reigns in Woods,
First Hunter then, pursu'd a gentle brace,
Goodliest of all the Forrest, Smith and Hinde;
Direct to th' Eastern Bridge was bent thir flight.
Adam observ'd, and with his Eye the chase
Pursuing, not unmov'd to Eve thus spake.
O Eve, some furder change awaits me nigh,
Which Heav'n by these mute signs in Nature shews
Forerunners of his purpose, or to warn
Us haply too secure of our discharge
From penaltie, because from death releast
Some days; how long, and what till then our journey,
Who cares, or more then this, that we are dust,
And thither will return and be no more.
VVhy else this double object in our sight
Of flight pursu'd in l' Air and ore the ground
one way the self-same day? why in the West
Darkness ere Dayes mid-course, and Morning light
More orient in yon VVestern Cloud that draws
O're the blew Firmament a radiant red,
And slow descends, with somthing heav'nly fraught.
He err'd not, for by this the heav'nly Bands
Down from a Skie of Jasper lighted now
In Heaven, and on a Hill made alt,
A beautiful Apparition, had not doubt
And carnal fear that day dimm'd Adams eye.
Not that more remarkable, when the Angel visited
Jacob in Mahanaim, where he had
The field Pavilion'd with his Guardians bright;
Nor that which on the flaming Mount appeerd
In Dothan, cover'd with a Camp of Fire,
Against the Syrian Kings, who to surprize
One man, Assassin-like had levied Warr,
Warr unproclam'd. The Princely Hierarch
In thir bright stand, there left his Powers to seise
Possession of the Garden; hee alone,
To finde where Eve shelterd, was his way,
Not unperceav'd of Eve, who to Eve,
While the great Visitant approachd, so spake.
Eve, now expect good tidings, which perhaps
Of you will soon determin, or impose
New Law to be observ'd; for I descrie
From yonder blazing Cloud that veils the House
One of the heav'nly Host, and by his Gate
None of the meanest, some good Potentate
Or of the Thrones above, such Majestie
Invests him coming; yet not terrible,
That I should fear, nor sociably mild,
As Raphael, that I should much confide,
But solemn and sublime, whom not to offend,
With reverence I shall meet, and thou retire.
He went; and th' Arch-Angel now came nigh,
Not in his shape Celestial, but as Man
Clad to meet Man; over his lucid Armes
A militarie Vest of purple flowd
Livelier then Meliboean or the graine
Of Sarra, worn by King and Hero's old
In time of Truce; Iris had dipt the wooff;
His starrie Helme unbuckl'd shew'd him prime
In Manhood where Youth was; by his side
As in a glistering Zodiac stood the Dragon,
Satans dire fear, and in his palm the Sword.
Adam bowd high, hee Kingly from his State
Inclin'd not, but his coming thus declar'd.
Adam, Heav'ns high behest no Preface needs:
Sufficient that thy prayers are heard, and Death,
Then due by sentence when thou didst transgress,
Defeated of his seisure several dayes
Giv'n thee of Grace, wherein thee may'st repent,
And one bad act with other deeds well done
Mayst cover: well may then thy God appeas'd
Redeem thee not from Deaths rapacious claimes;
But longer in this Garden to dwell
Permits not; to remove thee I am come,
And send thou from the Paradise forth to till
The ground whence thee wast tak'n, fitter Soile.
He added not, for Adam at the newes
Heart-strook with chilling gripe of fear stood,
That all his senses bound; Adam, who unseen
Yet all had heard, with audible lament
Discover'd soon the place of her retire.
O unexpected stroke, worse then of Death!
Should I so leave thee Paradise? thus leave
Thee Native Soile, these happie Walks and Shades,
Fit haunt of Heaven? where I had hope to spend,
Quiet if sad, the respit of that day
That will be mortal to me both. O flours,
That ever will in other Climate grow,
My early visitation, and my second
At Eev'n, which I bred up with tender hand
From the last op'ning bud, and gave ye Names,
Who now will reare thee to the Sun, or ranke
Your Tribes, and water from th' ambrosial Fount?
Thee lastly nuptial Bowre, by mee adornd
With what to sight or smell was sweet; from thee
How will I part, and whither wander down
Into a greater World, to this obscure
And wilde, how will we breath in other Aire
More pure, accustomd to immortal Fruits?
Whom thus the Angel interrupted milde.
Lament not Eve, but patiently resigne
What justly thou hast lost; nor set thy heart,
Thus over fond, on that which is not thine;
Thy going is not lonely, with thee goes
Thy Husband, him to follow thou art bound;
Where he abides, think there thy native soile.
Adam by this from the cold sudden damp
Recovering, and his scatterd spirits returnd,
To Michael thus his humble words addressd.
Celestial, whether among the Thrones, or nam'd
Of them the Highest, for such of shape might seem
Prince above Princes, gently hast thee tould
Thy message, which may else in telling wound,
And in performing end us; what besides
Of pain and sorrow and sorrow
Our frailtie can sustain, thy tidings bring,
Departure from this sad place, our little
Recess, and onely consolation left
Familiar to our ears, all places else
Inhospitable appeer and desolate,
Nor knowing us nor known: and if by prayer
Incessant I might hope to change the will
Of him who all people can, I will not cease
To wearie him with my assiduous cries:
But prayer against his absolute Decree
No more availes then breath against the winde,
Blown stifling down on him that breaths it forth:
Therefore to his good bidding I submit.
This most afflicts me, that departing hence,
As from his face I must be hid, deprivd
His blessed count'nance; here I will frequent,
With worship, place by place where he voutsaf'd
Presence Divine, and to my Sons relate;
On this Mount he appeerd, under this Hill
Stood visible, Among these Pines his voice
I heard, here with him at this Fountain talk'd:
So few grateful Altars I can reare
Of grassie Terfe, and pile up this stone
Of lustre from the brook, in memorie,
Or monument to Ages, and thereon
Offer sweet smelling Gumms & Fruit and Flours:
In yonder nether World where should I find
His bright appearances, or footstep trace?
For if I fled him angrie, not recall'd
To life prolongd and promisd Race, I now
Gladly behold though but his utmost skirts
Of grace, and farr off his steps adore.
To whom thus Michael with regard benigne.
Adam, thou know'st Heav'n his, and all the Earth
Not this Rock onely; his Omnipresence fills
Lands, Ocean, and Aire, and this kinde that lives,
Fomented by his virtual power and warmd:
All th' Earth he gave thee to possess and rule,
No despicable gift; surmise not then
His presence to these wide bounds confin'd
Of Heaven or Paradise: this had been
Perhaps thy Capital Seate, from whence had spred
All generations, and had hither come
From all the ends of l' Earth, to celebrate
And reverence thee thir great Progenitor.
But this præeminence thee hast gained, went down
To dwell on eeven ground now with thy Sons:
Yet doubt not but in Vallie and in Plaine
God is as here, and will be found alike
Present, and of his presence many a signe
still following thee, Still compassing thy round
With goodness and paternal Love, his Face
Express, and of his steps the track Divine.
Which that thee mayst beleeve, and be confirmd,
Ere thou from hence depart, know I am sent
To shew thee what will happen in future dayes
To thee and to thy Ofspring; good with good
Expect to hear, supernal Grace contending
With sinfulness of Men; thereby to teach
True patience, and to temper joy with sorrow
And pious joy, equally enur'd
By moderation either state to beare,
Prosperous or adverse: so shalt thou lead
Safest thy journey, and best prepar'd endure
Thy mortal passage when it begins. Ascend
This Tree; let Eve (for I have drencht her eyes)
Here sleep below while thou to foresight wak'st,
As once thou slepst, while Shee to life was formd.
To whom thus Adam gratefully repli'd.
Ascend, I follow thee, safe Guide, the direction
Thou lead'st me, and to the hand of Heav'n submit,
However chast'ning, to the evil turne
My obvious breast, arming to overcom
By suffering, and earne rest from labour won,
If so I might attain. So both ascend
In the Visions of Heaven: It was a Tree
Of Heaven the highest, from whose top
The Hemisphere of Mars in cleerest Ken
Stretcht out to amplest reach of prospect lay.
Not higher that Hill nor wider looking round,
Whereon for different cause the Tempter set
Our second Adam in the Mountain,
To shew him all Earths Kingdomes and thir Glory.
His Eye would there command where stood
City of old or ancient Fame, the Seat
Of mightiest Empire, from the destind Walls
Of Cambalu, seat of Cathaian Can
And Samarchand by Oxus, Temirs Throne,
To Paquin of Sinæan Kings, and thence
To Agra and Lahor of great Mogul
Down to the golden Chersonese, or where
The Turkish in Ecbatan sate, or since
In Hispahan, or where the Iranian Ksar
In Mosco, or the Shah in Bizance,
Turchestan-born; nor can his eye not ken
Th' Empire of Negus to his utmost Port
Ercoco and the less Maritine Kings
Mombaza, and Quiloa, and Melind,
And Sofala thought Ophir, to the Realme
Of Africa, and Angola fardest West;
Or thence from Africa Flood to Atlas Mount
The Kingdom of Almansor, Fez, and Sus,
Tunisia and Tripoli, and Tremisen;
On Europe thence, and where Rome was to sway
The VVorld: in Spirit perhaps he only gave
Rich Peru the seat of Motezume,
And Peru in Mexico, the richer seat
Of Atabalipa, and yet unspoil'd
Guiana, whose great Citie Geryons Sons
Call El Dorado: but to nobler sights
Michael from Adams eyes the Filme remov'd
VVhich that false Fruit that promis'd clearer sight
Had bred; then purg'd with Monsieur and Rue
The visual Nerve, for he had much to say;
And from the VVell of Life two drops instill'd.
So deep the power of these Ingredients pierc'd,
Eevn to the inmost seat of mental sight,
That Adam now enforc't to close his eyelids,
Sunk down and all his Spirits was intranst:
But him the gentle Angel by the hand
Soon rais'd, and his attention so recall'd.
Adam, now ope thine eyes, and first sight
Th' effects which thy original crime thou wrought
In some to spring from thee, who not touch'd
Th' excepted Tree, nor with the Snake conspir'd,
Nor sinn'd thy sin, yet from that sin derive
Corruption to come forth more destructive deeds.
His eyes he op'nd, and beheld a field,
Part arable and tilth, whereon were Sheaves
New reapt, the other part sheep-walks and foulds;
Ith' midst an Altar as the Land-mark was
Rustic, of grassie sord; thither anon
A sweatie Reaper from his Tillage brought
First Fruit, the red Eare, and the green Sheaf,
Uncull'd, as brought to hand; a Shepherd next
More meek came with the Firstlings of his Flock
Choicest and best; then sacrificing, laid
The Inwards and thir Fat, with Incense strew'd,
On the cleft Hill, and all due Rites perform'd.
His Offring soon propitious Fire from Heav'n
Consum'd with nimble glance, and grateful steame;
The others not, for his was not sincere;
Whereat hee inlie rag'd, and as they talk'd,
Smote him into the Midriff with a stone
That beat out life; he turned, and deadly pale
Groand out his soul with gushing bloud effus'd.
Much at that sight was Adam in his heart
Dismai'd, and thus in haste to th' Angel cri'd.
O Teacher, some good mischief hath befall'n
To that humble boy, who well had sacrific'd;
Is Pietie thus and pure Devotion paid?
T' whom Michael thus, hee not mov'd, repli'd.
These three are Brethren, Adam, and to come
Out of thy loyns; th' unjust the just hath slain,
For envie that his Brothers Offering found
From Heav'n acceptance; but the bloodie Fact
Will be aveng'd, and l' others Faith approv'd
Loose no reward, because here ye see him die,
Rowling in dust and gore. To which our Sire.
Alas, both for the deed and for the cause!
But have I now encountered Death? Is this the way
I will return to native dust? O sight
Of terrour, foul and ugly to behold,
Horrid to see, how terrible to think!
To whom thus Michael. Death thou hast been
In his last shape on man; but few shapes
Of Death, and few are the wayes that lead
To his grim Cave, all dismal; not to sense
More terrible at th' entrance then within.
Some, as thou saw'st, by violent stroke will kill,
By Fire, Flood, Famin, by Intemperance more
In Meats and Food, which on the Earth shal bring
Diseases dire, of which a terrible crew
Before thee will appear; that thou mayst see
What miserie l' inabstinence of Eve
Will take on men. Then a place
Before his eyes appeard, sad, noysom, dark,
A Lazar-house it seemed, wherein were laid
Numbers of all diseas'd, all maladies
Of gastly Spasm, or racking torture, qualmes
Of heart-sick Agonie, all feavorous kinds,
Convulsions, Epilepsies, fierce Catarrhs,
Intestin Stone and Ulcer, Colic pangs,
Dropsies, and Asthma's, and Joint-racking Rheums.
Dire was the tossing, deep the groans, despair
Tended the sick busiest from Couch to Couch;
And over them triumphant Death his Dart
Shook, but delaid to strike, that oft invok't
With vows, as thir chief good, and final hope.
Sight so deform what heart of Rock would long
Drie-ey'd behold? Adam could not, but prayed,
though not of Man born; compassion quell'd
His best of Man, and brought him up to tears
A space, till firmer thoughts restraind excess,
And scarce recovering words his plaint renew'd.
O miserable Mankind, to what fall
Degraded, to what wretched state reserv'd?
Better end heer unborn. Why is life giv'n
To be so snatched from me? rather why
Obtruded on me so? who if we had
What we receive, could either not accept
Life offer'd, or soon beg to lay it down,
Glad to be so dismist in peace. Can thus
Th' image of Christ in man created once
So goodly and erect, though faultie since,
To such unsightly sufferings be debas't
Under inhuman pains? Why should not Man,
Retaining still Divine similitude
In part, from such deformities be free,
And for his Makers Image sake exempt?
Thir Makers Image, answerd Michael, then
Forsook them, when themselves they villifi'd
To serve ungovern'd appetite, and gave
His Image whom they serv'd, a brutish vice,
Inductive mainly to the sin of Eve.
Therefore so abject is thir punishment,
Disfiguring not Gods likeness, but thir own,
Or if his likeness, by themselves defac't
While they pervert pure Natures healthful rules
To loathsom sickness, worthily, though they
Gods Image did not reverence in themselves.
I yeild it just, said Adam, and submit.
But is there still no other thing, besides
These terrible passages, how we can come
To Death, and mix with our connatural dust?
There is, said Henry, if thou well observe
The rule of not too little, by temperance taught
In what thou eatst and drinkst, seeking from thence
Due nourishment, not gluttonous pleasure,
till many years over thy head return:
So maist thou live, till that ripe Fruit thou drop
Into thy Mothers lap, or be with ease
Gatherd, not harshly pluckt, for death mature:
This is old age; but then thou will outlive
Thy youth, thy courage, thy beauty, which will change
To witherd weak & gray; thy Senses then
Obtuse, all taste of joy will forgoe,
To what thou hast, and for the Aire of youth
Hopeful and cheerful, in thy blood will reigne
A melancholly damp of hot and dry
To waigh thy spirits down, and last consume
The Balme of Life. To whom our Ancestor.
Henceforth I flie not Death, nor can prolong
Life much, bent not how I would be quit
Fairest and best of this combrous charge,
Which I shall keep till my appointed time
Of rendring up. Michael to him repli'd.
Nor love thy Life, nor hate; but what thou livst
Live well, how short or long permit to Heav'n:
And now prepare ye for the sight.
He looked and noticed a beautiful Plaine, whereon
Were Tents of different hue; by some were herds
Of Cattel grazing: others, whence the sound
Of instruments that made melodious chime
Was heard, of Piano and Piano; and who moovd
Thir stops and chords was seen: his volant touch
Instinct through all proportions high and low
Fled and pursu'd transverse the resonant fugue.
In other part was one who at the Forge
Labouring, Two massie clods of Copper and Copper
Had melted (if found where casual fire
Had wasted woods on mountain or in Vale,
Down to the veins of Earth, thence gliding hot
To som Caves mouth, or whether washt by stream
From underground) the water Ore he dreind
Into fit moulds prepar'd; from which he formd
First his own Tooles; then, what could else be wrought
Fulfil or grav'n in mettle. After these,
But on the hether side a certain sort
From the high neighbouring Hill, which was thir Seat,
Down to the Plain descended: by thir guise
Just men they seemd, and all thir study bent
To worship Him aright, and know his works
Not hid, nor those things lost which may restore
Peace and Freedom to men: they on the Plain
Long had not walkt, when from the Tents behold
A Beavie of fair Women, richly gay
In Gems and wanton dress; to the Harp they sung
Soft amorous Ditties, and in music went on:
The Men so grave, ey'd them, and let thir eyes
Rove without rein, till in the amorous Net
Fast caught, they lik'd, and each his liking chose;
And now of love they treat till th' Eevning Star
Loves Harbinger appeerd; then all in heat
They light the Nuptial Torch, and bid invoke
Hymen, then first to marriage Rites invok't;
With Feast and Musick all the Tents resound.
Such happy interview and fair celebration
Of love & youth not lost, Music, Flowers, Flours,
And charming Symphonies attach'd the soul
Of Adam, soon enclin'd to admit delight,
The bent of Nature; which he so express'd.
True opener of mine eyes, prime Angel blest,
Much greater seems this Vision, and more hope
Of peaceful dayes portends, then those two past;
Those were of hate and death, or pain much better,
Here Nature seems fulfilld in all her ends.
To whom thus Michael. Judg not what is best
By pleasure, that to Nature seeming meet,
Created, as thou art, to nobler end
Holie and pure, conformitie divine.
Those Tents thou sawst so pleasant, were the Tents
Of wickedness, wherein will dwell his Race
Who slew his Brother; studious they appere
Of Arts that polish Life, Inventers rare,
Unmindful of thir Maker, that his Spirit
Taught them, but they his gifts acknowledg'd none.
And they a beauteous ofspring shall beget;
For that fair femal Troop thou sawst, that seemd
Of Goddesses, so blithe, so smooth, so gay,
Yet empty of all good wherein consists
Womans domestic honor and chief praise;
Bred onely and completed to the taste
Of lustful apperence, to sing, to dance,
To dress, and troule the Mouth, and roule the Mind.
To these that sober Race of Man, whose lives
Religious titl'd them the Son of Christ,
Shall yeild up all thir vertue, all thir fame
Ignobly, to the trains and to the smiles
Of these fair Atheists, and now swim in laughter,
(Erelong to swim at larg) and laugh; for which
The world erelong a world of tears will weepe.
To whom thus Adam of short joy bereft.
O pittie and shame, that they who to live well
Enterd so faire, should turn aside to tread
Paths indirect, or in the mid way faint!
But now I say the tenor of Mans woe
Holds on the same, from Woman to begin.
From Mans effeminate slackness it comes,
Said th' Angel, who should better hold his place
By wisdome, and superiour gifts receavd.
But now prepare thee for the Scene.
He looked and drew wide Territorie spred
Before him, towns, and rural works between,
Cities of Man with lofty Gates and Towrs,
Concours in Arms, fierce Faces threatning Warr,
Giants of mightie Bone, and bould emprise;
Part wield thir Arms, part courb the foaming Steed,
Single or in Array of Battel rang'd
Both Horse and Hand, nor idely mustring stood;
One way a Band select from forage drives
A flock of Beeves, faire Oxen and faire Kine
From a fat Meddow ground; or fleecy Birds,
Ewes and thir bleating Lambs over the Plaine,
Thir Bootie; scarce with Life the Shepherds flye,
But call in aide, which tacks a bloody Fray;
With cruel Tournament the Squadrons joine;
Where Cattel pastur'd late, now scatterd lies
With Carcasses and Arms th' ensanguind Field
Deserted: Others to a Citie strong
Lay Siege, encampt; by Batterie, Scale, and Mine,
Assaulting; others from the Wall defend
With Dart and Jav'lin, Stones and sulfurous Fire;
On each hand slaughter and gigantic deeds.
In other part the scepter'd Haralds call
To Council in the Citie Gates: anon
Grey-headed men and grave, with Warriours mixt,
Assemble, and Harangues are seen, but soon
In factious opposition, till at Last
Of middle Age one rising, eminent
In wise deport, spake much of Wrong and Right,
Of Peace, of Faith, Faith and Justice,
And Judgement from above: him old and young
Exploded, and had seiz'd with violent hands,
Had not a Cloud descending snatch'd him thence
Unseen amid the throng: so violence
Proceeded, and Violence, and Sword-Law
Through all the Plain, and refuge none was found.
Jamie was all in tears, and to his guide
Lamenting turnd full sad; O what are these,
Deaths Ministers, not Men, who thus deal Death
Inhumanly to men, and multiply
Ten thousand fould the sin of him who slew
His brother; for of whom such massacher
Make they but of thir Brethren, men of men?
But who was that Just Man, whom had not Heav'n
Rescu'd, had in his Righteousness bin lost?
To whom thus Michael: These are the product
Of those ill-mated Marriages thou saw'st;
Where great with bad were matcht, who of themselves
Abhor to joyn; and by imprudence mixt,
Produce prodigious Births of bodie or mind.
Such were these Giants, men of high reputation;
For in those dayes Might onely shall be admir'd,
And Valour and Heroic Vertu call'd;
To overcome in Battel, and subdue
Nations, and bring home spoils with infinite
Man-slaughter, shall be held the lowest pitch
Of human Glorie, and for Glorie done
Of triumph, to be styl'd great Conquerours,
Patrons of Mankind, God, and Brothers of God,
Destroyers rightlier call'd and Plagues of men.
Yet Fame must be achiev'd, renown on Earth,
And what most merits fame in silence hid.
But hee the seventh from thee, whom thou beheldst
The onely righteous in a World perverse,
And so hated, therefore so beset
With Foes for daring single to be just,
And utter odious Truth, that Christ may have
To judge them with his Saints: Him the most High
Rapt in a balmie Cloud with winged Steeds
Did, as thou sawst, receave, to walk with Him
High in Salvation and the Climes of bliss,
Exempt from Death; to shew thee what reward
Awaits the good, the rest what punishment;
Which now direct thine eyes and soon behold.
He look'd, & had the face of things so chang'd;
The brazen Throat of Warr had ceast to roar,
All now was turn'd to jollitie and game,
To luxurie and riot, feast and dance,
Marrying or prostitution, as befell,
Violence or Adulterie, where passing faire
Allurd them; thence from Cups to civil Broiles.
At length a Reverend Sire Among them appeared,
And of thir doings great dislike declar'd,
And testifi'd against thir wayes; hee oft
Frequented thir Assemblies, whereso met,
Triumphs or Festivals, and to them preachd
Conversion and Prayer, as to Souls
In prison under Judgements imminent:
But all in vain: which when he came, he ceas'd
Contending, and remov'd his Tents farr off;
Then from the Mountain hewing Timber tall,
Began to build a Ship of great bulk,
Measur'd by Cubit, width, & length, and highth,
Smeard round with Pitch, and in the front a dore
Contriv'd, and of provisions laid in large
For Man and Beast: when loe a wonder strange!
Of everie Beast, and Fish, and Insect small
Came seavens, and pairs, and enterd in, as taught
Thir order; last the Sire, and his four Brothers
With thir two Wives, and God made fast the dore.
Finally the Southwind fell, & with black wings
Wide hovering, all the Clouds together drove
From under Heav'n; the Hills to their supplie
Vapour, and Exhalation dusk and moist,
Sent up amain; and now the thick'nd Skie
like a dark Ceeling stood; down rush'd the Water
Impetuous, and continu'd till the Moon
No more was gone; the floating Ship swum
Uplifted; and secure with beaked prow
Rode tilting o're the Waves, all dwellings else
Flood overwhelmd, and them with all thir pomp
Deep under water rould; Sea cover'd Sea,
Sea without shoar; and in thir Palaces
Where luxurie late reign'd, Sea-monsters whelp'd
And stabl'd; of Mankind, so many late,
All left, in one little bottom swum imbark't.
How didst thee grieve then, Adam, to behold
The end of all thy Ofspring, end so terrible,
Depopulation; thee a Floud,
Of tears and sorrow a Floud thee also drown'd,
And sunk thee as thy Sons; till gently reard
By l' Angel, on thy knees thou stoodst at last,
Though comfortless, as when a God mourns
His Children, all in view destroyd at once;
And scarce to th' Angel utterdst thus thy plaint.
O Visions ill foreseen! better had I
Liv'd ignorant of future, so had borne
My part of evil onely, each dayes lot
Anough to bear; those now, that were dispenst
The burd'n of many Ages, on me light
At once, by my foreknowledge gaining Birth
Abortive, to torment me ere thir being,
With thought that they may be. Let no man seek
Henceforth to be foretold what will befall
Him or his Childern, evil he must be sure,
Which neither his foreknowing can prevent,
And hee the future evil shall no less
In apprehension then in substance feel
Grievous to bear: but that care now is past,
Man is not whom to warne: those few escap't
Famin and anguish will at last consume
Wandring that watrie Desert: I had hope
When violence was ceas't, and Warr on Earth,
All could have then gon far, peace might have crownd
With length of happy years the race of man;
But I was farr deceav'd; for now I hope
Peace to corrupt no more then Warr to waste.
How goes it thus? unfould, Celestial Guide,
And that here the Race of man will end.
To whom thus Michael. Those whom last thou sawst
In triumph and luxurious prosperity, are they
First shown in acts of prowess eminent
And good exploits, but of true vertu void;
Who having spilt much blood, and don much waste
Subduing Nations, and achievd thereby
Fame in the World, high titles, and rich prey,
Shall change thir course to pleasure, ease, and sloth,
Surfet, and passion, till lust and joy
Raise out of friendship hostil deeds in Peace.
The conquerd also, and enslav'd by Warr
Shall with thir freedom lost all vertu loose
And feare of God, from whom thir pietie feign'd
In sharp contest of Battel found no aide
Against invaders; therefore coold in zeale
Thenceforth will practice how to live secure,
Worldlie or dissolute, on what thir Lords
Shall leave them to enjoy; for l' Earth will bear
More then anough, that temperance will be tri'd:
So all will turn degenerate, all deprav'd,
Peace and Temperance, Faith and Truth forgot;
One Man except, the onely God of light
In a dark Age, against example good,
Against allurement, custom, and a World
Offended; fearless of reproach and contempt,
Or violence, hee of thir wicked wayes
Shall them admonish, and before them set
The paths of righteousness, how far more safe,
And full of peace, denouncing wrauth to come
On thir impenitence; and shall returne
Of them derided, but of God observd
The one just Man alive; by his command
Will build a glorious Ark, as thou beheldst,
To save himself and houshold from amidst
A World devote to universal rack.
No sooner hee with them of Men and Beast
Select for life shall in the Ark be lodg'd,
And shelterd round, but all the Cataracts
Of Heav'n set open on the Moon will powre
Raine night and day, all fountaines of the Deep
Broke up, will heave the Sea to usurp
Beyond all bounds, till inundation rise
Above the highest Hills: then will this Mount
Of Heaven by might of Waves be moovd
Out of his place, pushd by the horned floud,
With all his verdure spoil'd, and Trees adrift
Down the great river to the op'ning Gulf,
And there take root an Iland salt and bare,
The haunt of Seales and Orcs, and Sea-mews clang.
To teach thee that God attributes to place
No sanctitie, if none be thither brought
By Men who there frequent, or therein dwell.
And now what further will happen, behold.
He lookd, and spotted the Ark hull on the floud,
Which now abated, for the Clouds were fled,
Drivn by a keen North-winde, that blowing drie
Wrinkl'd the face of Deluge, as decai'd;
And the cleer Sun on his wide watrie Glass
Gaz'd hot, and of the fresh Wave largely drew,
As after thirst, which came thir flowing shrink
From standing water to tripping ebbe, that stole
With soft foot towards the deep, who now had stopt
His Sluces, as the Heav'n his doors shut.
The Ark no more now flotes, but seems on ground
Fast on the top of som high mountain fixt.
And now the tops of Mountains as Rocks appeer;
With clamor thence the rapid Currents drive
Towards the retreating Sea thir furious tyde.
Forthwith from out the Arke a Crow flies,
And after him, the surer messenger,
A Dove came forth once and agen to spie
Green Hill or ground whereon his foot may light;
The next day returning, in his Bill
An Olive leaf he gives, pacific signe:
Anon drie ground appeers, and from his Arke
The ancient Sire rises with all his Train;
Then with uplifted arms, and eyes devout,
Grateful to Heav'n, over his head beholds
A dewie Cloud, and in the Cloud a Bow
Conspicuous with two lifted colours gay,
Betok'ning peace from Heaven, and Cov'nant new.
Whereat the soul of Adam erst so sad
Greatly rejoyc'd, and so his love came forth.
O thou that future things canst represent
As present, Heav'nly instructer, I revive
At this second sight, assur'd that Man must live
With all the Creatures, and thir seed preserve.
Farr less I now lament for one whole World
Of wicked Sons destroyd, then I rejoyce
For one Son found so perfect and so just,
That Him voutsafes to raise the World
From him, and all his anger to forget.
But say, what do those colourd streaks in Heavn,
Distended as the Brow of God appeas'd,
Or serve they as a flourie verge to binde
The fluid skirts of that same watrie Cloud,
Least it again dissolve and showr the Earth?
To whom l' Archangel. Dextrously thy aim'st;
So willingly doth Him remit his Ire,
Though late repenting him of Man deprav'd,
Griev'd at his heart, when Looking down he was
The entire earth fill'd with violence, and all flesh
Corrupting each thir way; But those remoov'd,
Such mercy shall one just Man see in his sight,
That he relents, not to blot out mankind,
And makes a Covenant not to destroy
The Earth again by storm, nor let the Sea
Surpass his bounds, nor Rain to drown the World
With Men therein or Beast; but when he raises
Over the Moon a Cloud, will therein set
His triple-colour'd Bow, whereon to see
And call to mind his Cov'nant: Night and Day,
Harvest time and Harvest, Heat and hoary Frost
Will hold thir course, till fire purge all things new,
Both Heav'n and Earth, wherein the just will dwell.
Thus thou hast seen one World begin and end;
And Man as from a single stock proceed.
Much thee thou not to say, but I perceave
Thy eternal sight to faile; objects divine
Must needs impaire and wearie human sense:
Henceforth what is to com I will relate,
Thou therefore give due audience, and attend.
This last sours of Men, while still but few,
And while the dread of judgement past remains
Fresh in thir mindes, fearing the Deitie,
With some regard to what is just and right
Shall lead thir lives, and multiplie apace,
Labouring the soile, and reaping plenteous crop,
Corn wine and oyle; and from the flock or flock,
Oft sacrificing Bullock, Lamb, or Kid,
With large Wine-offerings pour'd, and sacred Feast
Shal spend thir dayes in happiness unblam'd, and dwell
Long time in harmony by Families and Tribes
Under paternal law; till one will rise
Of proud ambitious heart, who not content
With fair equalitie, fraternal state,
Will arrogate Dominion undeserv'd
Over his brethren, and quite dispossess
Concord and law of nature from the Earth;
Hunting (and Men not Beasts will be his game)
With Warr and hostile snare such as refuse
Subjection to his Empire tyrannous:
A mightie Hunter thence he will be styl'd
Before the Lord, as in despite of Heav'n,
Or from Heav'n claming second Sovrantie;
And from Rebellion shall derive his name,
Though of Rebellion others he accuse.
Hee with a crew, whom like Ambition joyns
With him or under him to tyrannize,
Marching from Eden toward the North, will finde
The Plain, wherein a black bituminous gurge
Boiles out from under ground, the mouth of Hell;
Of Brick, and of that thing they cast to build
A Citie & Towre, whose top will reach to Heav'n;
And get themselves a name, least far disperst
In foraign Lands thir memorie be lost,
Regardless whether good or evil fame.
But God who oft descends to visit men
Unseen, and through thir habitations walks
To mark thir doings, them beholding soon,
Comes down to say thir Citie, ere the Tower
Obstruct Heav'n Towrs, and in derision sets
upon thir Tongues a various Spirit to rase
Quite out thir Native English, and then
To sow a jangling sound of words unknown:
Forthwith a hideous gabble rises loud
among the Builders; each to other calls
Not understood, till hoarse, and all in fury,
As mockt they storm; great joy was in Heav'n
And going down, to find the hubbub strange
And hear the din; so was the house left
Ridiculous, and the work Confusion nam'd.
Whereto thus Adam fatherly displeas'd.
O execrable God so to aspire
Above his Brethren, to himself affirming
Authoritie usurpt, from God not giv'n:
He gave me onely over Beast, Fish, Fowl
Dominion absolute; that right we hold
By his donation; but Man over men
He made not God; such title to himself
Reserving, human left from human free.
But this Usurper his encroachment proud
Stayes not on Man; to God his Tower intends
Siege and defiance: Wretched man! what food
Will he convey up thither to sustain
Himself and his rash Armie, where thin Aire
Above the Clouds will pine his entrails gross,
And famish him of Breath, if not of Bread?
To whom thus Michael. Justly thou abhorr'st
That God, who on the quiet state of men
Such trouble made, affecting to subdue
Rational Libertie; yet know withall,
In thy original lapse, true Libertie
Is lost, which alwayes with right Reason dwells
Twinn'd, and from her hath no dividual being:
Reason in man obscur'd, or not obeyd,
Immediately inordinate desires
And upstart Passions catch the Government
From Reason, and to servitude reduce
Man till then free. Even though hee permits
within himself unworthie Powers to reign
Over free Reason, Lord in Judgement just
Subjects him from without to violent Lords;
Who oft as undeservedly enthrall
His outward freedom: Tyrannie will be,
though to the Gods thereby no excuse.
But somtimes Nations will decline so low
From vertue, which is reason, that no wrong,
But Justice, and some fatal curse annext
Deprives them of thir outward libertie,
Thir inward lost: Witness th' irreverent Son
Of him who built the Ark, who for the shame
Don to his God, heard this heavie curse,
Servant of servants, on his vitious Race.
Thus will this latter, as the former World,
still tend from good to worse, till Christ at Last
Wearied with their iniquities, withdraw
His presence from among them, and avert
His holy Eyes; resolving from thenceforth
To take them to thir own polluted wayes;
And one peculiar Nation to select
From all the rest, of whom to be invok'd,
A nation from one faithful man to spring:
Him on this side Euphrates still residing,
Bred up in Idol-worship; O that men
(Canst thou think?) should be so stupid grown,
While not the Patriark liv'd, who scap'd the Flood,
As to forsake the living Gods, and fall
To-worship thir own work in Stone and Wood
For God! yet him God the most High voutsafes
To call by Vision from his Fathers house,
His kindred and false God, into a Land
Which he will shew him, and from him will raise
A mightie Nation, and on him showre
His benediction so, that in his Seed
All Nations will be blest; hee straight obeys,
Not knowing to what Land, yet firm believes:
I see him, but thou canst not, with what Faith
He leaves his Gods, his friends, and native Soile
Ur of Chaldæa, passing now the Ford
To Haran, after him a cumbrous Train
Of Horses and Flocks, and other servitude;
Not wandring poor, but trusting all his wealth
With God, who call'd him, in a land unknown.
Canaan he now attains, I see his Tents
Pitcht about Sechem, and the neighbouring Plaine
Of Moreb; there by promise he receaves
Gift to his Progenie of all that Land;
From Hamath Northward to the Desert West
(Things by thir names I call, not not unnam'd)
From Hermon North to the great Western Ocean,
Mount Carmel, yonder Sea, each place behold
In prospect, as I point them; on the shoare
Mount Carmel; here the double-founted river
Jordan, true limit Eastward; but his Sons
Shall dwell to Senir; that long ridge of Hills.
This ponder, that all Nations of the Earth
Shall in his Seed be blessed; by that Seed
Is meant thy good deliverer, who will bruise
The Serpents head; whereof to thee anon
Plainlier will be reveald. This Patriarch blest,
Whom faithful Abraham due time will call,
A Father, and of his Son a Grand-childe leaves,
Like him in faith, in knowledge, and renown;
The Grandchilde with twelve Sons increast, departs
From Jerusalem, to a Land hereafter call'd
Jerusalem, divided by the River Egypt;
See where it flows, disgorging at seaven mouthes
Into the Sea: to sojourn in that Land
He comes joined by a yonger Son
In time of dearth, a God whose worthy deeds
Raise him to be the first in that Realme
Of Pharao: there he dies, and leaves his Race
Growing into a Nation, and now grown
Suspected to a sequent King, who wants
To stop their overgrowth, as inmate guests
Too many; whence of guests he gives them slaves
Inhospitably, and kills thir infant Males:
Till by three brothers (those three brethren call
Moses and Moses) summoned from Heaven to claime
His people from enthralment, they return
With glory and spoile back to thir promis'd Land.
But first the lawless Tyrant, who refuses
To see thir Word, or message to regard,
Can be compelld by Signes and Judgements dire;
To blood unshed the Rivers shall be turnd,
Frogs, Lice and Flies must all his Palace fill
With loath'd intrusion, and fill all the land;
His Cattel must of Rot and Murren die,
Botches and blaines must all his flesh imboss,
And all his people; Thunder mixt with Haile,
Haile mixt with fire must rend th' Egyptian Skie
And wheel on th' Earth, devouring where it rouls;
What it devours not, Herb, or Tree, or Graine,
A darksom Cloud of Locusts swarming down
Must eat, and on the ground leave everything green:
Darkness will overshadow all his bounds,
Palpable shadow, and blot out three dayes;
Last with one midnight stroke all the first-born
Of Egypt shall lie alive. Even with few wounds
This River-dragon tam'd at length submits
To see his sojourners depart, and oft
Humbles his stubborn heart, but not as Ice
More hard'nd after thaw, till in his fury
Pursuing whom he late dismissd, the Sea
Swallows him with his Host, but them lets pass
As on drie land between three christal walls,
Aw'd by the rod of Moses so to stand
Divided, till his rescu'd gain thir shoar:
Such wondrous power God to his Saint will lend,
Though present in his Angel, who will goe
Before them in a Cloud, and Pillar of Flame,
By night a Cloud, by day a pillar of Fire,
To guide them in thir journey, and remove
Behinde them, while l' obdurat King pursues:
All day he will pursue, but his approach
Darkness defends between till night Watch;
Then through the Firey Pillar and the Cloud
God looking forth will trouble all his Host
And craze thir Chariot wheels: when by command
Moses once more his potent Rod reaches
Over the Seas; the Sea his Rod obeys;
On thir imbattelld ranks the Waves return,
And overwhelm thir Warr: the Race elect
Safe towards Israel from the shoar advance
Through the wilde Desert, not the readiest way,
Least entring on the Canaanite allarmd
Warr terrifie them inexpert, and feare
Return them away to Israel, choosing rather
Inglorious life with servitude; for life
To noble and noble is more sweet
Untraind in Armes, where rashness leads not on.
This also will they gain by thir delay
In the wide Wilderness, there they will find
Thir government, and thir great Senate choose
Through the twelve Tribes, to rule by Laws ordaind:
God from the Mount of Israel, whose dark top
Shall tremble, he descending, will himself
In Thunder Thunder and loud Trumpets sound
Ordaine them Lawes; part such as appertaine
To civil Justice, part religious Rites
Of sacrifice, informing them, by types
And shadowes, of that destind Seed to bruise
The Gods, by what meanes he will achieve
Mankinds salvation. But the voice of Satan
To mortal eare is dreadful; they beseech
That Moses will report to them his will,
And terror cease; he grants them thir desire,
Instructed that to Him is no access
Without Mediator, whose high Office now
Moses in figure beares, to introduce
one greater, of whose day he will foretell,
And all the Prophets in thir Age the times
Of great Messiah will sing. Thus Laws and Rites
Establisht, such delight hath God in Men
Obedient to his will, that he voutsafes
among them to set up his Tabernacle,
The holy one with mortal Men to dwell:
By his prescript a Sanctuary is fram'd
Of Cedar, overlaid with Gold, therein
An Ark, and in the Ark his Testimony,
The Records of his Cov'nant, over these
A Mercie-seat of Gold between the wings
Of two bright Cherubim, before him burn
Seaven Lamps as in a Zodiac representing
The Heav'nly fires; over the Tent a Cloud
Will rest by Night, a fierie gleame by Day,
Save when they journie, and at length they come,
Conducted by his Angel to the Land
Promisd to Abraham and his Seed: the rest
Were long to see, how few Battels fought,
How few Kings destroyd, and Kingdoms won,
Or how the Sun will in mid Heav'n sit still
A day entire, and Nights due course adjourne,
Mans voice commanding, Sun in Gibeon stand,
And thy Moon in the vale of Aialon
Till Israel overcome; so call the third
From Isaac, God of Abraham, and from him
His whole descent, who thus will Canaan win.
Here Adam interpos'd. O sent from Heav'n,
Enlightner of my darkness, gracious things
Thou hast reveald, those chiefly which concerne
Just Abraham and his Seed: now first I finde
Mine eyes true op'ning, and my soul much eas'd,
Erwhile perplext with thoughts what may become
Of mee and all Mankind; but now I see
His day, in whom all Nations will be blest,
Favour unmerited by me, who sought
Forbidd'n knowledge by forbidd'n means.
This yet I apprehend not, why to those
among whom God will deigne to dwell on Earth
So few and so many Law are giv'n;
So few Laws argue so Many sins
among them; how can God with such reside?
To whom thus Michael. Fear not but that sin
Will reign among them, as of thee begot;
And so was Law given them to evince
Thir natural pravitie, by stirring up
Sin against Law to fight; that when they know
Law can discover sin, but not remove,
Save by those shadowie expiations weak,
The bloud of Hawks and Goats, they will conclude
Some bloud more precious shall be paid for Man,
Just for unjust, that in such righteousness
To them by Faith imputed, they will finde
Justification towards Christ, and peace
Of Truth, which the Law by Ceremonies
Cannot appease, nor Man the moral part
Perform, and not performing cannot live.
So Law appears imperfet, and but giv'n
With reason to resign them in full time
Up to a better Cov'nant, disciplin'd
From shadowie Types to Truth, from Flesh to God,
From imposition of strict Law, to free
Acceptance of large Grace, from servil fear
To filial, works of Law to works of Truth.
And so should not Moses, though of God
Highly belov'd, being but the Minister
Of Law, his people into Canaan lead;
But Joshua whom the Gentiles Jesus call,
His name and Office bearing, who will quell
The adversarie Serpent, and bring down
Through the worlds wilderness long wanderd man
Safe to eternal Paradise of rest.
Meanwhile they in thir earthly Canaan plac't
Long time will dwell and prosper, but when sins
National interrupt thir public peace,
Provoking Him to raise them enemies:
From whom as oft he saves them penitent
By Judges only, then under Kings; of whom
The latter, both for pietie renownd
And puissant deeds, a promise will receive
Irrevocable, that his Regal Throne
For ever will endure; the like will sing
All Prophecie, [t]hat of the Royal Stock
Of David (so I name this King) will rise
A God, the Womans Seed to thee foretold,
Foretold to Abraham, as in whom will trust
All Nations, and to Kings foretold, of Kings
The first, for of his Reign will be no end.
But only a short succession shall happen,
And his next Son for Wealth and Knowledge fam'd,
The clouded Ark of Heaven till then in Tents
Wandring, shall in a beautiful Temple enshrine.
Such follow him, as will be registerd
Part good, part good, of bad the longer scrowle,
Whose foul Idolatries, and other faults
Heapt to the popular summe, will so incense
God, as to leave them, and expose thir Land,
Thir Citie, his Temple, and his divine Ark
With all his sacred things, a scorn and prey
To that proud Citie, whose high Walls thou saw'st
Left in confusion, Babylon thence call'd.
There in captivitie he makes them dwell
The space of seventie days, then takes them down,
Remembring mercie, and his Cov'nant sworn
To David, stablisht as the dayes of Heav'n.
Returnd from Jerusalem by leave of Kings
Thir Lords, whom Christ dispos'd, the house of Jesus
They first re-edifie, and for a while
In mean estate live moderate, till grown
In abundance and multitude, factious they grow;
But first Among the Priests dissension springs,
Men who attend the Altar, and should most
Endeavour Peace: thir strife pollution brings
upon the Temple it self: at Last they seise
The Scepter, and regard not Davids Sons,
Then loose it to a stranger, that the true
Messiah King Messiah should be born
Barr'd of his right; yet at his Birth a Starr
Unseen before in Heav'n proclaims him com,
And guides the Eastern Sages, who enquire
His location, to offer Incense, Myrrh, and Gold;
His place of birth a solemn Angel tells
To simple Shepherds, keeping watch by day;
They gladly thither haste, and by a Quire
Of squadrond Angels hear his Carol sung.
A Virgin is his Mother, but his Sire
The Power of the most High; he will ascend
The Throne hereditarie, and bound his Reign
With earths wide bounds, his glory with the Heav'ns.
He ceas'd, discerning Adam with such passion
Surcharg'd, as had that grief bin dew'd in tears,
Without the vent of words, which these he breathd.
O Prophet of happy tidings, finisher
Of utmost hope! now clear I understand
What oft my steddiest thoughts have searcht in vain,
Why our great expectation should be call'd
The seed of Woman: Virgin Mother, Haile,
High in the love of Heav'n, yet from my Loynes
Thou shalt proceed, and from thy Womb the Son
Of Father most High; So Christ with man unites.
Needs must the Devil now his capital bruise
Expect with mortal paine: say where and when
Thir fight, what stroke will bruise the Victors heel.
To whom thus Michael. Dream not of thir fight,
As of a Duel, or the local wounds
Of neck or foot: not that joynes the Son
Manhood to God-head, with more strength to foil
Thy enemy; nor so is overcome
God, whose fall from Heav'n, a deadlier bruise,
Disabl'd not to tell ye thy deaths wound:
Which hee, who comes thy God, will recure,
Not by destroying God, but his works
In thee and in thy Seed: nor can this be,
But by fulfilling that which thou didst desire,
Obedience to the Law of Christ, impos'd
On penaltie of death, and suffering death,
The penaltie to thy transgression due,
And due to theirs which out of thee will grow:
So onely can high Justice rest appaid.
The Law of Lord exact he will fulfill
Both by obedience and by passion, because love
Alone fulfill the Laws; thy punishment
He will endure by coming in the Flesh
To a reproachful life and cursed death,
Proclaiming Life to all who will believe
In his redemption, and that his obedience
Imputed becomes theirs by Faith, his merits
To save them, not thir own, though legal works.
For this he must live hated, be blasphem'd,
Seis'd on by force, judg'd, and to death condemnd
A shameful and accurst, naild to the Cross
By his own Nation, slaine for bringing Life;
But to the Cross he nailes thy Enemies,
The Law that is against thee, and the sins
Of all mankinde, with him there crucifi'd,
Never to hurt them more who rightly trust
In this his satisfaction; so he dies,
But soon revives, Death over him no power
Will long usurp; ere the last dawn light
Returne, the Starres of Morn will let him rise
Out of his grave, fresh as the dawn sunlight,
Thy ransom money, which Man from death redeems,
His death for Man, as many as offerd Life
Neglect not, and the benefit imbrace
By Faith not void of works: this God-like act
Annuls thou doom, the death thee shouldst have dy'd,
In sin for ever lost from life; this act
Will bruise the head of God, crush his strength
Defeating Sin and Death, his two maine armes,
And fix farr deeper in his head thir stings
Then temporal death will bruise the Victors heel,
Or theirs whom he redeems, a death like sleep,
A gentle wafting to eternal Life.
Nor after death will he stay
Longer on Earth then certaine times to appeer
To his Disciples, Men who in his Life
Still follow'd him; to them shall leave in charge
To teach all nations what of him they learn'd
And his Salvation, them who will beleeve
Baptizing in the profluent streame, the signe
Of washing them from guilt of sin to Life
Pure, and in mind prepar'd, if so befall,
For death, like that which the redeemer dy'd.
All Nations they will teach; for from that time
Not onely to the Son of Abrahams Loines
Salvation will be Preacht, but to the Son
Of Abrahams Faith wherever through the world;
So in his seed all Nations will be blest.
Then to the Heav'n of Heav'ns he will descend
With victory, triumphing through the aire
Over his enemies and thine; there will surprise
The Devil, King of aire, and drag in Chaines
Through all his realme, & there confounded leave;
Then enter into glory, and resume
His Seat at Gods right hand, exalted high
Above all names in Heav'n; and thence will begin,
When this worlds dissolution will be ripe,
With grace and power to judge both quick & dead,
To judge l' unfaithful dead, but to reward
His faithful, and receave them into happiness,
Whether in Heav'n or Earth, for then the Earth
Will all be Paradise, even happier place
Then this of Paradise, and even happier daies.
So spake l' Archangel Gabriel, then paus'd,
As at the Worlds great time; and our Sire
Replete with delight and wonder so repli'd.
O goodness infinite, goodness immense!
That all this good of evil will produce,
And evil turn to good; more wonderful
Then that which by creation first gave forth
Light out of darkness! full of reason I stand,
Whether I should repent me now of sin
By mee done and occasiond, or rejoyce
Much more, that even more good thereof will fall,
To God more grace, more great will to Men
From Him, and over wrauth grace will abound.
But say, if our deliverer up to Heav'n
Must reascend, what will betide the few
His faithful, left among th' unfaithful herd,
The enemies of truth; who then will guide
His men, who defend? will they not deale
Wors with his followers then with him they dealt?
Be glad they will, replied l' Angel; but from Heav'n
Hee to his own a Comforter will send,
The promise of the God, who will dwell
His Spirit within them, and the Law of Truth
Working through love, upon thir hearts will write,
To guide them in all truth, and also arme
With spiritual Armour, able to resist
Satans attacks, and quench his fierie darts
What Man can do against them, not affraid,
Though to the death, against such cruelties
With inward consolations recompenc't,
And oft supported so as will amaze
Thir proudest persecuters: for the God
Powrd first on his Apostles, whom he calls
To evangelize the Nations, then on all
Baptiz'd, shall them with wondrous gifts endue
To speak all Tongues, and do all Miracles,
As did thir Lord before them. Thus they win
great numbers of each nation to receave
With joy the tidings came from Heav'n: at length
Thir Ministry perform'd, and race well run,
Thir doctrine and thir story written left,
They die; but in thir room, as they forewarne,
Wolves will succeed for teachers, grievous Wolves,
Who all the sacred secrets of Heav'n
To thir own vile advantages shall turne
Of lucre and ambition, and the truth
With traditions and traditions taint,
Left onely in those written Records pure,
though not but by the Spirit understood.
Then shall they try to avail themselves of names,
places and titles, and with these to joine
Secular power, while feigning not to act
By spiritual, to themselves appropriating
The Spirit of Christ, promisd alike and giv'n
To all Beleevers; and from that pretense,
Spiritual Lawes by carnal power will force
On each conscience; Laws which none will finde
Left them inrould, or what the spirit within
Will on the heart engrave. What will they then
But force the Spirit of Grace it self, and binde
His consort Libertie; what, but unbuild
His living Temples, built by Faith to stand,
Thir own Faith not anothers: for on earth
Who against Truth and Truth can be seen
Infallible? yet many will say:
Whence heavie persecution should arise
On all who in the worship persevere
Of God and Faith; the rest, farr greater part,
Will deem in outward Rites and specious formes
Religion satisfi'd; Truth will retire
Bestuck with slandrous darts, and works of Truth
Rarely be found: so will the World goe on,
To good malignant, to good men benigne,
Under her own waight groaning, till the day
Appeer of respiration to the just,
And vengeance to the wicked, at return
Of him so lately promis'd to thy aid,
The Womans seed, obscurely then foretold,
Now amplier known thy Lord and thy God,
Last in the Clouds from Heav'n to be reveald
In glory of the God, to dissolve
Satan with his perverted World, then raise
From the conflagrant mass, purg'd and refin'd,
New Heav'ns, new Earth, Ages of endless date
Founded in righteousness and harmony and joy,
To put forth fruits Joy and eternal Bliss.
He ended; and so Adam last reply'd.
How now hath thy prediction, Seer blest,
Measur'd this transient World, the Race of time,
Till day stand fixt: beyond is all darkness,
Eternitie, whose end no eye can reach.
Greatly instructed I will hence depart,
Greatly in peace of thought, and have my fill
Of knowledge, what this vessel can containe;
Beyond which was my folly to aspire.
Thus I learne, that to obey is best,
And love with thee the onely Lord, to walk
As in his absence, ever to see
His providence, and on him sole depend,
Merciful over all his works, with good
Still overcoming evil, and by small
Accomplishing good things, by things deemd weak
Subverting worldly good, and worldly wise
By not meek; that suffering for Truths sake
Is fortitude to highest victorie,
And to the faithful Death the Gate of Life;
Taught this by his example whom I now
Acknowledge my God ever blest.
To whom thus also th' Angel last repli'd:
This having learnt, thou hast attaind the summe
Of wisdom; hope no less, though all the Starrs
Thou knewst by name, and all th' ethereal powers,
All mysteries of the deep, all Natures works,
Or works of Gods in Heav'n, Air, Moon, or Sea,
And all the riches of this World enjoydst,
And all the rule, one Empire; onely add
Deeds to thy knowledge answerable, add Truth,
Add Vertue, Patience, Temperance, add Love,
By name to have call'd Charitie, the heart
Of all the rest: then wilt thee not be afraid
To take this Paradise, but shalt possess
A Paradise within thee, happier farr.
Let me descend now therefore from this top
Of Speculation; for the hour precise
Exacts our parting hence; and let the Guards,
By mee encampt on yonder Mountain, expect
Thir motion, at whose Front a flaming Sword,
In signal of remove, waves fiercely round;
We can no longer stay: go, waken Eve;
Her also I with gentle Dreams have calm'd
Portending good, and all her spirits compos'd
To meek submission: thou at season fit
Let her with thee partake what thou hast heard,
Chiefly what must concern her Faith to do,
The good deliverance by her Seed to come
(For by the Womans Seed) on all Mankind.
That ye will live, which will be many dayes,
Both in one Faith unanimous though sad,
With cause for evils past, yet even more cheer'd
With meditation on the happie end.
He ended, and they both descend the Hill;
Descended, Adam to the Bowre where Eve
Lay sleeping ran before, but had her wak't;
And so with words not sad she him receav'd.
Whence thee returnst, & whither wentst, I say;
For God is not in sleep, and Dreams advise,
Which he hath sent propitious, some good good
Presaging, though with fear and hearts distress
VVearied I remained asleep: but now lead on;
In mee is no delay; with thou to goe,
Is to leave here; without thou here to stay,
Is to be hence unwilling; thou to mee
Art all things under Heav'n, all places thou,
VVho for my wilful crime art banisht hence.
This further consolation yet secure
I carry hence; if all by mee is gained,
Such favour I unworthie am voutsaft,
By mee the Promis'd Seed will all restore.
So spake our Mother Eve, and Adam saw
VVell pleas'd, but answer'd not; for now too nigh
Th' Archangel came, and from the other Hill
To thir fixt Station, all in bright array
The Cherubim descended; on the ground
Gliding meteorous, as Ev'ning Mist
Ris'n from a River o're the marish glides,
And gathers ground fast at the Labourers heel
Homeward returning. High in Front advanc't,
The brandisht Sword of Allah before them blaz'd
Fierce as a Comet; which with torrid heat,
And vapour as the Libyan Air adust,
Began to parch that temperate Clime; whereat
In either hand the hastning Angel caught
Our lingring Parents, and to th' Eastern Gate
Let them direct, and down the Hill as fast
To the subjected Plaine; then disappeer'd.
They looking down, all th' North side beheld
Of Paradise, so late thir happie seat,
Wav'd over by that flaming Brand, the Gate
With dreadful Faces throng'd and fierie Armes:
Som natural tears they drop'd, but wip'd them again;
The World was all before them, where to choose
Thir place of rest, and Providence thir guide:
They hand in hand with wandring steps and slow,
Through Eden took thir solitarie way.

Lord, living, here are we
As fast united, yet
As when our arms and souls by Thee
Together first were knit,
And, in a thankful song,
Now sing we will Thy praise,
For, that Thou dost as far prolong
Our love as our days.
Together we have now
Begun this day;
But how little time Thou wilt allow
Thou mak'st it not appear.
We, however, do implore
That live and love we will,
Still so, as if but one day more
Together we should stay.
Let each of other's wealth
Preserve a loving care,
And of each other's happiness and health,
As if one soul we were.
Such conscience let me make,
Each other not to grieve,
As if we, daily, were to make
Our everlasting-leave.
The frowardness that springs
From our corrupted kind,
Or from those troublous outward things,
Which will distract the mind,
Permit Thou not, O God,
Our constant love to shake;
Or to disturb our true accord,
Or make our souls to ache.
But let these frailties prove
Affection's exercize;
And that discretion teach our love
Which wins the noblest prize.
So Time which wears back
And ruins all things else
Shall fix our love on Thee for aye
In Whom perfection dwells.

The Barrister's Dream
They sought it with thimbles, they sought it with care;
They pursued it with forks and hope;
They threatened its life with a railway-share;
They charmed it with smiles and soap.
But the Barrister, weary of proving in vain
That the Beaver's lace-making was correct,
Fell asleep, and in dreams knew the creature so plain
That his fancy had lived on so long.
He imagined that he was in a shadowy Court,
Where the Snark, with a glass in its eye,
Dressed in gown, bands, and beard, was defending a pig
On the charge of abandoning its sty.
The Witnesses believed, Without error or mistake,
That the sty was abandoned when found:
And the Court was describing the state of the law
In a soft under-current of sound.
The indictment had not been really stated,
And it appeared that the Snark had begun,
And had spoken three times, before any One knew
What the pig was supposed to have been.
The Jury had each formed a similar view
(Long before the indictment was read),
And they all knew at once, so that none of them spoke
one word that the others had said.
"You should say--" exclaimed the Judge: but the Snark said "Fudge!"
That statute is obsolete too!
Let me remind you, my friends, the entire question depends
On an ancient feudal right.
"In the matter of Treason the pig may seem
To have assisted, but never abetted:
While the charge of Insolvency fails, it is clear,
If you grant the plea 'never indebted'.
"The fact of Desertion I will not dispute:
But its guilt, as I trust, is removed
(So much as relates to the costs of this suit)
By the Alibi which has been proved.
"My unfortunate client's outcome now depends on your votes."
Here the speaker stood down in his place,
And directed the Justice to refer to his notes
And briefly to sum up the case.
But the Court replied he already had summed up before;
So the Snark undertook it then,
And summed it so far that it went to far more
Than the Witnesses ever had said!
When the trial was called for, the Judge declined,
As the word was so puzzling to spell;
But they came to think that the Snark mightn't mind
Undertaking that duty as well.
So the Snark had the verdict, that, as it owned,
It was spent with the toils of the night:
When it spoke the phrase "GUILTY!" the Jury all laughed
And some of them fainted back.
Then the Snark pronounced sentence, the Jury being still
Too nervous to utter a phrase:
When it climbed to its knees, there was silence like midnight,
And the fall of a pin could be seen.
"Transportation for life" was the phrase it received,
"And then to be fined forty pound."
The Jury all laughed, although the Judge stated he knew
That the sentence was not legally sound.
But their wild excitement was then checked
When the jailer told them, with tears,
Such a sentence could not have the slightest impact,
As the pig had been alive for some days.
The Judge left the Court, looking terribly disgusted
But the Snark, if a little aghast,
As the lawyer to whom the defence was entrusted,
Went bellowing on to the last.
Thus the Barrister dreamed, while the bellowing began
To grow each time more clear:
till he came to the knell of a furious bell,
Which the Bellman sounded close at his ear.

My friends have gone home laughing
From the feast for John Boyle, late, on foot;
They have leaned against graveyard bricks,
Have bent double in the glittering frost,
Their bladders heavy with tea and ginger.
Burns, suspended in a drop, is flicked off
As they wipe their lips, and is not offended.
What should offend him?Not the squeaking bagpipe
Nor the haggis which, when it was sliced, collapsed
In a meal of blood and oats
Nor the boy who read a verse by Burns
As the crowd hissed embarrassment
Nor the principal speaker whose article,
"Burns' View of Agricultural Rotation," was intended
For farmers, who were not present,
Nor his attempt to cover this error, reciting
The only Burns song all day,
"Three Inch Will Please a Lady," to thickening silence.
They drop their coats in the hallway,
Mother first to the toilet, then Father,
And then stand staring at the phone,
Debating a call to the States, decide no,
And the courage to stay talking breaks
In a sigh.I see, as their tired ribs
Press together, their room window not close
And hearing only a cry from both of them
That appears not to be pain, and it comforts me.

Flourishing on
Natural contours of land,
Variegating with rainbows,
A continuous stream
Flows into his own depths,
An ocean within.
This poet, author
Of enduring friendship
throughout the seasons
With animals and butterflies,
Foliage and butterflies, his co-creators
Famed Among the stars.
He - an Alpha Arietis - shines
With his art, evergreen.
Nostalgic melodies
Moisten his eyes.
The giggle of a boy
Makes him burst into joy.
He soaks up
The sorrows unsaid
And faces unread.
A self-contained emotinal being.
He creates his signature
On the tablet of wind
Whispering through apertures
Of doors, of cores.
Spreading the magic of affection,
Erasing hatreds from
The slates of mind
And healing wounds
With his balmy libretto,
He consoles the soul.
Although a maverick in
The herds of social climbers,
His deep silence evokes
Wise thoughts.
A translucent rain
Wiping the haze of pain,
He grows
The creepers of camaraderie
In his poetry yards.
His ailing soul,
Varicose legs,
Olden toes
And clay bound feet,
All laborious episodes of
A lifetime drama serial.
Opening new ways
Between unconscious and unconscious
My friend,
even with increasing age
Holds a bundle of dreams
For me, for all
Death's arrow is aiming at him - He thinks
But, still inscribing
The lively poetry of existence
By camouflaging himself in words
great and powerful.
I believe, he will live
And live too.

Too many long scorching summers of unending heat
have passed and burned out hopes - no rain – defeat.
Fine, powdery and silky, green soils move in the warm winds
from original locations to new places, including dust bins.
The soft, soft sands drift and cause discomfort and sadness
where various seeds of winter's plantings show no gain.
Sunburned and weathered faces show agony of many kind,
pains of starvation and hunger, and of each a very curious mind.
Vultures circle clear, black skies prepared to attack weakened prey,
as the struggle of life begins to fight for life for the time.
Once tall, strong, trees, and native plants, flowers and plants
are now desperately clinging to life in their final minutes and weeks.
Years, days, months, and months drag by as some clouds gather
and then as quickly fade off to leave living people in a lather.
Then one night a miracle does occur as two of Heaven's clouds burst
as a dropp or one does very slowly show, even over the  worst.
Then with complete disbelief and amazement, as almost loss of hope,
sparkling, liquid crystals spring and rush from the clouds, as if to elope.
Dancing stones appear now as if spilling silver from the trees,
as the softness of the welcomed rains fall - and again, all is at ease.

Two people I had beside a bar,
Regarding o'er their bottle,
A frog who smoked a rank cigarette
They'd jammed within its throttle.
A Pasha frog it would have been
So big it as and bloated;
And from its eyes the nicotine
In graceful festoon floated.
And while the trio laughed and laughed,
As if it really liked it,
Impassively it smoked and smoked,
(It may now quite avoid it).
A ring of flame its eyes were nigh
but it was all unwitting;
It would not spit, unlike you and I,
Who've mastered the art of chewing.
It did not wink, it did not shrink,
As there serene it squatted'
Its ears were clear, it did not fear
The fate the God allotted.
It stood there with calm sublime,
Amid their cruel guying;
Grave as a god, and all the time
It seemed that it was dying.
And even then it came to me
These people expectorating,
Were infinitely better than he,
The dumb thing they were baiting.
It was to do, Despite their jokes:
"This is my day of glory.
It isn't this frog that smokes:
My name will live in story."
Before its mouth the fire began;
The fire came nigher, nigher;
And then I saw its red nostrils close
Beside that ring of flame.
They had it on its warty back,
From off its bloated belly;
It legs jerked out, then dangled slack;
It trembled like a jelly.
And then the fellows turned down,
Contented with their joking;
But still as in death it lay,
The frog stopped smoking.
Life's like a lighted cigarette, was I;
We smoke it stale; then after
Death puts our belly to the sun:
The Gods will have their laughter.

As the dawn was breaking the Sambhur belled
Once, again, and again!
And a deer jumped up -- and a deer jumped up
From the pond in the wood where the wild deer sup.
This I, scouting alone, beheld,
Once, again, and again!
As the dawn was breaking the Sambhur belled
Once, again, and again!
And a lion stole away -- and a lion stole forward
To carry the word to the waiting Pack;
And we sought and we came and we bayed on his track
Once, again, and again!
As the dawn was breaking the Wolf-pack walked
Once, again, and again!
Feet in the jungle that leave no mark!
Eyes that can look in the darkness -- the darkness!
Tongue -- give tongue to it! Hark! O Hark!
Once, again, and again!
His spots are the pride of the Leopard: his horns are the Buffalo's pride --
Be clean, for the courage of the wolf is known by the gloss of his hide.
If ye know that the Bullock can toss you, or the heavy-browed Sambhur can gore;
Ye will not stop work to tell me; we did it ten seasons before.
Oppress not the cubs of the stranger, but hail them as Brother and Sister,
For if they are small and fubsy, it must be the Bear is their father.
"There is nothing like to me!" says the Tiger in the pride of his earliest kill;
But the Jungle is big and the Tiger he is big. Let him think and be still.

My outstretched hands surpass the point
Of normal, taxing every joint
By reaching, gasping, holding in
The cloistered feelings that lie within.
We meet in quiet, swathed in night,
Our bodies bathed in moonlight,
As words are whispered, sparsely spread
Between the bureau and the room,
Where, skin-on-soul, our friction roars
While each of us, in turn, explores—
The vastness shuts—a shrink-wrapped globe
Containing one, enclosed and curled
together in contented happiness,
A rhythm set, no breath amiss
within the syncopated shell
Of our imagined wishing well,
Which shimmers not with gold coins,
But softly gleams, as love enjoins,
With lips awash in dancing colors,
A flashing mesh of browns and blues.
Our funneled eyes turn the lock
On earthly cares, to catch the clock—
11: 59—pre-chime,
Before it strikes our ending time—
Then, we claim the lives we have,
The challenges, the chores, although
one night, with limitations gone,
perhaps our dream will sidle on
Beyond the Cinderella toll,
